comparisons.note: NixOS generations are numbered; users often add profile comments externally.

decisions.title: jetos generation naming UX
decisions.gist: Choose how OS generations get human names.
decisions.story: Earl is about to install a GPU driver. He wants the previous generation to be clearly named before he switches, and rollback should show something more useful than an opaque hash.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet os switch laptop --name pre-gpu-driver
$ jet os generations
48  current  post-gpu-driver
47           pre-gpu-driver

options.name: Name at switch
options.detail: One moment to name the artifact while creating it. Clear and scriptable, but unnamed generations still need a default display.
options.code: $ jet os switch laptop --name pre-gpu-driver

options.name: Separate rename verb
options.detail: Lets users name after inspection, but creates a second mutation path for generation metadata.
options.code: $ jet os rename 47 pre-gpu-driver

options.name: Auto-name plus override (recommended)
options.detail: Every generation gets a stable auto name; --name overrides during switch. generations sorts newest-first and shows chosen or auto name. No separate rename path.
options.code:
$ jet os switch laptop
generation 48 "2026-07-06-1842"
$ jet os switch laptop --name pre-gpu-driver

decisions.title: How a `plugin` target declares its exported surface
decisions.gist: D-PLUGIN1=B + D-DEP-WASM1=A settled the substrate (sandboxed WASM Component Model). This picks how a plugin package declares which entry points the host may call — the .wit surface generation. Deferred at ratification as Owner Q1.
decisions.explainer: A plugin builds a typed Component Model .wit contract; the open question is what in the plugin's source or manifest declares that contract. A new in-source #Plugin marker joins the #Test/#Bench family and lets each export tag its role explicitly, at the cost of a new keyword (I7 entry). A manifest-level declaration reuses the existing target `entry:`/`export:` fields (D-TGT3/4) with no new syntax. A pure-convention rule takes all `pub` items in the entry module as the ABI, frozen like `api: stable` (D-CAP4) — no new surface at all, reusing the capability-freeze machinery Jet already has. Recommended: the convention path (pub surface = the contract, frozen via the existing api: freeze), optionally named by a manifest `export:` field, which avoids a new keyword while giving the host a stable, inspectable .wit. Whichever wins needs a decision ID + Syntax.rs I7 entry.
decisions.story: Sam ships a plugin package. He wants to say 'these functions are the plugin API' once, have the host see a typed contract, and get a clean error if he accidentally breaks it — without learning a new keyword if he does not have to.
decisions.inWild:
// a plugin package today: target: plugin, but no way to name its exports
// this decides the spelling that generates the .wit the host binds
decisions.detail: Substrate is fixed (D-PLUGIN1=B sandboxed WASM, D-DEP-WASM1=A wasmtime + Component Model, safe by default, no #Unsafe gate). This ballot is surface-only; it generates the typed .wit the PluginHost loads. Needs a decision ID + I7 entry in Syntax.rs and a formatter round-trip + fmt STABILITY test if it adds syntax. Pairs with D-PLUGIN-VERSION1 (the version handshake on the resulting contract).

options.name: Convention: `pub` entry-module surface, frozen via `api: stable`, named by a manifest `export:` (recommended)
options.detail: All `pub` items in the plugin's entry module are the exported ABI; the manifest `export:` field names the entry module; the surface is frozen with the existing D-CAP4 `api: stable` machinery so a breaking change is a diagnostic, not a silent ABI break. No new in-source keyword. The .wit is generated from the pub signatures. Reuses machinery Jet already has (I8).

options.name: New in-source `#Plugin { … }` marker
options.detail: A `#Plugin { export fn transform(...) ... }` block (joining #Test/#Bench) lists exports explicitly and can tag each export's role. Most explicit and self-documenting in-source; adds a new keyword and I7 entry, and a second place (besides `pub`) that means 'public', which brushes against I8.

options.name: Manifest-only `entry:`/`export:` list
options.detail: The plugin target block in pkg.jet names the exported functions/module directly, reusing D-TGT3/4 target fields; source stays unannotated. No new in-source syntax; the export list lives away from the code it describes, so drift between manifest and source is possible and the freeze/versioning must be manifest-driven.
options.code: target: plugin { entry: src/api.jet, export: [transform, reset] }

comparisons.note: The export set is exactly a .wit `world` — every option here is a spelling that generates that world; A derives it from pub signatures.
comparisons.code: world plugin { export transform: func(input: frame) -> frame; }

comparisons.note: Native plugins mark each export explicitly (option B's spirit). Component Model lets Jet derive the surface instead, which is why the convention path (A) is viable.

decisions.recommendation: A

decisions.title: Plugin load-time version / ABI compatibility handshake
decisions.gist: How the host detects an incompatible plugin at load and rejects it with a clean diagnostic (I2) instead of a crash. Deferred at D-PLUGIN1 ratification alongside the export surface.
decisions.explainer: A host loading a plugin built against a different contract must fail cleanly, never crash (I2 — the loader never speaks raw to users). Three shapes: a per-build ABI hash (exact-match, simplest, but any rebuild of either side breaks compatibility even when the interface is unchanged); a declared semver compatibility range on the plugin interface (flexible, familiar, but relies on authors versioning honestly); or reuse of the D-CAP4 `api: stable` capability-signature freeze as the frozen .wit interface contract, so compatibility is structural — the host checks the plugin's interface signature against what it expects. Recommended: the D-CAP4 freeze reused as the .wit contract signature (structural compatibility), because it makes 'compatible' mean 'same typed interface' rather than 'same build', and it reuses machinery Jet already ships. Mismatch is an E-code with the expected-vs-found interface, snapshot-tested.
decisions.story: A host app ships v2 and loads a plugin built for v1's interface. Instead of a segfault deep in wasmtime, the user sees a Jet error naming the interface that changed and how to rebuild the plugin.
decisions.inWild:
$ myapp --load ./plugins/old.wasm
error[E12xx]: plugin `old` was built for interface `plugin_api@1`,
  host expects `plugin_api@2`
  fix: rebuild the plugin against this host, or install a v2 build
decisions.detail: The handshake runs against the typed Component Model .wit contract from D-PLUGIN-EXPORT1. Mismatch must be a Jet diagnostic with an E-code + tests/ui snapshot (I2/I4), never a loader crash. Substrate fixed by D-PLUGIN1=B/D-DEP-WASM1=A.

options.name: Reuse D-CAP4 `api: stable` freeze as the frozen .wit interface signature — structural compatibility (recommended)
options.detail: The plugin's exported interface carries the D-CAP4 capability-signature freeze; the host checks the plugin's interface signature against the one it was built to expect. 'Compatible' means 'same typed interface', not 'same build' — a plugin rebuilt with an unchanged interface still loads. Reuses machinery Jet already ships (I8); mismatch is a clean E-code naming the interface delta.
options.code:
target: plugin { export: plugin_api, api: stable }
// host records the frozen signature of plugin_api; load checks it structurally

options.name: Declared semver compatibility range
options.detail: The plugin declares an interface version; the host declares the range it accepts; load checks the range. Familiar and flexible across many plugin builds. Correctness rests on authors bumping the version honestly — a silent breaking change under an unchanged version still crashes.
options.code:
target: plugin { interface_version: "1.2" }
// host: accepts plugins matching ^1.0

options.name: Per-build ABI hash (exact match)
options.detail: Hash the full interface + toolchain into an ABI tag; load requires an exact match. Zero ambiguity — any incompatibility is caught. But it is maximally brittle: any rebuild of host or plugin, even with an identical interface, invalidates every existing plugin, forcing lockstep redistribution.
options.code:
// plugin embeds abi_hash = sha256(interface + toolchain)
// host loads only if the hash matches its own

comparisons.note: A component's typed .wit world IS a structural contract — the host can check interface compatibility by shape, which is exactly option A's basis.
Native dylibs have no stable ABI across compiler versions, forcing exact-build matching (option C's brittleness) — the pain the Component Model + structural check (A) avoids.
comparisons.code: // rustc version mismatch -> UB on load

decisions.recommendation: A

decisions.gist: Which app is Jet's flagship CLI slice — the command-line program we ship, benchmark, and point people at.
decisions.story: Hank, a sysadmin who lives in a terminal, hears Jet is 'great for CLI tools.' He wants proof: one real tool he can build from source, run on his own files, and time against what he already uses. Whatever we ship here is that proof — it gets compared, benchmarked, and quoted.
decisions.detail: [Owner 2026-07-03: flagship slices deferred to END of Epoch 4 — jetpack development takes priority. Web-app slice candidate when resumed: recreate Tower itself in Jet (owner suggestion, recorded on card #9).]

options.name: jetgrep — recursive regex search (recommended)
options.detail: Grow the E2 GA jetgrep into a ripgrep-class searcher: globs, ignore rules, --count/--files/--context, colored TTY output, parallel directory scan. Invites the single highest-signal CLI benchmark that exists (vs grep/ripgrep) and exercises regex, fs walk, streaming stdin, args, color, exit codes.
options.code:
$ jetgrep "fn \\w+_test" src/ --count
src/lexer.jet: 14
src/parser.jet: 22

$ time jetgrep TODO ~/big-repo   # the benchmark people will actually run
real 0m0.41s

$ jetgrep "(unclosed" src/
error: invalid pattern: unclosed group
  fix: escape the parenthesis: \\(

options.name: jetstat — typed CSV/JSON data cruncher
options.detail: Reads CSV with a header row into typed rows, filters, aggregates, emits JSON. Showcases serde derives, iterator adapters, and typed-pipeline safety — the 'awk but typed' pitch. Weaker on raw-speed comparison; stronger on type-safety story.
options.code:
$ jetstat sales.csv --filter "amount > 100" --group region --out json
{"west": {"count": 1204, "total": 981223.50}, "east": ...}

$ jetstat sales.csv --filter "amont > 100"
error: no column `amont` in sales.csv
  fix: did you mean `amount`?

options.name: jetship — static site generator
options.detail: Markdown tree in, HTML site out: templates, front-matter, live rebuild via jet dev. Credible (Hugo/Zola class), touches text/fs/templating, and its output can host Jet's own docs. Benchmarks less crisply than search; templating surface is a bigger bite.
options.code:
$ jetship build site/
  42 pages -> public/ in 180ms
$ jetship dev site/
  serving http://localhost:8080  (rebuild on save)

options.name: jetwatch — parallel task runner / file watcher
options.detail: make-meets-watchexec: declares tasks in a typed manifest, runs them in parallel on file change. Shows tasks/channels and process control in a tool devs run all day. Overlaps `jet dev` conceptually — risks a second way to mean 'watch and rerun' (I8 adjacency).
options.code:
$ jetwatch test lint
[test] 132 passed  [lint] clean   (parallel, 2.1s)
[watch] src/parser.jet changed -> rerunning test

options.name: jetdu — parallel disk-usage analyzer
options.detail: ncdu-class: walks a tree in parallel, ranks by size, TUI summary table. Simple mental model, good parallel-fs and TUI-table showcase. Narrower feature spread than A-C (no regex/serde/templates).
options.code:
$ jetdu ~/Projects
  3.2G  jet/target
  1.1G  jet/.jet/store
  212M  photos/raw
scanned 148,201 files in 0.6s

decisions.comparisons: Rust's domain proof is ripgrep — one tool did more for Rust's CLI reputation than any doc. Go's is the gh/docker generation of CLIs. Zig points at its own build system. The pattern: one polished, benchmarkable tool per language.
decisions.rec: A — the grep head-to-head is the strongest single proof a language is fast and pleasant for CLI work, and the heritage jetgrep already GA'd once, so the slice measures polish, not feasibility.
decisions.recommendation: A — the grep head-to-head is the strongest single proof a language is fast and pleasant for CLI work, and the heritage jetgrep already GA'd once, so the slice measures polish, not feasibility.

decisions.gist: Which service is Jet's flagship server slice — the HTTP program that proves the backend story.
decisions.story: Doris runs a small team's internal tools on one VM. She'll adopt Jet for services the day she can read one real service — routes, database, logging, shutdown — deploy it as a single binary, and curl it. This slice is that service.
decisions.detail: [Owner 2026-07-03: flagship slices deferred to END of Epoch 4 — jetpack development takes priority. Web-app slice candidate when resumed: recreate Tower itself in Jet (owner suggestion, recorded on card #9).]

options.name: jetpaste — pastebin with TTL expiry (recommended)
options.detail: POST a paste, get a short id; GET raw or HTML; expiry via TTL sweep; /stats and /health. CRUD + persistence + time + concurrent clients is the minimum honest service, and every behavior goldens through curl. Exercises routes, SQLite, serde JSON, structured logs, per-request deadlines, graceful shutdown.
options.code:
$ jetpaste &
$ curl -d "hello world" localhost:8080/paste
{"id": "k3xq", "expires": "2026-07-03T12:00:00Z"}
$ curl localhost:8080/p/k3xq
hello world
$ curl localhost:8080/p/gone4
{"error": "not found or expired"}   # 404

options.name: jetlink — URL shortener with click stats
options.detail: Shorten, redirect, count clicks, top-N stats endpoint. Same persistence/serde spread as A plus redirects; slightly thinner domain logic (fewer honest error paths than paste bodies + expiry).
options.code:
$ curl -d '{"url": "https://jet.dev/docs"}' localhost:8080/shorten
{"short": "http://localhost:8080/r/a7Kq"}
$ curl -i localhost:8080/r/a7Kq
HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: https://jet.dev/docs

options.name: jetfeed — feed aggregator with background fetchers
options.detail: Background tasks poll RSS/JSON feeds via the HTTP client; the server serves a merged digest. Uniquely shows client+server+taskgroup in one program. Depends on outside networks for real runs, so its golden path needs local fixture feeds.
options.code:
$ jetfeed --feeds feeds.toml &
[fetch] lobste.rs ok (12 items)  [fetch] hn ok (30 items)
$ curl localhost:8080/digest | head -3
{"items": [{"title": "Jet 1.0 released", ...}

options.name: jetboard — kanban/task JSON API (pairs with the web slice)
options.detail: Boards/cards CRUD API. If the web slice is jettasks (D-FLAGSHIP3=A), this becomes its persistence backend — the two slices then demo a full-stack Jet story. Cost: the two pillars' fates couple; a change in one ripples into the other's goldens.

options.name: jetrelay — webhook receiver and fan-out
options.detail: Receives webhooks, verifies signatures (core.crypto), fans out to configured targets with retry. Ops-flavored and shows crypto + retry + concurrency; but its interesting behavior (retries, downstream failures) is the hardest to demo convincingly in a golden test.

decisions.comparisons: Go's proof was 'a static binary serving HTTP' (Docker, Caddy). Rust points at axum examples; TS at Express/Next starters. The convincing form is always a small, complete, deployable service — not a framework tour.
decisions.rec: A — CRUD + persistence + expiry covers the widest honest surface (db, serde, time, routes, logs, shutdown) while every proof stays curl-observable and golden-testable.
decisions.recommendation: A — CRUD + persistence + expiry covers the widest honest surface (db, serde, time, routes, logs, shutdown) while every proof stays curl-observable and golden-testable.

# window opens: ship rotates with arrows, fires with space,
# asteroid splits with a crack sound, score ticks to 250
$ jet run game/main.jet -- --replay demo.moves --headless

options.name: barnstormer — side-scrolling plane through obstacles
options.detail: Flappy-class: a biplane threads pylons, one-button input, parallax scroll, high score. Aviation-perfect and instantly playable; smaller mechanical spread than A (no rotation math, one input axis, fewer entity kinds).

# plane dips on space, clips a pylon, prop-sputter sound, "score 23"
$ jet run game/main.jet -- --replay run.moves --headless
frames: 640  score: 23  checksum: 51c09be7

options.name: contrail — snake, native and windowed
options.detail: Snake where the body is a jet's contrail. Great name, dead-simple rules, fixed-array grid state shows off [T#N]. The most modest visual/audio workout of the menu — grid steps, no rotation, minimal sound.

decisions.title: Browser event and storage API for jettasks
decisions.gist: How Jet web apps bind DOM events and persist browser state.
decisions.story: Betty is replacing a React TodoMVC with Jet. She wants the add box, checkbox toggles, filters, and reload-persistent tasks to live in Jet code, not handwritten JavaScript glue. This choice decides whether the browser slice proves Jet as an app framework or only as a compute/render island.
decisions.detail: Current friction: `jettasks` can render through exported #Js functions, but Jet code cannot bind DOM events or browser storage itself. Host-page JS can call exports, yet that leaves app ownership outside Jet. If A is ratified, implementation touches `crates/jet-sema/src/Sema/CheckerCoreLib.rs`, `crates/jet-codegen/src/Codegen/Web.rs`, `crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/DomRuntime.js`, `examples/apps/jettasks/*`, `tests/web_build.rs`, and `tests/slices.rs`; proof is fake-DOM event/storage harness plus static web build and TodoMVC reducer/output goldens.

options.name: Typed core.web events plus storage (recommended)
options.detail: Add a first-party browser Core surface: typed selectors, event objects, input values, and localStorage/sessionStorage wrappers. Beginner path stays direct, expert path can still drop to #Js exports when needed. One canonical browser-side mechanism.
options.code:
use core.web as web
web.on("#toggle-3", "click", (_) => toggle(3))
web.storage.local.set("tasks", json)
json :: web.storage.local.get("tasks") ?? "[]"

options.name: Host-page JavaScript drives exported #Js functions
options.detail: Keep Jet web output as exported functions called by handwritten JS in index.html. Avoids new Core API, but the flagship app would not prove Jet owns browser interaction or persistence.
options.code:
<script type="module">
  import { addTask, toggle } from "./app.js";
  input.addEventListener("keydown", e => addTask(input.value));
</script>

options.name: Component callbacks inside core.ui nodes
options.detail: Events are attached as properties on UI nodes. Strong long-term component ergonomics, but requires the view tree to become the source of event wiring and storage still needs a separate answer.
options.code: ui.input(value: title, on_key: (ev) => { if ev.key == "Enter" { add(title) } })

options.name: Do not persist browser state yet
options.detail: Events land, storage stays out. This cannot satisfy TodoMVC persistence and would weaken the web flagship proof.
options.code:
web.on("#new-task", "keydown", add_from_input)
// reload loses tasks

comparisons.note: Events are declared in component code and state persistence usually uses localStorage through typed wrappers or hooks.
Events are typed messages; ports are used for browser APIs like storage.
Event handlers live in markup and storage is ordinary browser API.

decisions.comment: Components also should have events, like react and typescript

decisions.title: MMIO write API for metal
decisions.gist: How low-level Jet writes to memory-mapped hardware registers.
decisions.story: Earl is bringing up a tiny board. Reading a status register is not enough; he must write a byte to UART data and stream the Life transcript. Jet needs this power, but only inside an audited unsafe region so beginners never see the footgun.
decisions.detail: Current friction: `core.mem` has `volatile_read` and target-profile MMIO validation, but no write operation and no pointer-deref assignment lvalue. Without a write, `metal` cannot emit UART serial bytes. If A is ratified, implementation touches `crates/jet-foundation/src/Syntax.rs`, `crates/jet-sema/src/Sema/CheckerCoreLib.rs`, `crates/jet-codegen/src/Codegen/TIR/{subset,lower,emit}.rs`, diagnostics/tests for unsafe gating, `examples/apps/metal/*`, and `tests/slices.rs`; proof is gated `mem.volatile_write` plus freestanding/QEMU-oriented serial transcript path.

options.name: mem.volatile_write(ptr, value) (recommended)
options.detail: Pair the existing volatile_read with an audited write helper. It is gated by use core.mem plus #Unsafe, validates against target-profile MMIO ranges, and reads naturally in UART code.

options.name: Pointer assignment p.* = value
options.detail: Looks like ordinary assignment through a pointer. Compact, but expands lvalue grammar and makes volatile semantics less visible at the call site.

options.name: mem.mmio(region).write(offset, value)
options.detail: More structured and profile-aware. Strong for experts, more ceremony for first bring-up, and a second API alongside raw Ptr unless it replaces Ptr use entirely for MMIO.

options.name: Keep read-only volatile for now
options.detail: Cannot ship the metal UART proof because the app cannot write serial bytes.
options.code:
mem.volatile_read(status)
// no write path

comparisons.note: Volatile writes are explicit unsafe operations.
Volatile pointer writes are explicit in the pointer type/access.

decisions.title: core.raylib bridge completion boundary
decisions.gist: How the game slice proves real raylib without making CI depend on a display.
decisions.story: Earl runs the game at a club and wants a window, sprites, sound, input, and replay. CI still needs to verify the same rules without opening a display server. This choice sets the first real raylib bridge boundary.
decisions.detail: Current friction: `core.raylib` is a typed no-op skeleton: `window_open` returns a struct, `should_close` returns true, and no texture/audio/input bridge exists. If A is ratified, implementation touches `crates/jet-sema/src/Sema/CheckerCoreLib.rs`, `crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/CoreLib.rs`, `crates/jet-codegen/src/Codegen/TIR/{subset,lower,emit}.rs`, `Source/CmdCompile.rs`/link handling as needed, `examples/apps/jetfighter/*`, `tests/corelib.rs`, and `tests/slices.rs`; proof is real display bridge when available plus headless replay transcript in CI.

options.name: Real bridge plus headless replay verifier (recommended)
options.detail: Window/audio/input are real when display and raylib are present; CI runs the same game logic through a headless replay backend with frame transcript and budget checks. Strong proof without flaky display dependency.
options.code:
$ jet run examples/apps/jetfighter/main.jet
# opens window when raylib/display available
$ jet run examples/apps/jetfighter/main.jet -- --headless --replay fixtures/demo.moves

options.name: Headless core.game only

decisions.title: Jai-style message loop and mutation: should Jet ever let metaprograms rewrite user code?
decisions.gist: Decide whether full Jai-style mutation/macros stay rejected or become a future gated feature.
decisions.story: Frank admires Jai’s message loop because it can rewrite declarations and inject custom behavior across a program. His enterprise reviewer sees a different problem: reading a file no longer tells you what compiles. Jet needs a clear answer before this card drifts forever.
decisions.detail: 2026-07-06 two-facet pass: beginner local reasoning and expert power both prefer a non-mutating default. Recommendation strengthened: reject compiler-state mutation, but explicitly include additive overlays/generators, front-end APIs, DSL blocks, and policy passes as the powerful path.

options.name: Reject mutation; complete the non-mutating power stack (recommended)
options.detail: No AST mutation/message loop/user macros in compilation. Practical Jai use cases are covered by additive generated modules, registered targets/actions, read-only program/build graph enforcement, stdlib DSL whitelist, public front-end APIs, and optional additive overlay modules that materialize as source.

options.name: Audited additive overlays as a named subfeature
options.detail: Metaprograms may propose generated overlay modules only; user source is never mutated. This is compatible with A but could be ratified separately if the owner wants a first-class overlay term.
options.code:
overlay :: b.add_overlay("service_policies", generated: make_policy_layer(b.program))
return b.plan(include: [overlay])

options.name: Full message loop behind policy
options.detail: Build code can inspect and rewrite declarations before compile under explicit policy. Maximum Jai similarity, but reading a file no longer tells beginners or reviewers what compiles.

options.name: Post-self-host research only
options.detail: Do not decide the mechanism now; keep the card frozen until self-hosting proves which compiler-internal extension points are stable.
options.code: // No user-facing mutation design before e8/self-host evidence.

comparisons.note: Message-loop metaprogramming can inspect and alter program declarations.
Procedural macros transform token streams, with audit/debuggability costs.
Roslyn analyzers are read-only diagnostics, close to Jet rung B.

decisions.title: How is a whole-graph effect PROHIBITION spelled on a function signature?
decisions.gist: D-PROP1=A ratified that a function can forbid one effect across its entire reachable call graph, on the same propagation engine as the positive `#(Net)` effect set. This decides only how that prohibition reads. It must not collide with the positive effect-set syntax already in `#(...)`.
decisions.explainer:
The positive surface is the effect set `#(Net, Io)` (D-EFF1/D-QUAL1). A prohibition is the inverse walk: it names one effect the function and every reachable callee may NOT use. Purely surface; no new engine machinery (I3 holds, erased in codegen). Blast radius: parser marker/effect-tag grammar + Syntax.rs.

Recommendation: A — `!` is the universal 'not' sigil, keeps both polarities in one readable set, reuses `#(...)` with no new marker.
decisions.story: Nora writes audit tooling. `audit_log` may write local files, but must never reach the network through any helper. She wants that promise visible on the function, and she wants the compiler to name the callee path if someone later adds `http.post` deep inside.

options.name: Negation inside the effect set: `#(!Net)` (recommended)
options.detail: `!` before an effect name means this function and every reachable callee must not use that effect. Positive and negative facts stay in one `#(...)` list.

options.name: Dedicated marker: `#Forbid(Net)`
options.detail: Very explicit, but splits effect facts across two markers. Readers must merge `#(Io)` and `#Forbid(Net)` mentally.
options.code:
#Forbid(Net)
#(Io) fn audit_log(event: Event) -> () ? Error { ... }

options.name: Minus inside the set: `#(-Net)`
options.detail: Compact, but `-` reads like set subtraction and is less consistent with Jet’s existing `!` boolean-not spelling.
options.code: #(Io, -Net) fn audit_log(event: Event) -> () ? Error { ... }

comparisons.note: Effects are listed on function types; absence of an effect is meaningful. Jet already has positive effect sets, so prohibition should live near that set.
comparisons.code: fun f() : <console> ()  // cannot do network if net absent

comparisons.note: Deny rules are often explicit policy entries. Good for manifests, too heavy for a local function guarantee.

decisions.title: What surface declares a request/response protocol, and how is a generated handle used?
decisions.gist: D-PROTO1=A ratified that the compiler generates ordered Client/Server handle types over linear (`#SingleUse`) + typestate (`state`/`#Transition`). This decides the declaration spelling. The exchange should read top-to-bottom as a sequence — that readability is the point.
decisions.explainer:
D-LIN1 and D-STATE1 are ratified; this is the declaration surface + the handle threaded. Blast radius: a new top-level construct in the parser + Syntax.rs and codegen lowering to linear+typestate. I8: one canonical mechanism for ordered protocols.

Recommendation: A — `protocol` is the plain word a beginner reads right, keeps the exchange in one block, generates both sides as D-PROTO1=A requires.
decisions.story: Sam implements a payment terminal handshake. The client must send `Hello`, wait for `Ack`, then send `Charge`, then wait for `Receipt`. If a handler tries to charge before ack, Sam wants a type error, not a runtime protocol bug.

options.name: `protocol Name { ... }` ordered messages (recommended)
options.detail: One declaration generates typed client/server handles. The block reads like the wire conversation. Out-of-order sends become typestate/linear-use errors.

options.name: `session Name { ... }` ordered messages
options.detail: Same semantics with the research term. Precise for experts, but `session` also means login/session state to web developers.

options.name: No protocol block; write `state` + `#Transition` by hand
options.detail: Reuses existing machinery, but users must manually keep both endpoint types dual. That loses the main product win: one readable source of truth.

comparisons.note: Protocols are usually written as an ordered conversation and compile to endpoint types. Jet wants that power but with a plain block.
comparisons.code: Client -> Server: Hello; Server -> Client: Ack;

comparisons.note: Great for request/response shapes, weak at enforcing multi-step order in the type system.

decisions.title: What is the marker name for the replay-soundness function marker?
decisions.gist: D-REPLAY1=A ratified a function marker that rejects any reachable un-mockable `#(Time/Rand/Net/Io)` via inverse propagation. This is a low-stakes rubber-stamp of the NAME, matching the `#Pure`/`#Test` convention.
decisions.explainer:
Pure naming; no semantics at stake. PascalCase `#`-marker (D-CASING1) on a function. Blast radius: Syntax.rs keyword, parser, one ui snapshot, examples.

Recommendation: A — `#Replayable` matches the property-reading marker family and states what the guarantee buys without over-claiming.

options.name: `#Replayable`
options.detail:
Names the guarantee.

Matches the `-able` 'property of this fn' convention; says exactly what it buys.
options.code: #Replayable fn settle(order: Order, clock: Clock) -> Receipt { ... }

options.name: `#Deterministic`
options.detail:
Names the underlying property.

Accurate but over-claims (effect-free ≠ fully deterministic) and is longer/more abstract.
options.code: #Deterministic fn settle(...) -> Receipt { ... }

options.name: `#Replay`
options.detail:
Bare noun.

Terse, but reads as a command/mode, not a property the fn HAS.
options.code: #Replay fn settle(...) -> Receipt { ... }

comparisons.note: Temporal-style workflow engines use replayability as the contract for deterministic reruns.

decisions.bestCurrent: Workflow engines: Temporal-style workflow engines use replayability as the contract for deterministic reruns.
decisions.recommendation: Use `#Replayable`. It names the user goal directly: this function is safe to record and replay.

decisions.title: How should Jet track taint, PII, secrets, and audited release without becoming a full IFC research language?
decisions.gist: Extend `#Tainted` to a closed label set (`.Input`, `.PII`, `.Secret`, `.Credential`) with one taint engine and an audited declassify gate. This ballot ratifies the label taxonomy only — four follow-on ballots are required before implementation: `declassify` syntax (I7 registration), `#Sanitizer(.Kind)` specificity, sink policy declaration mechanism, and interprocedural scope. Bare `#Tainted` (D-TAINT1) must be designated sugar for `#Tainted(.Input)` with a teaching-error migration to avoid the I8 coexistence hole.
decisions.explainer: Owner question answered: the cohesive best-in-class shape is one taint mechanism, not separate #Pii/#Secret systems and not a full Jif lattice by default. Values carry a small set of labels (`#Tainted(.Input)`, `#Tainted(.PII)`, `#Tainted(.Secret)`) that flow through existing taint propagation and are checked only at sinks. Experts get control through sink policies, org labels, audit reports, and required declassify reasons. Adversarial pass: label sets can explode and become compliance theater. Patch: built-in labels stay closed in the language; org labels live in policy; diagnostics fire at sinks, not at every assignment; full principal lattices are deferred unless Epoch 6 explicitly funds them.
decisions.story: A signup form stores an email. The web package marks it `#Tainted(.PII)`. Passing it to `log.info` fails until the developer redacts or declassifies with a reason. Security can grep every declassification and can add an org label like `.HIPAA` without changing the language.
decisions.detail:
Owner Q: How can we give full control while keeping the system as small as it can be without cutting functionality? Can we turn #Tainted into something like `#Tainted(.PII)`?
Agent answer: Updated D-IFC1 around `#Tainted(.Kind)`. Best system: one taint mechanism, label set on values, built-in labels first (.Input, .PII, .Secret, .Credential), audited `declassify("reason", .Kind)`, sink policies, later org labels through policy. Devil's advocate: labels can explode and become compliance theater. Patch: closed built-ins in language, org labels only in policy, no principal lattice in Epoch 3, diagnostics at sinks only, declassification reports generated from semantic graph.

Adversarial pass (2026-06-28): Five concrete implementation blockers: (1) `declassify` syntactic form is undefined — must be I7-registered as a keyword or redesigned as a three-argument core library fn. (2) .Kind label type is unresolved — value-position dot requires a known expected type (D-ENUMDOT2=A); where is it declared and how does a caller use it? (3) Bare #Tainted (D-TAINT1, ratified + implemented) and `#Tainted(.Kind)` (Option B) coexist as two spellings for overlapping semantics — I8 violation with a safety hole (sink policy filtering .Input does not catch bare #Tainted). (4) `#Sanitizer fn` (D-TAINT-SAN, ratified) strips all labels, breaking label-aware declassification — a SQL sanitizer must not strip .PII. (5) Sink policy declaration mechanism is entirely absent from the ballot.

options.name: `#Tainted(.Kind)` closed label taxonomy + audited declassify gate (taxonomy decision only) (recommended)
options.detail: Ratify the label taxonomy: one taint engine, four built-in labels (`.Input`, `.PII`, `.Secret`, `.Credential`), an audited declassify gate (static string reason required), per-label sink policies (Db/Exec/Net for `.Input`; Log/Fs/Net for `.PII`/`.Secret`). This decision ratifies ONLY the label taxonomy and opt-in scope. Four follow-on ballots are required before implementation: (1) `declassify` syntactic form — keyword or three-arg core library fn, must be I7-registered; (2) `#Sanitizer` specificity — whether `#Sanitizer fn` strips all labels or becomes `#Sanitizer(.Kind)` to preserve other labels; (3) sink policy declaration mechanism — how core library fns declare their denied-label set; (4) interprocedural scope — whether labels propagate through unannotated fn parameters. Bare `#Tainted` (D-TAINT1, ratified + implemented) becomes sugar for `#Tainted(.Input)` with a teaching-error migration; I8 gap is closed by this designation.

options.name: Label-propagating distinct-type wrappers via D-DIST1 machinery
options.detail: Define `PII<T>`, `Secret<T>`, `Input<T>` as generic distinct wrapper types (D-DIST1/D-DIST3). The label IS the type; propagation is enforced by the existing type-checker without a new sema pass. Passing `PII<String>` where `String` is expected raises E0127 (distinct-type mismatch) with no new diagnostics. Declassification is an audited method: `email.declassify("support trace") -> String`. Costs: no multi-label without a union type; generic fns over `T` must propagate label type through signatures.

options.name: Defer rich information-flow to Epoch 6
options.detail: Keep today's one-bit #Tainted/sanitizer model (D-TAINT1, ratified and implemented). In Epoch 6, revisit the full label/policy/declassify system with real compliance workloads. Ship no new label taxonomy until then.

comparisons.note: Full principal lattice. Very expressive, but annotation-heavy and not mainstream.
Strong declassify discipline validates Jet’s audited release gate, but dynamic current-label semantics are too invasive for normal Jet.
Practical industry model: sources, sinks, sanitizers, labels. Jet can make this compile-time and type-aware instead of external analysis.

decisions.bestCurrent: Jif: Jif supports label-based information-flow control with principals and declassification, but its surface is heavy.
decisions.recommendation: Ratify `#Tainted(.Kind)` label taxonomy now; four follow-on ballots before implementation (Option A). This decision ratifies the label set and taint-engine scope only — not the syntax of declassify, #Sanitizer specificity, sink policy, or interprocedural propagation.

decisions.title: Should Jet express resource/time budgets as types and statically warn when a called function exceeds them — and if so, in what form?
decisions.gist: A render-frame loop wants a 16ms CPU budget that the compiler can enforce. But sound static timing/cost inference (WCET) is research-grade and undecidable in general — you cannot prove a wall-clock bound from source. The honest split: decline it as a type, ship a foundational #Budget that is really an effect/capability ceiling (forbid known-expensive effects in a hot region), or commit to full RAML-style cost inference as a post-Epoch research track.
decisions.explainer: Real timing budgets are a runtime property of a specific machine, inputs, and cache state; proving a 16ms bound at compile time is the worst-case-execution-time (WCET) problem, which is undecidable in general and, where tractable, requires whole-program loop-bound annotations and a hardware cost model (Ada/SPARK + aiT, RAML's amortized analysis). None of that is an Epoch-3 feature, and none of it composes with I8 without inventing a parallel mechanism. The pragmatic insight: most frame-budget blowups in practice come from doing forbidden *kinds* of work in a hot path — heap allocation, IO, syscalls, unbounded loops. Jet already has the exact machinery to forbid effect categories in a region (#(…) bounds, #Caps(…) ceilings, E0740/E0741). A #Budget region is therefore not a timing proof at all — it is an effect ceiling with a cost-oriented name that bans Alloc/Io/Net and flags unbounded loops, giving real, sound guarantees (no allocation in the render path) without claiming a millisecond it cannot honor. Full cost inference (option C) stays an honest research item; the runtime deadline path (option A's pointer to D-DEADLINE1) is the sanctioned way to get actual wall-clock enforcement today.
decisions.story: I'm writing render_frame for a 60fps game and I keep blowing my 16ms budget because some helper deep in the call graph quietly allocates and hits the filesystem to lazy-load a texture. I want the compiler to tell me — at the call site, before I ship — that this hot path is doing something it must never do, instead of finding it in a profiler at 11fps.

options.name: Decline budgets-as-types — sanction the runtime path (D-DEADLINE1)
options.detail: Do not add any budget type or marker. A wall-clock budget is a runtime fact, so enforce it at runtime: the existing latency/deadline-propagation card (D-DEADLINE1) carries a deadline on #Context and cancels work past it, and ordinary profiling catches regressions. The compiler makes no timing claim it cannot prove. Honest about undecidability; smallest surface; risks leaving the 'no alloc in the hot path' guarantee that game/audio devs actually want unserved.

options.name: Foundational #Budget marker — a cost-oriented effect ceiling (Epoch 3)
options.detail: Ship #Budget(name) as a region/function marker that is a thin policy layer over the existing effect ceiling (#Caps / #(…)). A budget profile names forbidden effects (default: Alloc, Io, Net, Fs) and requires every loop in the region to have a statically known bound. Reuses E0741's machinery; new diagnostics E0746 (forbidden effect in budget) and E0747 (unbounded loop in budget). It is NOT a timing proof — it proves the region does no expensive *kind* of work and has no unbounded iteration, which is the sound, decidable core devs can rely on. Composes with effect ceilings under I8 (one mechanism: effect bounds), not a parallel system. Names the limit honestly: a budget is a no-alloc/no-IO/bounded-loop contract, not 16ms.

options.name: Full static cost-bound inference (RAML-style, post-Epoch research)
options.detail: Commit to real comptime cost inference: a #Budget(16ms) (or abstract cost units) that the compiler discharges by inferring an amortized worst-case cost bound for each function and proving the called set fits. This is automatic amortized resource analysis (RAML) plus a hardware/instruction cost model — research-grade, requires loop-bound annotations or a termination/ranking analysis, an LP solver in comptime, and is undecidable in general (only sound on an annotated, restricted fragment). Highest value if it lands, but it cannot ship in Epoch 3, would pull a solver into the I6-clean compiler, and risks promising millisecond bounds the model can't honor across machines. Keep as a flagged research track that option B's effect ceiling forward-composes into.

comparisons.note: Real-time systems express priorities/deadlines; full static cost inference is rare and niche.

The hard-real-time world separates the two halves Jet must not conflate: the *language* (Ravenscar profile) statically forbids dynamic constructs in critical tasks — no unbounded allocation, no unbounded loops, restricted tasking — which is exactly option B's effect/capability ceiling. The actual *16ms timing proof* is done by a separate external WCET tool (aiT) over the binary with a CPU model, never by the type system. This is the prior-art case for declining timing-as-a-type while shipping the restriction profile.
comparisons.code:
-- Ravenscar restricts the language for the hot path (≈ option B):
pragma Profile (Ravenscar);   -- no dynamic alloc, bounded tasking
-- The 16ms bound is proven OUTSIDE the type system, by aiT WCET analysis on the binary.

comparisons.note: Two contrasting points. EVM proves cost only by *running* with a runtime gas counter that aborts when exhausted — dynamic, not static — mirroring option A's runtime-deadline path; even there the static bound is undecidable so it's metered live. Koka shows the decidable, sound thing you CAN infer: it infers *effect rows* (which effects a function has), not costs — confirming that effect membership is tractable and composable while cost magnitude is not. Jet's #Budget(B) leans on the Koka-style effect inference it already has, and leaves the EVM-style magnitude question to runtime.

decisions.bestCurrent: RTSJ / Ada: Real-time systems express priorities/deadlines; full static cost inference is rare and niche.
decisions.recommendation: Use a foundational `#Budget` marker, not full cost inference. Jet can connect budgets to effects/deadlines now and leave exact proofs to research.

decisions.title: Should Jet pursue machine-checked formal verification, and if so as a bounded foundational checker, a full proof-carrying-code engine, or not at all?
decisions.gist: A request to attach machine-checked proofs to functions and refuse to ship if the proof fails. The decision currently conflates three distinct capabilities under 'Option B': (1) exhaustive enumeration of finite domains — genuinely machine-proven, I6-safe, and unique; (2) randomized sampling of infinite domains — already provided by D-TEST1 property tests, a duplicate mechanism; and (3) build-time contract enforcement — blocked by the current comptime scope. The honest question is narrower: should Jet add exhaustive-enumeration-only build-gate checks for truly finite types (the one thing B can do that D-TEST1 cannot), or should the Epoch 3 investment go to lightweight require/ensure contracts that every expert verification tool already reads as input and that beginners can understand without a quantifier DSL?
decisions.explainer: Owner question answered: B cannot do what full proof tools do. B gives bounded/exhaustive finite-domain checks and randomized contracts through Jet-owned test/comptime machinery. C can prove universal properties: constant-time behavior, overflow absence for all inputs, functional correctness, and proof-carrying APIs. Adversarial pass: B risks being marketed as proof when it is only evidence. Patch: diagnostics and docs must call it bounded verification; C remains a separate expert prover tier, likely Epoch 6, with external solver errors translated into Jet diagnostics.
decisions.story: I'm writing a constant-time comparison for a password check. I write the function, mark it #Verify(constant_time), and `jet build` either proves the timing is input-independent and ships, or refuses with a diagnostic pointing at the branch that leaks. I never install a solver, never learn Dafny, and a teammate who's never heard of formal methods can read the marker and know exactly what's guaranteed. The day my logic stops being checkable by the bounded checker, Jet tells me plainly instead of silently downgrading to 'probably fine'.
decisions.detail:
Owner Q: What are the tradeoffs of going with B over C? What could experts do with C that they can't do with B?
Agent answer: B can exhaustively check finite domains and sample large domains through Jet's own comptime/test engine. C can prove universal properties over infinite/huge domains: real constant-time claims, no overflow for all inputs, functional correctness against pre/postconditions, and proof-carrying APIs. What B preserves: zero solver in the compiler, no default build tax, no solver error leakage, and a direct extension of #Test.

Adversarial pass (2026-06-28): (1) E0710 collision: the proposal reuses E0710, already assigned to effects-bound violations in syntax-decisions.md — assign a new code before ratifying. (2) `? VerifyError` in function signatures is wrong: #Verify is a build gate, not a runtime type; the return type must not change. (3) D-TEST1 overlap: the "large domain → sample" case duplicates what #Test fn already does; honest scope of #Verify is exhaustive-only. (4) Comptime engine scope gap: ratified comptime scope is "bindings only, no fn annotations" — evaluating arbitrary user functions exhaustively at build time requires an unapproved extension. (5) No enumeration cap defined: behavior at U16×U16 (4B cases) is unspecified. (6) Missing Option E (require/ensure contracts): simpler Epoch 3 step, already the foundation of every production verification language, cleaner I8 story.

options.name: `require`/`ensure` contracts + `#Verify` exhaustive finite-domain checker (recommended)
options.detail: Ship `require` (precondition) and `ensure` (postcondition) as first-class function contract annotations: checked eagerly in debug/test builds, treated as property-test generators by `jet test` (same engine as D-TEST1, no I8 cost — contracts are typed sugar over the existing test engine). No quantifier DSL, no enumeration engine beyond what D-TEST1 already provides. For finite-domain exhaustive proofs: add `#Verify(forall x: U8, y: U8 => predicate)` that exhaustively enumerates finite Cartesian products at compile time up to a build-time cap (default 1M; configurable). Domains exceeding the cap are a type error at the `#Verify` site — never silent fallback to sampling (that's D-TEST1's job). Assign a fresh diagnostic code from E08xx or E09xx (not E0710, which is already taken by effects-bound violations). Drop `? VerifyError` from function signatures — a failed `#Verify` is a build error, not a runtime type.

options.name: Decline — testing + property testing + #Unsafe audit is the floor
options.detail: No contracts, no #Verify. Constant-time and invariant claims are handled by #Unsafe("reason") audited regions plus property-style #Test blocks. Honest ceiling: Jet can never *prove* a property without an external solver; crypto/safety-critical users reach for SPARK/Dafny/F* and FFI the result in.

options.name: Defer to Epoch 6
options.detail: No contracts or verification now. Revisit in Epoch 6 when the solver/proof infrastructure and real production verification workloads exist. Choosing defer blocks the `require`/`ensure` foundation that every production verification language ships first — do not defer without an explicit plan for what fills the expert-guarantee story in the interim.
options.code:
// Only #Test and #Unsafe audit now.
// Epoch 6 revisit: require/ensure contracts + #Verify + optional SMT tier

comparisons.note: Dafny gives machine-checked pre/postconditions and proofs, but it is a verification language.

Verification-aware language: you write requires/ensures specs and Dafny discharges them via Z3 at compile time; verification is mandatory and the solver is core, not opt-in. Jet can't adopt this default-on model — it would put an SMT solver in every build (I6/beginner-path violation). Closest to Option C but without the expert gate.
comparisons.code:
method CtEq(a: array<byte>, b: array<byte>) returns (r: bool)
  requires a.Length == b.Length
  ensures r == (forall i :: 0 <= i < a.Length ==> a[i] == b[i])
{ ... }  // Z3 proves the ensures or the build fails

comparisons.note: Subset of Ada with contracts proved by an external prover (GNATprove/Why3); proof is opt-in per unit and layered (stone->gold->platinum). This is the closest precedent for Jet's Option C: a safe language where formal proof is an explicit, gated tier over normal compilation rather than the default — exactly the 'never in the default path' shape.

Bolt-on verifiers, none in rustc itself: Kani is a bounded model checker (finite unrolling — directly the Option B flavor), Prusti/Creusot are deductive SMT-backed (Option C flavor). All are separate opt-in tools you install and invoke, never part of `cargo build`. Validates that the foundational/bounded subset and the heavy prover can be cleanly separated, and that the prover lives outside the core toolchain.

Full dependently-typed proof assistants: maximal power (functional-correctness proofs, used for HACL* verified crypto), maximal cost — proofs are part of the source and the checker IS the compiler. This is beyond even Option C; cited to mark the far end of the gradient and why Jet would never embed a proof assistant in Source/ (it would BE an external proof kernel, the sharpest I6 collision).
comparisons.code:
let ct_eq (a b: bytes) : Pure bool
  (requires length a == length b)
  (ensures fun r -> r <==> equal a b) = ...
(* the F* typechecker discharges this; the proof ships with the code *)

decisions.bestCurrent: Dafny: Dafny gives machine-checked pre/postconditions and proofs, but it is a verification language.
decisions.recommendation: `require`/`ensure` contracts as the Epoch 3 foundation + `#Verify(finite-domain)` exhaustive checker for truly provable finite-type cases (Option A). `require`/`ensure` forward-composes into Option C's eventual proof language without redesign.

decisions.title: Should Jet support reversible/constraint-solved values — write `width = parent.width - padding*2` and let the compiler solve for `padding` given a target `width` — and if so, as a general language feature or only as a scoped UI-layout library?
decisions.gist: A forward expression is normally a one-way function: you give inputs, you get an output. Reversible computation flips that — you state a relationship once and the system solves for whichever side is unknown, like spreadsheet goal-seek or a layout engine resolving sizes from constraints. The question is whether Jet adopts this as a general semantic capability, ships a narrow linear-constraint solver scoped to UI layout, or declines it and keeps plain functions + the reactive stack as the only paths.
decisions.explainer: General reversibility is a deep semantic change: an `=` would stop meaning 'bind this computed value' and start meaning 'assert this relationship, solve for the hole', which collides head-on with I8 (one canonical meaning) and forces a constraint solver into the language core. Any real solver (Z3-class SMT, or even a robust Cassowary linear solver) is a substantial dependency — in the compiler that violates I6, and even as stdlib it is heavy. The honest split: the *foundational, shippable* slice is a bounded LINEAR (Cassowary-style) solver delivered as a library scoped to UI layout, where the problem is well-posed, the math is tractable, and it slots into the reactive-UI stack already queued for Epoch 3 (D-REACTUI1) — this is a layout engine, not a language primitive, and `=` keeps its meaning everywhere. The *general* version (solve arbitrary forward constraints over arbitrary types) is open-ended research with no bounded solver and unclear semantics; it belongs post-Epoch if ever. Declining is defensible: plain functions already invert by hand, and reactive `derived` already propagates layout forward.
decisions.story: I'm building a settings panel. I write `panel = VStack.{ padding: 16 }` and a row inside it, and I want the row to fill the panel minus the padding. Today I compute that by hand: `row.width@ = panel.width.get() - 32`, and if the panel resizes I re-derive it. What I *want* is to state the relationship once — `row.width == panel.width - panel.padding*2` — pin the row's minimum, and let the layout pass solve the rest, the way Auto Layout does, so I never hand-thread which value drives which.

options.name: Decline — plain functions + reactive derived are the sanctioned paths
options.detail: Do not add reversibility or a solver as a language feature. Inverting a relationship stays an explicit, user-written function; layout that must react to inputs uses `core.reactive` (`derived`) to propagate forward. Keeps I6 (no solver dependency anywhere in the compiler), keeps I8 (`=` means one thing — bind a computed value), and keeps the surface small. Cost: layout authors hand-thread direction and hand-write any inverse; there is no goal-seek.

options.name: Foundational subset — bounded LINEAR constraint solver, library-scoped to UI layout (Epoch 3)
options.detail: Ship `core.layout`: a Cassowary-style incremental solver for LINEAR equalities/inequalities over numeric layout values, with weak/medium/strong/required priorities and `@suggest` edits — exactly the Auto Layout model. It is a library, not a language primitive: `=` keeps its meaning; the solver only runs inside an explicit `layout.solve.{ … }` region over declared layout values, and it ties into the reactive-UI stack (D-REACTUI1). Bounded math means a tractable, std-only implementation is realistic (no SMT). Scope is deliberately narrow — linear, numeric, layout — so it does not become a general reversibility back door (I8 honored: the one canonical job is 'resolve a layout').

options.name: Full general reversible computation / constraint solving (post-Epoch research)
options.detail: A first-class `@reversible` annotation turns a forward expression into a relation the compiler can solve in either direction over arbitrary types — goal-seek for the whole language. Requires a general solver (SMT/Z3-class), which is a hard I6 violation in the compiler and a heavy stdlib dependency, plus a deep semantic shift: `=` inside a reversible region asserts a relationship with a hole rather than binding a value (I8 tension — two meanings for one symbol). No bounded solver, undecidable in general, error/diagnostic story unsolved (rustc must never see it — I2). Powerful, but open-ended research with no clear Epoch-3 landing.

comparisons.note: The proven model for Option B: an incremental LINEAR solver with required + weak/medium/strong priorities and editable 'suggested' values. Scoped to layout, fast, well-understood, std-implementable. This is the sweet spot Jet's layout library would target.

The Option C end of the space. Janus programs run backward by construction (every statement reversible); MiniZinc/Z3 solve arbitrary constraints via a heavy external solver. Both show the cost: a solver dependency and a programming model where statements are relations, not assignments — exactly the I6 + I8 + semantic-depth problems C inherits.

decisions.gist: Expose Cassowary-class layout as typed constraint values. Two open language gates must be resolved first: whether comparison operators may return non-Bool on closed built-in types, and whether core.layout.Var enters the compiler's closed type family. If both gates ratify, the ideal design is a static `layout { }` block (beginner face) desugaring to first-class typed constraint handles (expert layer), with axis-typed variables (`HVar`/`VVar`/`LengthVar`) that make cross-axis constraints compile errors. This is strictly better than Apple Auto Layout: readable authoring, inspectable/named/removable constraints, axis safety at compile time, and a structured conflict diagnostic rather than a runtime dump. If the language gates are declined, a method-only builder (Option A) is the safe fallback consistent with all ratified decisions.
decisions.story: Elena is building a settings panel. She wants the label column to be at least 80px wide, the input column to fill the rest, and a 16px gap between them. She writes these as constraints rather than calculated values so the layout adjusts automatically when the panel resizes.

comparisons.note: Auto Layout expresses UI constraints as linear equations and inequalities over anchors, the strongest production layout solver model.

options.name: `layout { }` block + typed-axis variables — gated on two language gates (recommended)
options.detail: A `layout { }` block desugars to first-class typed `Constraint` handles (each line is a named, removable, prioritizable handle). Layout variables are axis-typed: `HVar` (horizontal), `VVar` (vertical), `LengthVar` (unsigned scalar). Cross-axis constraints (`label.left >= label.height`) are compile errors — statically safe, zero-runtime-overhead axis checking; no existing constraint system offers this. Static layouts (all values comptime-known) can be solver-evaluated at compile time, emitting zero runtime solver. Expert escape: capture handles, adjust priorities, call `solver.suggest()`. GATE 1 (required): comparison operators may return non-Bool on specific closed built-in types — required for `>=`/`==`/`<=` on Var types to produce `Constraint`. GATE 2 (required): `core.layout.Var` and `core.layout.Length` enter the compiler's closed type family. If either gate is declined by the owner, fall through to Option B (method-only builder, unblocked today).

options.name: Method-only builder — no language gate (unblocked today)
options.detail: All constraints are explicit method calls: `Constraint.gte(a, b)`, `Constraint.eq(a, b)`. No comparison-operator overloading; no new compiler type family. Compatible with all ratified decisions (D-SIMD2, D-VECARITH1). Verbose relative to infix, but every constraint is a named, typed, inspectable value. Axis typing (G) can be added as a type-level distinction on top. The correct base layer for Option A's sugar if the language gates are later approved.
options.code:
c1 :: Constraint.gte(label.width, 80.px).named("label min")
c2 :: Constraint.eq_sum([label.width, Length(16.px), input.width], form.width)
solver.add([c1, c2])

options.name: Defer constraint solver to Epoch 6
options.detail: Ship only stack/grid/form presets for the UI stack now. Full Cassowary-based solver, constraint handles, and `layout { }` blocks defer to Epoch 6. Beginner presets cover common form/grid layouts without any solver dependency.
options.code:
Form.columns(label_min: 80.px, gap: 16.px)
// Epoch 6 revisit: full Cassowary solver + layout {} blocks

decisions.recReason: Infix operators on layout vars are the most ergonomic and don't require new syntax. Option B is good for tooling (inspectable constraints) but verbose. Option C needs a new compiler-blessed block (new syntax surface without clear I8 advantage over A).
decisions.explainer: Owner question answered: best current practice is Cassowary/Auto Layout: linear constraints, priorities, edit variables, and conflict explanation. Jet can improve with typed `Constraint` values: math-like authoring for layout vars, but every constraint remains a named/removable/inspectable value. Adversarial pass: infix constraints can look like general operator overloading. Patch: only `core.layout.Var`/`Length` get blessed builders; ordinary user types still cannot overload operators.
decisions.bestCurrent: Apple Auto Layout: Auto Layout expresses UI constraints as linear equations and inequalities over anchors, the strongest production layout solver model.
decisions.recommendation: `layout { }` block desugaring to typed axis-safe Constraint handles — F+G combined (Option A) — gated on two owner decisions. If either gate is declined, Option B (method-only builder, no language gate) is the unblocked fallback.
decisions.title: What is Jet’s constraint-layout API surface?
decisions.detail:
Owner Q: Consider the best approach currently in any language, then improve on it from a functionality & ergonomics perspective.
Agent answer: Updated. Best current model is Cassowary/Auto Layout: linear constraints, priorities, edit variables. Jet improves with typed Constraint values: math-like authoring, every constraint inspectable, removable, named, prioritized, and traceable. Devil's advocate: math operators look like global operator overloading. Patch: only core.layout.Var/Length comparison/arithmetic builders are blessed; no general user operator overloading.

Adversarial pass (2026-06-28): PRIMARY BLOCKER: `>=` returning `Constraint` instead of `Bool` requires comparison-operator return-type overloading — explicitly not covered by D-SIMD2 or D-VECARITH1. This is a language-level gate, not an API choice, and must be balloted separately before Option B can be implemented. MISSING FEATURES: no conflict-resolution story — the defining pain point in all constraint systems. core.layout.Var carries no axis type, allowing cross-axis constraints that are geometrically nonsensical. STRINGLY-TYPED: `form.var('label_width')` conflicts with U13 preference — name should be inferred from the :: binding. OPTION G (typed-axis model) is the "better than any existing language" angle the ballot is missing.

Adversarial pass complete: options hardened, challenges documented in detail field.
Ballot tightened: collapsed to 3 options, Option A is the unified optimal recommendation (adversarial pass + recommendation fused), rec moved to A.

decisions.title: Ratify the two language gates required for D-LAYOUT1 option A?
decisions.gist: D-LAYOUT1=A needs two compiler extensions: comparison ops that return Constraint on layout types, and axis-typed layout variables in the closed type family.
decisions.explainer: D-LAYOUT1 ratified option A (typed-axis layout block) conditionally on two compiler language gates. If both gates are ratified here, the full design ships. If either is declined, core.layout falls back to a method-only builder (D-LAYOUT1 option B), which is implementable today without any language change.
decisions.story: Sandra is building a form layout. She wants to write  and have Jet catch  (cross-axis mix) as a compile error. Both features require the compiler to treat layout variable types specially.

comparisons.note: Uses NSLayoutConstraint builder; no axis safety
frame/padding modifiers; no constraint model

options.name: Ratify both gates — ship full typed-axis layout (recommended)
options.detail: GATE 1: comparison operators (>=, ==, <=) may return Constraint (not Bool) when both operands are closed layout variable types (HVar, VVar, LengthVar). Like D-SIMD2's closed-operator blessing, this is limited to the compiler-provided family only. GATE 2: HVar, VVar, LengthVar, Constraint, and LayoutHandle enter the compiler's closed type family (recognized by core_type_known). Both gates are tightly scoped and follow existing precedent (SIMD/D-SIMD2, distinct types/D-DIST2).

options.name: Decline gates — use method-only builder
options.detail: Keep comparison operators Bool-only and keep the closed type family as-is. core.layout ships as a method-only builder (no layout {} block, no axis safety). Implementable today with no language change. Axis errors are runtime conflicts, not compile errors.

log.text: Raised as follow-up to D-LAYOUT1=A (two language gates required to implement full design).

decisions.title: Does `|` bind tighter than `||`/`&&` in match arms, and are parens required or cosmetic?
decisions.gist: D-MATCHARM1=A ratified the split: `|` alternates values, `||`/`&&` combine with booleans, parens group. This decides precedence between `|` and `||`/`&&`, and whether parens are load-bearing or cosmetic. It changes how an unparenthesized head parses.
decisions.explainer:
For `400 | 404 && fresh`: if `|` binds tighter it reads `(400|404) && fresh`; if `&&` binds tighter, `400 | (404 && fresh)`. Blast radius: parser arm-head precedence + the D-PAT `&&` guard rule (confirm the two `&&` unify). Beginner note: a silently-misread head is a footgun.

Recommendation: B — Beginner-first: a mixed head can be silently misread, so forcing parens there removes the footgun while simple heads stay clean.

options.name: `|` tighter; parens optional (cosmetic)
options.detail:
`|` tightest, then `&&`, then `||` (C-family). Parens only override.

Familiar, fewest keystrokes — but a reader must know the table.

options.name: `|` tighter; parens REQUIRED on a mixed head
options.detail:
Same precedence, but mixing `|` with `||`/`&&` demands explicit parens (teaching error otherwise).

No silent misread; costs parens on rare mixed arms. Most beginner-safe.
options.code:
400 | 404 -> ok                 // fine
(400 | 404) && fresh -> retry   // required
400 | 404 && fresh -> // ERROR: group with parens

options.name: Flat left-to-right; parens the only grouping
options.detail:
No precedence; strictly L-to-R, parens the sole grouping.
Simplest rule to state, but L-to-R surprises anyone expecting `&&` over `||` and still allows confusing mixes.

comparisons.note: Rust gives `|` in patterns its own grammar and requires guards after `if`, avoiding ambiguous boolean/pattern mixtures.

decisions.bestCurrent: Rust: Rust gives `|` in patterns its own grammar and requires guards after `if`, avoiding ambiguous boolean/pattern mixtures.
decisions.recommendation: Require parens on mixed heads. Jet keeps compact alternation while making mixed boolean logic impossible to misread.

decisions.title: Should Jet add a structured select combinator for channels, timers, task handles, and I/O events?
decisions.gist: Select must provide a single, coherent construct that specifies what to wait for AND what to do when each arm fires. The open questions before any option is implementable: what type does the wait produce, how does the builder's lifetime bind to the taskgroup scope, and what label replaces the keyword-conflicting `as:`. A if-fused form that reuses ratified if-subject arm syntax may resolve all three without new surface.
decisions.explainer: Owner question answered: syntax should be cohesive with task scopes and avoid a second `case` mini-language. A scoped fluent builder keeps ownership under the nursery/taskgroup and lets losing waits deregister safely. Adversarial pass: fluent chains can get long and hide arm identity. Patch: formatter keeps one wait arm per line, every arm has an explicit result tag, and reusable select sets can become values later without new syntax.
decisions.story: I am writing a WebSocket hub. For each connection I need to react to whichever happens first: a client message, a broadcast channel message, a heartbeat timer, or server shutdown. I want one structured wait that cleans up the losing waits automatically.
decisions.inWild:
taskgroup g {
    ev :: g.select()
        .recv(inbox, as: .Message)
        .read(conn, as: .ClientData)
        .after(ms: 30_000, as: .Heartbeat)
        .cancelled(as: .Shutdown)
        .wait()?
    handle(ev)?
}
decisions.detail:
Owner Q: I like A but don't like the syntax. Please provide an updated ballot with more cohesive options and much better syntax.
Agent answer: Updated. New syntax recommendation: fluent scoped select, `g.select().recv(...).read(...).after(...).wait()?`. Avoids `case`/block syntax, keeps ownership under the taskgroup, gives each event an explicit result tag. Devil's advocate: fluent chains can get long. Patch: formatter keeps one arm per line, each arm has a stable typed result.

Adversarial pass (2026-06-28): (1) `as:` label is syntactically invalid — KW_AS is a reserved keyword in Syntax.rs; every Option A example needs a different label. (2) Option A's return type is unspecified — a blocking design gap that if-fused Option F resolves by inheriting match's existing type rules. (3) .cancelled() in Option A conflicts with D-DEADLINE1=A's #Context propagation — two mechanisms for the same cancellation event. (4) Select-vs-race boundary must be drawn explicitly (I8): if `select` can race task handles, `race(handles)` is redundant. (5) Option E's Epoch 6 target is a category error; E6 = CI/docs, not language surface features; correct target is E3 after D-NURSERY1 ships.

options.name: If-fused select: `if g.select() { .recv(ch) -> val: ...; }` (recommended)
options.detail: Reuse the ratified if-subject arm syntax (S68, D-IF1, D-MATCHARM1=A, D-MATCHARM2=B) directly as the select surface. `g.select()` is the match subject; each arm names the event source and binds the result inline. Arm handlers are co-located with their declarations. Return type is the union of the arm handler return types — exactly what match already computes (no new type rule needed). Taskgroup `g` owns registration; losing arms deregister when any arm fires. No new language statement (avoids the parser cost the current ballot assigns to the `select { }` block option). No reserved-word collision (`as:` is not used — arm binding is direct in the match form). Extensibility: any type implementing a `Selectable` trait is a valid arm source. Gate: D-NURSERY1 must ship first (taskgroup/nursery primitive must exist).

options.name: Fluent `g.select().recv(...).after(...).wait()?` builder
options.detail: No new language statement; scoped to the taskgroup. Four blocking design gaps must be resolved before implementation: (1) Return type of `.wait()` — pre-declared user enum, compiler-synthesized tagged union, or match extension; (2) `as:` label must be renamed (`as` is KW_AS, reserved); (3) Builder lifetime relative to taskgroup must be specified; (4) Select/race boundary must be drawn (which sources belong here vs `race/any/all`). These resolutions tend to converge toward the if-fused form (Option A).
options.code:
ev :: g.select()
    .recv(inbox, tag: .Message)    // "as:" renamed — KW_AS is reserved
    .read(socket, tag: .Data)
    .after(ms: 50, tag: .Timeout)
    .wait()?

options.name: Defer select to after D-NURSERY1 ships
options.detail: Do not add a select API until the taskgroup/nursery primitive is implemented and the runtime's event polling model is operational. Fallback: `race/all/any` over helper tasks, which incurs task-allocation overhead and is less ergonomic. The correct defer target is Epoch 3 after D-NURSERY1 ships — not Epoch 6 (which is CI/docs, not language surface).

comparisons.note: select is central to channels, cancellation, timers, and server loops. It is powerful but a distinct language statement.
tokio::select! handles futures and channels, but macro/future ceremony leaks into user code.
receive expresses actor mailbox selection; great for actors, less general for typed channels, timers, and native I/O under one model.
comparisons.code: receive Msg -> handle(Msg) after 5000 -> timeout end

decisions.bestCurrent: Go select proves event choice belongs in the core concurrency toolbox; Tokio select proves the same need for async runtimes.
decisions.recommendation: If-fused select using the ratified if-subject arm syntax — no new language statement, return type resolved, no keyword conflicts (Option A). Option B (fluent builder) has four unresolved design gaps that converge on the same design anyway.
