decisions.title: Inside `.{ }` / `T.{ }` literals, adopt Zig-style `.field = val` member syntax to enable LSP dot-completion?
decisions.gist: D-DOTCTOR1/2 (ratified 2026-06-25) established `T.{ }` and `.{ }` as the struct literal spellings with `field: val` syntax. This card reopens only the inside-the-braces field syntax: should fields use a leading dot (`.field = val`) to enable LSP completion when the user types `.`, or stay with the current `field: val` colon style?
decisions.explainer: D-DOTCTOR1=A (ratified, not yet implemented) uses `field: val` inside braces, matching named-parameter and record-update patterns elsewhere. Changing to `.field = val` would require a different tokenization rule inside literal braces (dot-name-equals vs name-colon) and amend D-DOTCTOR1. The LSP motivation is real: when a user types `.` inside `T.{ }`, completion engines can offer field names. However, LSP can also complete after the bare `field` token using the expected type from context — the leading dot is not strictly required for completion. Adding `.field =` also introduces a third sigil family inside braces. I8: if `field: val` and `.field = val` coexist, that is two ways to mean the same thing — reject unless one fully replaces the other.
decisions.story: I type `Server.{` and then `.` and the IDE shows me exactly which fields are available. It feels like autocomplete in a GUI form — the dot is the trigger that says 'I want a field name here'.

options.name: Keep `field: val` (status quo, D-DOTCTOR1=A)
options.detail: The ratified spelling stands. LSP completion is implemented in the server using the expected type from context — no dot trigger needed. Consistent with named-parameter syntax elsewhere. No I8 issue. Recommend.

options.name: Adopt `.field = val` Zig-style, replace `field: val` in literals
options.detail: Amend D-DOTCTOR1 so struct literal fields use `.name = value`. The leading dot is a uniform trigger inside any `{ }` context (struct literal vs block) that LSP and parsers can key on. Creates a syntactic split: `fn foo(field: val)` named args use colon, struct literals use `.field =`. Introduces inconsistency across two very similar contexts.

options.name: Allow both (reject — I8 violation)
options.detail: Permit either `field: val` or `.field = val` inside literals. Violates I8 — two spellings for one job. Beginners will encounter both in real code and wonder which is right. Reject.

comparisons.note: Zig uses `.field = value` inside struct literals, enabling dot-completion and distinguishing member names from locals.
Zig uses `.field = value` inside struct literals uniformly. The leading dot is the LSP completion trigger and creates a consistent rule: dot-anything inside braces is a field init.
Rust struct literals use bare `field: value` with no leading sigil. IDEs complete field names from the struct definition without needing a dot trigger.

decisions.bestCurrent: Zig: Zig uses `.field = value` inside struct literals, enabling dot-completion and distinguishing member names from locals.
decisions.recommendation: Keep `field: value`: Jet already uses `:` for named association across fields, args, maps, and types. Zig wins completion, but Jet wins one-path consistency; LSP can still complete from expected type.

decisions.title: Add a blessed core library type for loading/pending/unknown async states, or leave to user enums?
decisions.gist: Async UIs often need a four-state value: not-asked, loading, ok(T), error(E). Jet has `T?` (optional) and `T ? E` (fallible). Should Jet add a blessed `Loadable<T>` or `AsyncState<T, E>` enum in the stdlib, or leave this pattern to user-defined enums?
decisions.explainer: The four-state pattern is already expressible today with a user enum and a `match`. Adding a blessed type risks I8: it's a second optional-like container alongside `T?` and `T ? E`. A stdlib enum (B) is lower cost than a language keyword (C) and avoids I1/I8 issues, but it still adds surface area to the beginner namespace. The case for it is that UI/reactive code is a target domain (replace-Swift lens) and the pattern is ubiquitous enough to warrant a canonical name. The case against: one extra enum is not a hardship, and a blessed type could fragment — `Loadable` in one codebase, user enum in another, both in the stdlib docs.
decisions.story: Every screen in my app has a data-fetch lifecycle: not loaded yet, loading spinner, loaded data, error banner. I want a type that models this cleanly without me defining the same four-variant enum in every project.

options.name: Leave to user enums (status quo)
options.detail: No new stdlib type. The pattern is one enum away. Documentation in the cookbook shows the canonical four-variant shape so every project lands on the same idiom. Keeps surface small (I8). The reactive library (D-REACT1) can export its own `Signal<T>` without a generic Loadable. Recommend.

options.name: Ship a blessed `Loadable<T, E>` stdlib enum
options.detail: Add `core.async.Loadable<T, E>` (or `core.ui.AsyncState`) to the stdlib with variants Idle / Loading / Loaded(T) / Failed(E). Consistent naming across all Jet projects. Cost: adds a type to learn, risks being wrong for some use cases (no Idle? two error types?), and may become the 'official' way even when a user enum is clearer.

options.name: Language-level pending state / keyword
options.detail: Make `pending` a first-class language concept: `T | pending` or a `?~` suffix. Deep integration — the compiler knows what 'pending' means, enabling flow-sensitivity. Very high cost, hard to reverse, I8 concern (third optional-like mechanism), and the motivating UI use cases don't require language-level semantics. Reject.

comparisons.note: Elm has no stdlib Loadable; the community converged on a `RemoteData` package with four variants (NotAsked / Loading / Failure e / Success a). A library, not a language feature.
comparisons.code:
type RemoteData e a
    = NotAsked
    | Loading
    | Failure e
    | Success a

comparisons.note: Swift has no canonical async-state type. Every team defines their own. The fragmentation pain is real — it's one argument for a blessed stdlib enum.

decisions.title: Method name inside impl Type.Display
decisions.gist: What is the method name inside impl Type.Display { }?
decisions.story: Doris is building a Color type for a design tool. She wants Color to print as "rgb(255, 0, 128)" when used in string interpolation. She writes impl Color.Display { } — what method name goes inside?

options.name: fn display(self) -> String (recommended)
options.detail: Method name matches the trait name exactly. No collision with any existing Jet built-in. Reads like the trait. Consistent with how fn restore matches the Rollback trait.

options.name: fn to_string(self) -> String
options.detail: Familiar from Rust/Java/Kotlin/Swift. But to_string is a common name users already write as helpers on their own types — high collision risk. Also implies conversion, not display.

options.name: fn format(self) -> String
options.detail: Evokes string formatting but in most languages "format" means formatting with arguments/patterns. A zero-argument fn format reads as if it takes a format string.

decisions.comparisons:
Rust:       impl fmt::Display for Color { fn fmt(&self, f: &mut Formatter) -> fmt::Result }
Swift:      var description: String { "rgb(...)" }   // CustomStringConvertible
Python:     def __str__(self) -> str
Java:       public String toString()
Kotlin:     override fun toString(): String
Go:         func (c Color) String() string

decisions.title: Field-level marker to exclude a field from Debug auto-derive output
decisions.gist: What marker hides a sensitive field from Debug auto-derive output?
decisions.story: Walter's User struct has a password_hash and a stripe_token. He never wants these in debug output, log files, or error messages. Debug auto-derives for all structs. What annotation hides a specific field?

options.name: #[Redact] field marker (recommended)
options.detail: General-purpose privacy marker. Not just for Debug — signals that this field contains sensitive data across all serialization, logging, and display contexts. PascalCase per D-CASING1. A single marker teaches one concept: "this field is sensitive."

options.name: #[Debug.skip] field marker
options.detail: Scoped specifically to Debug output. Clear intent but introduces a new dotted-name marker form not used anywhere else in Jet. Also, a developer might want a field to be skipped in JSON too — they would then need both #[Debug.skip] and a separate serialization marker.
options.code:
struct User {
    id:            Int
    email:         String
    #[Debug.skip]
    password_hash: String   // hidden from Debug but still in JSON?
    #[Debug.skip]
    stripe_token:  String
}

options.name: No v1 field exclusion — implement Display manually to filter
options.detail: Conservative. Users who need redaction override impl Type.Display themselves. No new marker. But Debug still leaks the field — you cannot hide a field from auto-derived Debug without a language mechanism.

decisions.comparisons:
Rust:           #[allow(dead_code)]  — doesn't hide from Debug
                derive(Debug) with manual impl — only way to hide
                serde:          #[serde(skip)] / #[serde(skip_serializing)]
Python:         override __repr__ manually — no field-level annotation
Swift:          no field-level skip; override debugDescription manually
Java:           @JsonIgnore (Jackson) — serialization only, not debug
Go:             omitempty tag — JSON only

decisions.title: User-type for-loop iterable hook: beginner .each/.to_list + expert Iterable protocol
decisions.gist: Beginners iterate custom collections with .each(fn) or .to_list() — no protocol required. Experts who want `for x in mytype` without copying implement Iterable + Iterator.
decisions.story: Betty built a BTree<T> for sorted data. As a beginner she writes `bt.each(fn(val) { print(val) })` or `for val in bt.to_list()` and it just works. When she needs zero-copy in-order walks, she adds `impl BTree.Iterable` and `for val in bt` becomes native.

options.name: Beginner .each/.to_list defaults + expert Iterable hook (recommended)
options.detail: Two tiers, one path. Default: any collection exposes `.each(fn(T))` for callback iteration and `.to_list() -> [T]` when a list is needed — no trait impl, no syntax surprise. Expert opt-in: `impl Type.Iterable { fn iter(self) -> Cursor }` plus `impl Cursor.Iterator { fn next(~self) -> T? }` enables `for x in mytype` without allocating a copy. Built-in `[T]`/`Map` keep `for` natively. Custom types without the protocol never silently copy — callers choose `.each` or `.to_list()` explicitly. Matches Jet's beginner-magic / expert-control split.

options.name: impl Type.Iterator only — type is its own cursor
options.detail: Single protocol on the collection. Simpler surface but fuses collection and cursor — two simultaneous `for` loops over the same value break (shared mutable state). Rejected for the expert tier when Iterable+Iterator is the safe pattern.

options.name: Defer v1 — .to_list() / .each() only, no for-in hook
options.detail: No iterable protocol in v1. Forces copies or manual `.each` forever. Rejected now that the dual-tier design gives beginners ergonomics without obligating experts to implement anything.
options.code:
for val in bt.to_list() { print(val) }   // only path
bt.each(fn(val) { print(val) })

decisions.recommendation: Beginner `.each`/`.to_list()` out of the box; expert `impl Iterable` + `Iterator` unlocks zero-copy `for x in mytype` (Option A).
decisions.comparisons:
Rust:       IntoIterator + Iterator — two traits; beginners use .iter()/.into_iter()
Python:     __iter__ + __next__ — experts implement; beginners use list()
Swift:      Sequence + IteratorProtocol — same split
Kotlin:     Iterable + Iterator — for-in requires Iterable
Jet (A):    .each/.to_list() without protocol; for-in with Iterable opt-in

decisions.title: User-type square-bracket indexing: beginner .get/.set + expert Index hook
decisions.gist: Built-in List/Map keep `m[k]` out of the box. Custom types use `.get(k)` / `.set(k, v)` by default; experts who want bracket syntax implement Index (+ optional IndexMut).
decisions.story: Earl built a SparseMatrix. Beginners call `m.get(3, 7)` and `m.set(3, 7, 42.0)` — explicit, always works. When he wants `m[3, 7]` sugar, he adds `impl SparseMatrix.Index` and bracket syntax lights up.

options.name: Beginner .get/.set defaults + expert Index hook (recommended)
options.detail: Built-in `[T]` and `Map` keep native `xs[i]` / `map[k]` with no impl. User-defined types without a protocol use named `.get(k) -> V?` and `.set(k, v)` — clear, fallible, no magic. Expert opt-in: `impl Type.Index { fn get(self, k: K) -> V? }` enables `mytype[k]`; optional `impl Type.IndexMut { fn set(~self, k: K, v: V) }` enables `mytype[k] = v`. D-SIMD2's closed built-in `[]` rule stays; only user types with an explicit impl gain brackets.

options.name: impl Type.Index + IndexMut required for all indexing
options.detail: Even built-ins would route through protocols — too much ceremony for beginners. Rejected: List/Map already have blessed `[]` and should not require impl blocks.
options.code: // Would force impl on every collection type — rejected

options.name: Defer — .get/.set only forever
options.detail: No bracket hook for user types. Rejected now that the dual-tier design keeps beginners on explicit methods while experts get brackets when they want them.

decisions.recommendation: Built-in `[]` for List/Map; `.get`/`.set` for custom types by default; expert `impl Index` unlocks `mytype[k]` (Option A).
decisions.comparisons:
Rust:       Index/IndexMut traits — opt-in for user types; Vec has built-in []
Python:     __getitem__/__setitem__ — always protocol-based
Swift:      subscript — explicit on each type
Kotlin:     operator get/set — opt-in
Jet (A):    built-in [] for List/Map; .get/.set default; Index opt-in for experts

decisions.title: Unit construction: dot-constructor spelling, not a literal-suffix hook
decisions.gist: No new literal-suffix protocol. #UnitFamily unit types construct with dot-construction like every other Jet value: `px.{100}`, `Em.{1.5}`.
decisions.story: Hank wants typed lengths in UI styles. He should write `width: px.{100}` — same dot-constructor family as `Point.{x: 3, y: 4}` — not CSS `100px` suffixes and not a hidden coercion protocol.

options.name: Dot-constructor on unit types — no literal-suffix hook (recommended)
options.detail: Close the literal-suffix hook item. D-QUAL3 #UnitFamily already provides typed units. Construction uses the ratified dot-constructor form (D-DOTCTOR1): `px.{100}`, `Em.{1.5}`, `Pct.{50}` when the target type is known from context (`width: Px = px.{100}`). No grammar suffix, no `from_int_literal` coercion protocol, no second mechanism. Consistent with struct/enum construction everywhere else in Jet.

options.name: Bless fn from_int_literal(n: Int) -> T coercion protocol
options.detail: Context-driven implicit coercion: bare `100` routes to different unit constructors depending on inferred type. Fights I8 (one path) and hides which conversion ran. Rejected in favor of explicit `px.{100}`.

options.name: CSS-style grammar suffix `100px`
options.detail: Tier-4 grammar extension. D-EXT1 already rejected user-defined literal suffixes. Would be a second construction path beside dot-constructors.
options.code: width :: 100px   // rejected — not Jet's constructor family

decisions.recommendation: Unit values construct with dot-construction `px.{100}`; remove literal-suffix hook from card #41 (Option A).
decisions.comparisons:
Jet structs:  Point.{x: 3.0, y: 4.0}  — same dot-constructor family
Jet enums:    Color.Red / .Variant     — leading dot
CSS:          width: 100px            — rejected suffix grammar
Kotlin:       100.px                   — extension property, not constructor
Rust:         Px::new(100)             — function, not dot-constructor

decisions.title: Should Jet codify a written core library ergonomic-laws checklist?
decisions.gist: The deeper question is not whether to write a doc — it is what enforcement mechanism Jet's rubric uses. Written guidelines enforced by PR review is the Rust model; it is explicitly weaker than what Jet already achieves (type-by-construction per D-DBDRIVER1, namespace separation per D-RANDSPLIT1). Jet's answer should be mechanical: encode each ergonomic law as a named lint, make the lint the source of truth, and generate the doc from it. A pure doc-checklist reviewed by humans is one pressure-filled review away from being ceremonial.
decisions.explainer: The checklist would live in docs/ (not the spec) and be referenced in PR review. It codifies things we already believe — like 'make misuse a type error', 'never accept raw strings where a path object works', 'CSPRNG and PRNG must not share a namespace' — so reviewers have a checklist rather than relying on institutional memory. It has no syntax impact and no I8 risk. It does require someone to author and maintain it; the risk is it becomes stale or ceremonial. This is a process/docs decision, not a language feature.
decisions.story: I keep catching the same API shape mistakes in review — raw strings instead of typed path objects, functions that are easy to call wrong. I want a short checklist I can point to instead of re-litigating the same principles every time.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass (2026-06-28): (1) Option A as written is the Rust social-convention model, not the Jet structural-safety model — add rule taxonomy and lint-graduation plan or it will calcify. (2) D-RINGLAYER1 (open) makes any "valid core library API" rubric incomplete until ring layering is decided; reserve a ring-placement section. (3) Option C (lints-first) is the stronger Jet-native answer: encode each rule as a named jet-lint, generate the doc from lint annotations so it cannot go stale — and closes the ecosystem coverage gap since lints apply to jetpack packages too. (4) Option D needs a concrete trigger condition (D-RINGLAYER1 ratified + D-IFC1 ratified + 20 Core APIs across 3 domains) rather than a vague epoch reference.

options.name: Lints-first: named jet-lints, doc generated from annotations (recommended)
options.detail: Encode each ergonomic law as a named compiler lint (e.g. `jet::core::stringly-typed-arg`, `jet::core::csprng-namespace-leak`). The rubric doc is auto-generated from lint metadata — name, why-clause, fix suggestion — so it cannot go stale. CI runs the lint set on every core library addition as a required gate; lints are optionally enabled for jetpack packages ecosystem-wide. Start with 5 high-value lints covering patterns already surfaced by prior decisions. Ring-placement rules become ring-qualified lint attributes once D-RINGLAYER1 is ratified; no prose reserve section needed. This is I8-clean: one mechanical path, not a social-convention document.

options.name: Author a tiered rubric doc (no lint generation)
options.detail: Write a ~10-rule doc in docs/ classifying rules as compiler-enforced, lint-tracked, or convention. Human-reviewed in PR. Weaker than A: doc can go stale, enforcement is social, ring-placement and taint-sink rules cannot be added until D-RINGLAYER1/D-IFC1 settle.

options.name: Defer — capture emerging patterns as one-off lint proposals until Epoch 6
options.detail: No rubric now. File individual lint proposals as patterns surface; revisit a unified rubric in Epoch 6 when D-RINGLAYER1, D-IFC1, and 20+ Core APIs across 3 domains are stable. Until then, institutional knowledge lives in PR comments and individual lint PRs.
options.code:
// No rubric doc; defer to Epoch 6
// Pattern surfaced → file lint proposal → implement if approved

comparisons.note: Rust API Guidelines codify naming, ownership, error, and trait conventions so std/crates feel coherent across teams.

Rust has a published API guidelines doc (rust-lang.github.io/api-guidelines) that is explicitly required for std contributions. It catches naming, error handling, and ergonomics issues before they land.
Swift has a mandatory API design guidelines doc. Every new core library addition is checked against it, enforcing naming clarity and call-site readability.
comparisons.code:
// Swift guideline: "Prefer method and function names that make use sites form grammatical English phrases"
array.insert(x, at: i)   // not array.insert(i, x)

decisions.bestCurrent: Rust: Rust API Guidelines codify naming, ownership, error, and trait conventions so std/crates feel coherent across teams.
decisions.recommendation: Encode each ergonomic rule as a named jet-lint; generate the rubric doc from lint annotations so it cannot go stale (Option A). Ecosystem-wide: lints apply to both core library and jetpack packages.

decisions.title: Should `jet fmt` preserve author-written grouping parentheses?
decisions.gist: Authors sometimes write parentheses to clarify sub-expression grouping even when they are not required by precedence rules. Currently it is unclear whether `jet fmt` strips these. The decision is whether the formatter should preserve or remove redundant-but-intentional parentheses.
decisions.explainer: This touches the formatter's normalization policy. D-FMT1 established single-line/multi-line preservation as respecting author intent; this is the same principle applied to grouping parens. The formatter-roundtrip-required memory note means any change here requires a stability test. Option A (preserve all author parens) is safest for intent but may accumulate noise. Option C (preserve only where precedence is non-obvious) requires the formatter to reason about precedence ranks — more complex but more principled. Option B (strip to minimal) matches classical formatter behavior but erases intent.
decisions.story: I wrote `(a + b) * c` and `jet fmt` rewrote it as `a + b * c` — technically the same but now I can't tell at a glance that the grouping was intentional. The formatter should not second-guess me.

options.name: Preserve all author parens
options.detail: The formatter never removes any parentheses the author wrote. Intent is always respected. Simple rule: if the author put parens there, keep them. Risk: accumulated unnecessary parens over time in auto-generated or refactored code.

options.name: Normalize to minimal parens
options.detail: Strip any parentheses that are not needed for correct parsing. Produces the most compact output. Risk: erases author intent and can silently change apparent meaning even when actual meaning is the same.

options.name: Preserve only non-obvious precedence parens
options.detail: The formatter keeps parens when operators of differing precedence are mixed across a threshold of 'obvious' (e.g. arithmetic vs bitwise, bitwise vs boolean). Strips parens that are redundant within a single precedence group. Requires a precedence-obviousness table but is the most principled option.

comparisons.note: Prettier removes subjective formatting but preserves parentheses when they change parsing or remove real ambiguity.
Prettier strips all redundant parens by default. This is a known complaint — authors use parens for documentation and Prettier removes them silently.
rustfmt preserves most author parens, removing only the truly degenerate cases (double-parens around a literal). Generally considered the right call.
comparisons.code:
// rustfmt keeps: let x = (a + b) * c;
// rustfmt removes: let x = ((42));  → let x = 42;

decisions.bestCurrent: Prettier: Prettier removes subjective formatting but preserves parentheses when they change parsing or remove real ambiguity.
decisions.recommendation: Preserve non-obvious grouping parens only. Jet keeps fmt deterministic like Prettier while preserving author intent where it materially improves scanability.

decisions.title: Should Jet build a copy-paste-drift lint, and if so, when?
decisions.gist: When N near-identical blocks exist in a codebase and one diverges from the rest, it is almost always a missed update. Detecting structural duplication with drift requires a semantic index to compare AST subtrees across a file or project. No such lint exists in Jet today. The question is whether to pursue it and at what phase.
decisions.explainer: This lint cannot be a single-file sema pass — it requires a global view of the codebase (cross-file AST similarity). That means it depends on the semantic-index API, which is not yet landed. Building it standalone (as a separate tool) avoids the dependency but creates a parallel infrastructure. The high false-positive risk (similar-looking code is not always copy-pasted) makes opt-in the right default. Given the dependency, deferring until the semantic-index API lands is the practical choice — but the decision to pursue it at all should be made now so it gets a slot.
decisions.story: I copy-pasted a validation block for three new fields, updated two of them, and shipped a bug in the third for six months. If the compiler had seen four nearly-identical blocks and flagged the diverging one, I would have caught it immediately.

options.name: Defer: plan it now, build after semantic-index lands
options.detail: Record the intent as a roadmap item gated on the semantic-index API. Once the index exists, build this as an opt-in lint on top of it — no standalone tool, no parallel infrastructure. This is the right sequencing: don't block, don't build twice.

options.name: Standalone external tool now
options.detail: Build a separate `jet dup-check` command that does its own AST traversal independent of the semantic index. Ships sooner but creates duplicate infrastructure that must be maintained and eventually unified. Against I8 (two mechanisms for the same job).
options.code:
$ jet dup-check src/
warning: near-duplicate blocks detected
  src/validators.jet:3 and src/validators.jet:6 differ by 1 statement

options.name: Don't pursue
options.detail: High false-positive risk, complex implementation, depends on infrastructure not yet built. The cost may not be worth the benefit compared to other lint investments. Defer indefinitely.
options.code: // No lint ever. Users rely on code review to catch drift.

comparisons.note: SonarQube's CPD (copy-paste detection) engine runs as a separate analysis pass over the full codebase AST. It is effective but requires a project-wide index — the same dependency Jet would have.
comparisons.code:
# sonar-project.properties
sonar.cpd.exclusions=**/generated/**
# CPD fires on blocks > 10 tokens that appear 2+ times

comparisons.note: jscpd is a standalone copy-paste detector that works on token streams, not a semantic index. Fast but produces more false positives on intentional similar-looking code.
comparisons.code:
npx jscpd src/ --min-lines 5 --min-tokens 50
# Clone found: src/a.ts (12-18) ~ src/b.ts (34-40)

decisions.title: How does interpolation select the Debug hook instead of the default Display hook?
decisions.gist: Debug formatting needs a selector that signals "compiler-known protocol hook, not a field or method call." The key constraints that the current ballot underweights: (1) all `#`-markers are PascalCase and `#` infix means "pinned number" — Option B's `{value#debug}` violates both unless explicitly amended; (2) don't create a format mini-language by a different route; (3) the selector must compose cleanly in multi-value interpolations. The owner asked for non-member-looking operators; this ballot adds a casing conflict and an infix contract problem that must be resolved before any option is ratified.
decisions.explainer: Owner question answered: the ballot now has six non-member-looking selectors. `{value#debug}` marks Debug as a compiler-known interpolation feature, not a field or method. Adversarial pass: `#` inside interpolation is new and could invite a mini-language. Patch: selector set is closed (`#debug` only unless a future decision adds another), formatter round-trips it exactly, and unknown selectors produce Jet diagnostics.
decisions.story: Nora writes a CLI tool. Normal output should be clean and user-facing, but a debug log needs the full structural representation with variant names and field labels. She wants one interpolation selector that is obvious at the call site and cannot be confused with a field or method.
decisions.detail:
Owner Q: Try a method operator with different sigils that could identify it as a non-member/feature rather than a field. Give me multiple options.
Agent answer: Updated with six method/operator-style selectors. New rec: `{value#debug}`. Marks Debug as a compiler-known formatting feature, not a field or method. Restrict to a tiny closed selector set, formatter round-trips it, sema errors on unknown selectors.

Adversarial pass (2026-06-28): `#` INFIX CONTRACT: S76 + VERSION-# established that `#` in infix position "introduces a pinned number" ([T#N], pkg#1.2.0). `{value#debug}` breaks this contract — debug is not a number; needs explicit ratification in syntax-decisions.md. D-CASING1 CONFLICT: every #-marker is PascalCase; `{value#debug}` (lowercase) violates D-CASING1; `{value#Debug}` (corrected) looks like applying an attribute marker in expression position. OPTION E PARSING BUG: `{a | b | debug}` is ambiguous — parser cannot distinguish `debug` as a variable from a selector without reserved-word treatment. MINI-LANGUAGE RISK IS SYMMETRIC: reserving `#repr`/`#pretty` by decision creates the same format-spec mini-language as Option A, just slower. MISSING OPTION H: `{value:Debug}` — PascalCase protocol name after `:`; consistent with D-CASING1, no new sigil, unambiguous in interpolation context.

Sprint-readiness sweep: story and inWild filled so the ballot is complete for owner decision.

options.name: `{value@Debug}` — PascalCase selector suffix (ratified)
options.detail: Inside interpolation, suffix the value expression with `@Debug` to select the Debug hook: `{value@Debug}`. Bare `{value}` remains Display. This honors the owner correction away from `:Debug`, keeps selector casing PascalCase, avoids a format mini-language, and mirrors Jet marker-suffix visual grammar without making `Debug` look like a field or method.

options.name: `{#Debug value}` — marker-style prefix selector
options.detail: Use Jet's marker visual language inside interpolation: a PascalCase `#Debug` prefix names the protocol hook, then the value follows. This avoids member-call shape and avoids Rust's `:?` mini-language hint. Tradeoff: `#` inside interpolation becomes a new selector form even though `#` elsewhere marks declarations/blocks/types, so this must stay a closed interpolation-only grammar.

options.name: `{Debug user}` — protocol-name prefix selector
options.detail: Put the PascalCase protocol name first with no sigil: `{Debug user}`. It reads like "render this value with Debug" and cannot be mistaken for a field or method. Tradeoff: interpolation grammar must treat a leading PascalCase name plus following expression as a selector form, so `{Point x}`-style expressions need a clear parse rule or teaching error.
options.code:
print("user={Debug user}")
print("plain={user} debug={Debug user}")

// Display can be explicit if desired:
print("user={Display user}")

comparisons.note: Rust interpolation uses `{}` for Display and `{:?}` for Debug, a compact convention developers already know.

decisions.bestCurrent: Rust: Rust interpolation uses `{}` for Display and `{:?}` for Debug, a compact convention developers already know.
decisions.recommendation: Ratified owner amendment: use `{value@Debug}` for Debug interpolation; bare `{value}` stays Display.

decisions.title: Should the PRNG and CSPRNG APIs be structurally separated to prevent misuse?
decisions.gist: `core.random` (fast, seedable PRNG) and `core.crypto` (CSPRNG) already exist but their naming and structural relationship may not make the security boundary unmistakable. Using a PRNG for secrets (session tokens, keys, nonces) is a critical security bug. The decision is whether to add structural guards — naming, types, lints — that make misuse a compile-time or lint-time error.
decisions.explainer: This is a misuse-resistant API design problem. The PRNG is not secret-safe; the CSPRNG is. If both are called `random`, a developer searching for 'random' may pick the wrong one. The fix is: distinct namespaces (already partially true), a type-level or lint-level guard that blocks PRNG output from flowing into crypto-context parameters, and clear naming. This interacts with D-STDRUBRIC1 (the ergonomic checklist would catch this pattern). A lint that fires when PRNG output is used where a CryptoRand is expected is the highest-value addition. No new syntax — this is API shape + a lint.
decisions.story: I grepped for 'random' and used `core.random.int()` to generate a session token. It looked right. Six months later a security audit found it. I want the compiler to tell me I'm using the wrong thing.

options.name: Distinct namespaces + typed outputs + misuse lint
options.detail: Keep `core.random` for PRNG and `core.crypto.random` for CSPRNG. Give them distinct return types (`PrngBytes` vs `CryptoBytes`). Add a lint that fires when `PrngBytes` flows into a parameter typed `CryptoBytes` or any parameter named `token`, `key`, `nonce`, `secret`. Docs and error messages call out the distinction explicitly.

options.name: Single random module with a security flag
options.detail: One `random` module; caller passes a security level flag. Simpler API surface but violates I8 (one module doing two jobs with a flag) and makes misuse easy — the default flag is the unsafe one.

options.name: Status quo: docs and naming only
options.detail: Keep the existing split as-is. Add clearer documentation. No types, no lint. Risk: documentation is not read at the call site; misuse continues silently.

comparisons.note: Rust separates seeded PRNGs from OS entropy and uses typed RNG traits, making deterministic and cryptographic randomness visibly different.
Python's `secrets` module is explicitly for cryptographic use; `random` is for simulations. The naming makes the split clear. There is no lint — misuse is silent.
comparisons.code:
import secrets, random
token = secrets.token_bytes(32)   # correct
token = random.randbytes(32)      # wrong, no warning

comparisons.note: Go separates CSPRNG (`crypto/rand`) from PRNG (`math/rand`) at the package level. Different import paths make confusion less likely but not impossible. No lint either.

decisions.bestCurrent: Rust: Rust separates seeded PRNGs from OS entropy and uses typed RNG traits, making deterministic and cryptographic randomness visibly different.
decisions.recommendation: Split PRNG/CSPRNG structurally and lint misuse. Jet can make the safe choice clearer than Rust by putting deterministic tests and crypto APIs behind different names and return types.

decisions.title: Should we maintain a desugaring map doc that records what each surface feature lowers to?
decisions.gist: No written record exists of which surface forms Jet lowers and to what TIR node. Jet has no desugaring phase (unlike Haskell/GHC); "lowering" happens at the checked-AST→TIR boundary inside jet-codegen. A lowering map would: (a) enforce I8 by making it immediately visible when a new surface form duplicates an existing TIR path; (b) anchor crate-seam contracts by telling each crate author what it receives and what it emits; (c) give contributor onboarding a one-page reference instead of four-file grepping. The core question is whether to maintain it as an enforced spec artifact (like I4/I5) or rely on TIR type definitions and code comments. A prose doc without CI enforcement is neither: it adds maintenance cost without providing reliability.
decisions.explainer: A desugaring map disciplines I8 directly: if a new feature proposal would introduce a second mechanism that lowers to the same kernel form as an existing one, the doc makes that visible immediately. It also anchors the compiler-seams work (the 7-crate workspace under crates/) by giving each crate a clear contract for what it receives and emits. The doc is a living spec artifact, not a one-shot writeup — it must be updated whenever a surface feature is added or changed. Cost: author time per feature; benefit: prevents silent I8 violations and aids new contributors reading the compiler.
decisions.story: I'm reading the sema crate trying to understand what `for x in xs { }` desugars to. There's no doc — I have to grep through four files and guess whether the lowering is canonical or accidental. A one-page map would have answered this in ten seconds.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass (2026-06-28): (1) Jet has no desugar pass; "for x in xs" lowers at TIR, not via AST rewriting. The doc records TIR lowerings, not AST desugarings — the title and framing should reflect this. (2) The inWild example shows Rust text output, which violates R7; entries must be TIR-level. (3) Without a CI check, Option A degrades to B within one development cycle — all Jet spec artifacts (I4 ui snapshots, I5 golden tests) are machine-enforced. (4) Option C (machine-verifiable lowering tests, a tests/lowering/ suite) should be evaluated and potentially combined with A. (5) Option D needs an explicit trigger condition ("E6 sema feature-set freeze") rather than a vague epoch reference.

options.name: docs/spec/desugaring.md + tests/lowering/ CI suite (recommended)
options.detail: Create docs/spec/desugaring.md recording each surface construct and the TIR node(s) it lowers to — at TIR level, not Rust output, so the doc survives an R7 backend swap. Simultaneously add tests/lowering/ where each surface construct has a canonical TIR expectation test. CI fails if a new surface form lacks a lowering test — matching how I4 (ui snapshots) and I5 (golden examples) work. The doc is human-readable index; the test suite is enforcement. Add "desugaring.md + lowering test updated" to the CLAUDE.md workflow done criteria.

options.name: Inline lowering notes in architecture.md (no new file)
options.detail: Add a "surface-to-TIR lowering" section to the existing architecture.md. Single-source-of-truth benefit: no contributor has to know a separate file exists. Drawback: architecture.md grows and lacks CI enforcement unless a lowering test suite is added anyway. If a lowering test suite is added, Option A and B are equivalent; prefer A because the standalone doc is more discoverable and easier to scope-limit in a grep.

options.name: Skip or defer to Epoch 6
options.detail: Do not create a lowering map now. Revisit when the sema feature set is frozen for v1 API stability. Risk: the surface exceeds 40 constructs by then; contributors in E2–E5 work without the map; I8 violations (two paths to the same TIR node) are invisible until caught by a late reviewer.
options.code:
// Status quo: grep four files to find the lowering.
// grep for_in crates/jet-sema/src  -- 6 files, no canonical answer

comparisons.note: Rust Reference + MIR make many surface-to-core lowerings explicit, giving implementers and tool authors shared truth.
The Kotlin spec maintains explicit desugaring rules for lambdas, for-loops, destructuring, and delegates. It is the authoritative reference for contributors and tooling authors.
GHC's 'desugaring' phase is formally documented in the Commentary wiki. Designers check it when evaluating new syntax for overlap with existing mechanisms.
comparisons.code:
-- GHC desugars do-notation:
-- do { x <- m; rest } => m >>= \x -> rest

decisions.bestCurrent: Rust: Rust Reference + MIR make many surface-to-core lowerings explicit, giving implementers and tool authors shared truth.
decisions.recommendation: Lowering map doc + CI-enforced tests/lowering/ suite (Option A). The doc alone would rot; machine enforcement keeps it current at zero marginal cost per new feature.
