Adversarial pass complete: options hardened, challenges documented in detail field.
Ballot tightened: collapsed to 3 options, Option A is the unified optimal recommendation (adversarial pass + recommendation fused), rec moved to A.

decisions.title: Should Jet provide a single quality/performance fidelity knob that apps can read and respond to under load?
decisions.gist: A 'fidelity signal' is a single scalar (0.0–1.0) that represents current quality budget. The runtime or platform sets it based on load; app code reads it and degrades gracefully (lower resolution, skip effects, reduce particles). This is a New/library-level idea, closely related to D-ADAPTRT1 (adaptive runtime).
decisions.explainer: This is simpler than D-ADAPTRT1 — rather than a full environmental-signals API, it is one number apps read. The hard question is who sets it: the runtime (automatic, opaque) or the developer explicitly (manual, testable). A library pattern where the fidelity signal is readable and also manually overridable is both useful and auditable. Folding this with D-ADAPTRT1 makes sense — they are the same concept at different granularities. If D-ADAPTRT1 is deferred, defer this too. References: approximate-algorithms and budgets-as-types cards may interact (fidelity budget as a typed value).
decisions.story: My renderer runs at 60fps on a fast machine but stutters on low-end hardware. I want one place in my code to check 'what quality level should I be running at right now' and scale every effect accordingly — without if-else chains spread through every render path.

options.name: Library fidelity signal (read + manual override)
options.detail: Stdlib exposes `Perf.fidelity() -> f32` (set automatically by the runtime based on frame time, or manually by the app for testing). App code reads it and applies its own degradation. Simple, auditable, foldable with D-ADAPTRT1.

options.name: Runtime-managed automatic degradation
options.detail: The runtime detects load and automatically disables features annotated with a fidelity level. App code is unaware of what got disabled. Hard to debug, harder to test.

options.name: Fold into D-ADAPTRT1 / defer
options.detail: Decide this together with the adaptive-runtime card. Not worth a separate ballot slot.
options.code: // Deferred — see D-ADAPTRT1

comparisons.note: Exposes 'scalability groups' (shadow quality, effects quality) as integer levels the engine reads. App code checks `Scalability.GetQualityLevels()`. Explicit, readable, testable.

decisions.title: Should Jet expose carbon-intensity and battery-state signals as stdlib APIs?
decisions.gist: The idea: runtime policies that respond to grid carbon intensity and battery state — pause heavy tasks when carbon is high or battery is low, prefer green windows for scheduled work. This is a New/library-level idea. Carbon intensity requires an external API (not available from the OS). Battery state is OS-provided on most platforms.
decisions.explainer: Battery state is straightforward — every major OS exposes it. Carbon intensity is not: it requires calling an external service (electricityMap, WattTime) or using a locale-derived static estimate. Embedding a live carbon API into stdlib creates an external network dependency inside the language runtime, which is a significant commitment. The simpler approach: expose battery state as a stdlib signal, provide a carbon-intensity hook that apps wire to their preferred data source. This folds cleanly under D-ADAPTRT1. If D-ADAPTRT1 is deferred, defer this too.
decisions.story: I'm running a nightly ML training job. I want it to start only when both the battery is above 80% (or plugged in) and the grid carbon intensity is below a threshold — without writing platform-specific scheduler code.

options.name: Stdlib battery signal + user-provided carbon hook
options.detail: Stdlib provides `Env.battery()` (OS-backed, cross-platform). Carbon intensity is a user-registered hook: app code fetches from its preferred source and registers it. No network dependency inside stdlib. Clean, auditable.

options.name: Full stdlib carbon + battery runtime policies
options.detail: Stdlib bundles a carbon-intensity client (or estimates from locale). Runtime uses both signals to auto-schedule or throttle. Adds external network calls to the language runtime — fragile, hard to test, region-specific accuracy varies wildly.

options.name: Fold into D-ADAPTRT1 / defer
options.detail: Same decision space as adaptive-runtime. Not worth a separate ballot. Decide together.
options.code: // Deferred — see D-ADAPTRT1

comparisons.note: Platforms expose battery/performance hints; carbon intensity is usually app/service-provided.
Exposes 'low power mode' and 'battery level' via OS API; scheduler hints (prefersExternalPower) let the OS choose timing. No carbon signal — Apple uses its own internal heuristics.
The standard carbon-intensity data source. Requires API key, network call, locale. Not embeddable in a stdlib without user opt-in.

decisions.bestCurrent: Browser / mobile APIs: Platforms expose battery/performance hints; carbon intensity is usually app/service-provided.
decisions.recommendation: Fold into adaptive runtime later. Jet should not standardize environmental signals before the runtime policy surface exists.

decisions.title: Reopen procedural macros / arbitrary AST injection for Jet?
decisions.gist: D-METADEPTH1 and D-CTCODEGEN1 rejected user-defined AST rewriting for v1. The question is whether to revisit that rejection — either now, gated, or as a post-self-host research track. Current coverage comes from `#[derive]`, reflection, and `$splice` inside `comptime {}` blocks.
decisions.explainer: Proc macros let user code transform the AST of arbitrary other code before semantic analysis. They were rejected because they create an unbounded second surface of syntax and type rules that the front end no longer fully owns — violating I8 (one canonical mechanism) and making tooling (the LSP, diagnostics) unreliable. The safe cases are covered by `#[derive]` for structural code generation and `$splice` for comptime value injection. Reopening requires revisiting D-METADEPTH1 and D-CTCODEGEN1. Any gated form would interact with the user-derives card and the full-jai-metaprogramming track (c154).
decisions.story: I want to write a library that generates a state machine from an annotated enum without forking the compiler — right now I have to hand-write the expansion or wait for an official derive.

options.name: Keep rejected for v1
options.detail: Derives, reflection, and `$splice` cover the safe-structural cases. Full proc macros give arbitrary user code control over the AST before sema, which breaks I8 (a new syntax surface per macro) and I2/I3 (sema can no longer own all checking). No new action needed.

options.name: Allow gated proc macros (opt-in, audited)
options.detail: A library marks a function `@proc_macro` and it receives an AST token tree, transforming it before sema. Gated behind `#[Grant(ProcMacro)]` at the call site so readers see the risk. Still violates I8 — it is a second expansion surface running before the canonical checker.

options.name: Far-horizon: post-self-host research
options.detail: Park the idea as a research item under the full-jai-metaprogramming track (c154). Revisit only after Jet is self-hosted and the AST/sema boundary is stable enough to define a safe proc-macro API. No current action; decision stays rejected.

comparisons.note: Proc macros operate on raw `TokenStream` before type checking. They can produce invalid code that causes cryptic rustc errors, and IDEs struggle to provide completions inside macro-generated spans.
Zig has no proc macros; comptime functions operate on fully-typed values. This is closer to Jet's `$splice` model — safe, checkable, no separate AST surface.

decisions.title: Reopen library-defined sigils, keywords, or grammar (reader macros) for Jet?
decisions.gist: D-EXT1 classified grammar mutation (Tier 4 extensions) as a global footgun and rejected it. Reader macros let libraries introduce new sigils, keywords, or syntax rules. The question is whether any sandboxed form is worth reopening, or whether the rejection stands.
decisions.explainer: Reader macros change the tokenizer or parser table for the duration of a module or file. They violate I7 (every user-typeable sigil lives in Source/Syntax.rs with a decision ID) and I8 (grammar becomes per-library, not one surface). Tooling — the LSP, formatter, syntax highlighter — cannot reason about code it has not seen the grammar for. Even a sandboxed form requires the parser to be extensible, which is a major architectural commitment. Marked DSL blocks (`#[Sql] { ... }`) are the stdlib-only safety valve already ratified under D-EXT1. No new prerequisites exist for a gated form.
decisions.story: I want to write a parsing library that introduces `<< >>` as stream operators without waiting for a language proposal — like Haskell's `do` notation or Raku's grammar system.

options.name: Keep rejected — grammar is fixed
options.detail: I7 requires every sigil in Source/Syntax.rs. Reader macros would mean any library could silently redefine what `<<` or `>>` mean in a file. DSL blocks handle the common case; new operators go through the ballot process. Strong recommendation.
options.code:
// Error if user lib tries to add a sigil:
error[E0900]: unknown sigil `<<` in expression
  --> src/stream.jet:4:12
   |
 4 |   let x = buf << 16;
   |              ^^ not a defined operator
   |   hint: define operators via the ballot process, not reader macros

options.name: Allow grammar extensions in an isolated scope
options.detail: A `#[Grammar(ext)]` block opts a file into a named grammar extension published as a package. The parser downloads and applies the extension grammar. This is sandboxed per-file but breaks the LSP, formatter, and any tool that assumes a fixed grammar. Violates I7/I8.

options.name: Far-horizon: post-v1 grammar versioning research
options.detail: Park as research under a grammar-versioning track. Before any extension mechanism, Jet would need content-addressed grammar snapshots and tooling APIs for grammar consumers. Not actionable now; rejection stands.

comparisons.note: Reader macros dispatch on arbitrary characters before tokenization. They are expressive but mean any Lisp file's syntax can be completely foreign to a reader who does not know its reader macro set.
Grammars are first-class and composable, making Raku highly expressive — and nearly unreadable across different grammar extensions in practice.

decisions.title: Treat 'structural merge by meaning' as a distinct card, or fold into D-STRUCTMERGE1?
decisions.gist: This card and the structural-merge card (D-STRUCTMERGE1) describe the same idea from two angles: merging by AST identity vs. merging by program meaning/semantics. Keeping two cards creates duplicate tracking and splits owner attention on what is effectively one research item.
decisions.explainer: D-STRUCTMERGE1 captures AST/semantic structural merge. This card adds the 'meaning' framing — understanding whether two edits are semantically equivalent even if textually different. In practice, any structural merge tool would need to handle both: identity-based merge for renames/moves, and meaning-based equivalence for refactors. They are not independent research tracks. Consolidating them into one card (D-STRUCTMERGE1) eliminates the I8 violation of two mechanisms for one job and keeps the owner's ballot queue shorter. The distinction between 'identity' and 'meaning' is an implementation detail of the one tool, not a reason for two cards.
decisions.story: I don't want to review two separate ballot cards for what is clearly the same future tooling feature — one entry on the research backlog is enough.

options.name: Fold into D-STRUCTMERGE1 (consolidate)
options.detail: Close this card. Add a note to D-STRUCTMERGE1 that 'meaning-based equivalence' is part of the same research track. One far-horizon item, one owner decision, no duplicate ballot entries. Directly respects I8 at the process level.

options.name: Keep as a distinct card
options.detail: Argue that 'merge by identity' (rename detection) and 'merge by meaning' (semantic equivalence) are distinct research problems that may require different tools and timelines. Track separately. Creates two far-horizon items where one would do.

comparisons.note: Most issue trackers close duplicate cards with a 'duplicate of #N' tag. The standard practice is to consolidate and add notes to the canonical card rather than run parallel tracks for the same research question.
comparisons.code:
# CLOSED as duplicate of D-STRUCTMERGE1
# Added to D-STRUCTMERGE1 scope:
#   - meaning/semantic equivalence detection
#   - not just AST identity

decisions.title: Should the leading enum-variant dot also apply in value position when the expected type is known?
decisions.gist: D-ENUMDOT1=A ratified the leading dot on enum-variant patterns in match arms (`.Circle(r)`). This decides whether that dot extends to VALUE position when the expected type is known (`c@ Color = .Red` alongside `Color.Red`). A coherent but separate extension the owner flagged for an explicit ruling.
decisions.explainer:
Today value-position is `Color.Red` (S30); the dot was added only to match arms (S31). Extending it mirrors dot-construction (`.{ }`, D-DOTCTOR) — type-directed authoring (Blueprint north-star). The dot resolves only where the expected type is known (annotated binding, return, typed arg). Blast radius: parser expression grammar, expected-type elaboration, every enum literal in canon/examples.

Recommendation: A — Extending the dot mirrors dot-construction and the owner's type-directed anti-repetition direction, while keeping `Color.Red` where no expected type exists.

options.name: Extend the dot to value position (both spellings)
options.detail:
`.Red` allowed anywhere the expected type is known; `Color.Red` stays valid everywhere.

Mirrors dot-construction and the match-arm dot; type-directed, less repetition. Rule: 'use the dot when the type is known.'
options.code:
c@ Color = .Red
fn default() -> Color { .Red }
paint(.Red)
x@ = Color.Red   // no expected type -> qualified form

options.name: Keep the dot match-arm-only
options.detail:
Value position stays `Color.Red`.

Smallest surface, no new ambiguity — but the dot means 'inferred member' in patterns yet is absent in the symmetric value case.
options.code:
c@ Color = Color.Red
match shape { .Circle(r) -> ... }

options.name: Require the dot everywhere; retire `Color.Red`
options.detail:
`.Red` the single spelling where the type is known; drop `Color.Red`.
One canonical spelling (I8-pure) but breaks the no-expected-type case and churns every `Type.Variant` literal.

comparisons.note: Swift allows `.case` when the enum type is known, making assignments and calls concise without losing type context.

decisions.bestCurrent: Swift: Swift allows `.case` when the enum type is known, making assignments and calls concise without losing type context.
decisions.recommendation: Extend dot to value position. Jet already chose dot for inferred enum patterns; value-position parity gives Swift’s ergonomics with one inferred-member rule.

decisions.title: What is the ratified syntax and access gate for labeled stored-reference fields?
decisions.gist: Stored reference fields let structs carry zero-copy views into owner values; owner selected marker syntax `#Ref(Label)`.
decisions.explainer: The recovered #100 concern is not an unresolved dangling-reference bug. E2-M5 hardened stored refs. The remaining issue is governance: `ref[label] field: T` is user-typeable, documented by diagnostics, and absent from syntax-decisions.md. I7 requires every keyword/sigil to have a decision ID. This ballot either ratifies that syntax, replaces it, or removes it until a better tier-2 stored-reference model exists.
decisions.story: Earl builds a parser over a large input buffer. He wants tokens and slices to point into that buffer without allocating new strings, while the compiler still proves the buffer outlives every view.

options.name: Ratify `ref[label] field: T` behind `use core.mem` (recommended)
options.detail: Purpose: this is for structs that store a view into another value, e.g. parser tokens pointing into an input buffer, graph edges pointing into arena-owned nodes, or zero-copy packet/header views. The normal Jet memory model lets functions borrow during a call, but v1 intentionally disallows storing/returning references in beginner code. `ref[label] field: T` is the expert-tier opt-in that exposes that power while naming the owner relationship. It does not make unsafe memory possible by itself; sema must still reject dangling/escaping views. Gate it behind `use core.mem` so beginners never encounter stored-reference vocabulary accidentally.

options.name: `#Ref(Label)` field marker, no import gate (ratified)
options.detail: Stored reference fields use normal Jet marker syntax on the field: `#Ref(arena) name: T`. The label names the owner relationship sema must prove. No `use core.mem` gate is required per owner choice; safety still comes from sema rejecting dangling or escaping views. This gives experts zero-copy stored views that call-time `&`/`~` capabilities cannot express, while avoiding a new bracket keyword form.

options.name: Remove labeled ref fields until tier-2 references are redesigned
options.detail: Delete or hide current syntax and diagnostics until a full tier-2 stored-reference model is designed. Avoids ratifying a syntax that may need to change when the broader owned/borrowed reference system (post-v1) is specified. Breaks existing examples and tests that use `ref[label]`.
options.code: // no stored reference fields until tier-2 reference model is designed

comparisons.note: Rust encodes stored-reference relationships with lifetimes; Jet intentionally has no lifetime syntax in v1.
Swift mostly avoids stored borrowed references in safe user code; ownership features are explicit advanced syntax.

decisions.bestCurrent: Rust proves stored references need explicit relationship tracking; Jet should keep that explicit but hide it behind an expert gate.
decisions.recommendation: Ratified owner amendment: use `#Ref(Label)` on the field, with no `use core.mem` gate (Option B as amended).

log.text: Owner amendment applied: stored-ref fields use `#Ref(Label)` syntax.
Owner asked purpose/control question; ballot expanded to explain zero-copy stored views and why call-time capabilities are insufficient.
Ballot tightened: collapsed to 3 options, Option A is the unified optimal recommendation, rec set to A.

decisions.comment: Use syntax `#Ref(Label)` instead of `ref[label]`; no import gate.

decisions.title: Reopen C FFI syntax or keep S59/D-CFFI2-SYN?
decisions.gist: C FFI syntax is already ratified. This decides whether `#Lang_C`-style blocks are better enough to reopen that surface.
decisions.explainer: C FFI syntax is already ratified. This decides whether `#Lang_C`-style blocks are better enough to reopen that surface. The ballot is a proceed/reopen check so tomorrow's agents know whether to implement, document, or leave the existing design alone.
decisions.story: A systems programmer binds a small C header. They want the boundary to read clearly as C interop without importing C syntax into normal Jet code.

options.name: Keep C FFI, but spell blocks `#Extern module` (ratified)
options.detail: Keep the ratified C FFI model (`use c.<lib> as alias`, generated bindings, same safety gates) but update the marker spelling to Jet-canonical `#Extern module`, per owner comment. This preserves one C-binding mechanism while aligning with PascalCase marker syntax; `@extern` becomes retired teaching syntax.

options.name: Add `#Lang_C { ... }` C-FFI block
options.detail: A marker block visually names the foreign language. Risk: looks like a syntax island and may imply raw C declarations parse inside Jet braces (they do not). I8 concern: `#Lang_C { }` and `@extern module` both declare C bindings — two mechanisms for one job. Only justified if user research shows `@extern module` is consistently misread.

options.name: Docs-only: teach "C binding block" terminology without new syntax
options.detail: Keep current syntax; rename the docs section and examples to use "C binding block" as the teaching term. No syntax change, no I8 cost. Correct if the issue is terminology, not syntax.
options.code:
// docs: "C binding block"
@extern module libc { fn puts(s: *U8) -> Int }

comparisons.note: Existing ratified decisions are the baseline; reopening needs a clear safety/readability win.

decisions.bestCurrent: Jet ratified surface unless this ballot identifies a stronger beginner-safe, one-path design.
decisions.recommendation: Ratified owner amendment: keep the existing C FFI model, but spell the binding block `#Extern module`, not `@extern module`.

log.text: Owner ratified A with amendment: use `#Extern` instead of `@extern`; option text updated.
Ballot tightened: collapsed to 3 options, Option A is the unified optimal recommendation, rec set to A.

decisions.comment: update to use #Extern instead of @extern

decisions.title: Should Jet add a compact counted-loop header with semicolon-separated parts?
decisions.gist: The question is not `for` as an alias; it is whether loop setup, bound, and increment need a compact header form.
decisions.explainer: Jet already chose one `loop` keyword and no visible semicolons. This decides whether Odin-style `for`/`;` loop headers are worth reopening. The ballot is a proceed/reopen check so tomorrow's agents know whether to implement, document, or leave the existing design alone.
decisions.story: Hank writes a byte scanner. He wants one line to name the index, set its bounds, and say how it advances. A beginner should still understand which part starts the loop, which part stops it, and which part changes each turn.
decisions.inWild:
loop i in 0..len step 4 { scan(bytes[i]) }

loop i := 0; i < len; i += 4 { scan(bytes[i]) }

options.name: Keep range + `step` as the compact counted loop (recommended)
options.detail: Preserve the ratified shape: `loop i in start..end step n`. It already gives a one-line iterator variable, range, and increment for the common counted-loop case, without making semicolons user-visible. More complex state changes stay in the loop body where they are explicit.

options.name: Add a semicolon header under `loop`
options.detail: Keep Jet's `loop` keyword, but allow a C/Odin-style counted header: initializer; condition; afterthought. Semicolons would be legal only inside this header, not as statement separators. This gives experts compact control over non-range increments, but it creates a second counted-loop mechanism beside `loop i in range step n`.

options.name: Add a named-header form without semicolons
options.detail: Use labels inside the loop header instead of punctuation: `from`, `while`, and `step` name the same three jobs. This keeps visible semicolons out of Jet, but adds new contextual words and still overlaps with the current range form.

options.name: Expert-only counted loop marker
options.detail: Keep beginner loops unchanged and put arbitrary counted headers behind an explicit expert marker, e.g. `#Counted loop init; cond; step`. This surfaces the control when needed without making it the everyday loop form, but it is heavier and still spends semicolon syntax.

comparisons.note: One `loop` keyword; counted loops use inclusive ranges and `step`.
Initializer, condition, and afterthought share one header separated by semicolons.

decisions.bestCurrent: Jet ratified surface unless this ballot identifies a stronger beginner-safe, one-path design.
decisions.recommendation: Keep `loop i in range step n` as the compact counted-loop path (Option A). It already carries iterator, bounds, and increment in one line while preserving Jet's no-visible-semicolon rule. Option B is the direct answer if the owner wants full C/Odin header control.

log.text: Owner clarified the proposal: semicolon-separated loop header parts, not a `for` alias. Ballot rebuilt around compact counted-loop syntax.
Ballot tightened: collapsed to 3 options, Option A is the unified optimal recommendation, rec set to A.

decisions.title: Should Jet support switch/case fallthrough?
decisions.gist: Jet rejected C-style `switch`/`case` and uses multi-arm `if`. This decides whether fallthrough exists at all or grouped arms are the only path.
decisions.explainer: Jet rejected C-style `switch`/`case` and uses multi-arm `if`. This decides whether fallthrough exists at all or grouped arms are the only path. The ballot is a proceed/reopen check so tomorrow's agents know whether to implement, document, or leave the existing design alone.
decisions.story: A C programmer wants two HTTP status codes to share handling. Jet should make the shared handling obvious without hidden control flow from one arm into the next.

options.name: No fallthrough; shared handling via grouped arms (recommended)
options.detail: Jet's multi-arm if syntax (`400 | 404 -> handle_client()`) handles all cases where C fallthrough is used for shared logic — with no implicit fall-through, no hidden control flow, and exhaustiveness checked. Do not add `fallthrough`. Teaching: when a C programmer asks "how do I fall through?", the diagnostic or docs point to the grouped-arm form. This is unambiguously the safer, cleaner path.

options.name: Explicit `fallthrough` statement
options.detail: Allow an arm to jump into the next arm only when it writes `fallthrough`. Familiar to switch users who expect it, but adds a second control-flow edge (arms can now have two exits), complicates exhaustiveness analysis, and reintroduces a class of bugs (wrong arm order changes behavior silently). Only justified if a use case cannot be expressed with grouped arms — which has not been demonstrated.
options.code:
400 -> { log("client"); fallthrough }
404 -> handle_client()

options.name: Reopen `switch/case/default` with fallthrough semantics
options.detail: Bring back switch vocabulary, case arms, and optional fallthrough. Conflicts with S24/D-IF1 teaching policy, adds a third pattern-dispatch surface (I8), and brings C fallthrough's bug class back into the language. Not recommended under any circumstances — this is the pattern Jet's multi-arm if was designed to replace.

comparisons.note: Existing ratified decisions are the baseline; reopening needs a clear safety/readability win.

decisions.bestCurrent: Jet ratified surface unless this ballot identifies a stronger beginner-safe, one-path design.
decisions.recommendation: No fallthrough — grouped arms (`400 | 404 -> ...`) cover all shared-handling use cases safely (Option A). C-style fallthrough is a well-documented footgun; Jet eliminated it intentionally.

log.text: Ballot tightened: collapsed to 3 options, Option A is the unified optimal recommendation, rec set to A.

decisions.title: Does Jet need general union types or `Any`, and how should dynamic cases be served?
decisions.gist: Jet already has enums, optionals, fallible values, generics, traits, and data values. This decides whether to add a general dynamic escape or keep unions closed and explicit.
decisions.explainer: Jet already has enums, optionals, fallible values, generics, traits, and data values. This decides whether to add a general dynamic escape or keep unions closed and explicit. The ballot is a proceed/reopen check so tomorrow's agents know whether to implement, document, or leave the existing design alone.
decisions.story: A library author parses JSON and plugin messages. Some values are only known at runtime, but most app code should stay statically typed and beginner-safe.

options.name: No general `Any`; document the correct mechanism per use case (recommended)
options.detail: Jet already has: closed unions via enums (JSON parsing, plugin messages), polymorphism via traits/generics (algorithm abstraction), absence via T? and T?E, and data values (DataTree from D-SERDE2) for truly dynamic untyped trees. A general `Any` top type adds a second optional-like mechanism (I8) and a second polymorphism mechanism (I8), while weakening static guarantees for beginners. The correct path: a compiler diagnostic that recognizes "I need to hold anything" patterns and points at the right tool for the specific use case.

options.name: Closed union type syntax
options.detail: A type-level syntax for a fixed set of alternatives: `Int | String`. More compact than defining an enum for short-lived unions. Risk: overlaps with enum (I8: two ways to define closed unions), and pattern matching rules must extend to the union form. Only justified if enum definition for 2-3 variant unions is demonstrably too verbose in common code.

options.name: `Any` only at interop/dynamic-data boundaries (expert-gated)
options.detail: A boxed dynamic value (like DataTree but for arbitrary types) gated behind `use core.interop`. Required explicit downcast before use; compile error outside interop scope. The narrowest possible escape hatch for FFI/plugin/serde edges. Distinct from D (full Any): upcasting to Any requires explicit invocation; the beginner surface is untouched. Only justified if DataTree + enums provably cannot cover a critical interop use case.

comparisons.note: `any` is the default escape for JS interop and gradual migration; `unknown` is the safer closed form requiring narrowing before use.
comparisons.code:
function handle(x: any) { return x.foo }  // no error
function safe(x: unknown) { return (x as {foo: string}).foo }

comparisons.note: Pre-generics, `interface{}`/`any` was the only way to write generic containers and JSON boundaries; post-generics it shrank but never disappeared at FFI/JSON edges.
`Any`/`AnyObject` for heterogeneous collections and ObjC interop; app code is encouraged toward typed enums/protocols instead.
comparisons.code:
let items: [Any] = [1, "hi", UIView()]
let n = items[0] as? Int

comparisons.note: No std `Any` top type for years; `dyn Trait` for open polymorphism, `enum`/`serde_json::Value` for closed/dynamic data. `Box<dyn Any>` exists but is niche (type-id downcasts).
comparisons.code:
enum Value { Null, Bool(bool), Number(f64), String(String) }
// or trait objects: Box<dyn Display>

comparisons.note: `Any`/`Object` is the root of the class hierarchy — every reference type is implicitly an `Any`, which powers collections and reflection but erases static guarantees.
comparisons.code:
val list: List<Any> = listOf(1, "x")
val s = list[1] as String

comparisons.note: Dynamic trees via `Data`/`DataTree`; closed sums via enums (+ ratified `A | B` unions); open polymorphism via traits/generics; absence via `T?`; interop stays explicit.

decisions.bestCurrent: Jet ratified surface unless this ballot identifies a stronger beginner-safe, one-path design.
decisions.recommendation: No general `Any` — existing mechanisms (enums, traits, generics, T?, data values) cover all dynamic cases without a top type (Option A).

decisions.title: Keep Jet fallback control flow or add an Odin-style `or_` suite?
decisions.gist: Odin has a family of `or_` control operators; this maps each case to today's Jet and decides whether Jet needs another family.
decisions.explainer: Jet already has `?? return` for fallback/early return. This decides whether an Odin-style `or_return` spelling adds clarity or just a second way to mean it. The ballot is a proceed/reopen check so tomorrow's agents know whether to implement, document, or leave the existing design alone.
decisions.story: Mara writes a log shipper. Missing config should use a default, bad records should skip the current loop turn, a closed stream should break the loop, and startup failure should return from the function. She needs the error path to stay visible without learning four unrelated spellings.

options.name: Keep Jet's existing fallback/control suite (recommended)
options.detail: Do not add Odin-style `or_` words. Jet already covers the suite with one fallback operator plus control words: value fallback is `x ?? default`, early return is `x ?? return value`, loop break is `x ?? break`, loop continue is the ratified loop shorthand `x?continue`, and normal propagation remains `x?`. The only rough edge is documentation: the ballot now names the whole map so users are not left comparing only `or_return`.

options.name: Unify all local exits under `?? <control>`
options.detail: Keep `??` as the single fallback operator, but complete the control-word family so loop skip is `x ?? continue` instead of the special `?continue`. Then fallback, return, break, and continue all read as "use the value, or do this control action." This is the most Jet-shaped path if the current `?continue` shorthand feels like an exception.

options.name: Add explicit `or_*` keywords as teaching-only diagnostics
options.detail: Reserve/recognize `or_return`, `or_break`, `or_continue`, and `or_else` only to emit teaching errors that point at the Jet spelling. No accepted second spelling reaches formatted source. This helps Odin users migrate while preserving I8.

options.name: Accept an Odin-style `or_*` suite as real syntax
options.detail: Add `or_else`, `or_return`, `or_break`, and `or_continue` as accepted postfix forms. This is familiar to Odin users and very explicit, but it duplicates `??`, `?`, and `?continue` semantics with another family of spellings. It should only win if the owner chooses that readability over the one-path rule for error control.

comparisons.note: Uses `or_`-style postfix control helpers around optional/error-returning operations.
`??` is the fallback operator; `?` propagates; loop skip has ratified `?continue`.
comparisons.code:
value :: parse(raw)?continue
other :: parse(raw) ?? return fallback

decisions.bestCurrent: Jet ratified surface unless this ballot identifies a stronger beginner-safe, one-path design.
decisions.recommendation: Keep Jet's existing suite (Option A): it covers fallback, return, break, continue, and propagation without adding a second family. If the `?continue` exception bothers us, Option B is the cohesive Jet-shaped amendment.

log.text: Owner asked for the whole Odin-style `or_` suite; ballot expanded to map fallback/return/break/continue/propagation and added cohesive Jet alternatives.
Ballot tightened: collapsed to 3 options, Option A is the unified optimal recommendation, rec set to A.

decisions.title: Retire S25 `||` comparison-distribution shorthand?
decisions.gist: Ratify that `||` no longer distributes comparisons; comparator value alternatives use single `|` (`x == 1 | 2`) in arm heads, while `&&`/`||`/`==`/`!=` remain boolean arm conditions.
decisions.explainer:
S25 was ratified on 2026-06-11 as “comparison distribution”: inside a boolean chain, a bare value to the right of a comparison reused the nearest comparison on its left. The old spelling used boolean operators, e.g. `status == 400 || 404` meant `status == 400 || status == 404`. This ballot retires that `||`/`&&` distribution rule.

Ratified shape: single `|` is the value/pattern-alternative separator against the comparator, e.g. `status == 400 | 404 ->` in an arm head. `||` and `&&` do not distribute comparisons; they combine full boolean expressions/guards. `==` and `!=` remain explicit boolean comparisons/guards in arm heads.
decisions.story: A reader sees `status == 400 || 404` and should not have to know that `404` secretly reuses `status ==`. Retiring S25 makes `||` a boolean operator only. The compact comparator-alternate form is still available where Jet pattern matching lives: `status == 400 | 404 ->` or, under an inferred comparator, `400 | 404 ->`.

options.name: Retire S25 `||` distribution (recommended)
options.detail: Delete comparison distribution from `||`/`&&`. Write full boolean comparisons in ordinary expressions. Keep single `|` for value/pattern alternatives against the comparator in arm heads, and keep `&&`/`||`/`==`/`!=` as boolean condition syntax inside arm heads.

options.name: Keep S25 expression shorthand
options.detail: Allow bare values in `||`/`&&` chains to reuse the nearest comparison. Compact, but `||`/`&&` would carry a Jet-only value-distribution rule instead of being boolean-only. Arm `|` alternatives and arm boolean guards still stay exactly as described above.

options.name: Retire S25 and design membership later
options.detail: Remove S25 `||`/`&&` distribution now, then separately decide whether Jet needs `in`/set/range membership sugar for common equality lists. This still preserves arm `|` alternatives and arm boolean guards.

comparisons.note: D-MATCHARM1/2 uses single `|` for alternatives against the comparator in arm heads and `&&`/`||`/`==`/`!=` for boolean arm conditions; retiring S25 keeps that compact arm syntax but removes hidden comparison reuse from `||`/`&&`.
Boolean operators combine Bool expressions only; repeated comparisons are explicit unless a separate membership operator exists.

decisions.comment: Owner ratified: retire S25 `||`/`&&` comparison distribution; comparator alternatives are single `|` (`x == 1 | 2`), not `||`.

log.text: Owner ratified A and clarified comparator alternatives are `x == 1 | 2`, not `x == 1 || 2`.
Clarified scope: ballot only retires ordinary-expression S25 shorthand; arm `|` alternatives and `&&`/`||`/`==`/`!=` boolean arm conditions are explicit non-goals.
Reopened: agent incorrectly ratified after answering owner question; owner had not selected an option.
Question answered and ballot expanded: S25 defined as comparison distribution with before/after examples.

decisions.title: Counted loop separator: what replaces semicolons?
decisions.gist: D-LOOP-SEMICOLON1=C retired semicolons from counted loop headers; pick the replacement separator.
decisions.explainer: D-LOOP-SEMICOLON1=C kept compact counted loops but deferred the separator choice. The ratified S6-R law bans visible semicolons; we need a different separator for the three-part header (init; condition; afterthought).
decisions.story: Gerald is porting a tight inner loop from C and wants the three-part form. He knows Jet has no semicolons, so he needs to know exactly what punctuation to type between the init, condition, and step.

comparisons.note: Semicolons in for-loop header
Semicolons in for-loop header
No three-part for; use while
comparisons.code: var i = 0; while i < n { i += 1 }

options.name: Comma separator (recommended)
options.detail: Use commas between the three parts. Commas already appear in function call arguments and tuple construction; reusing them here keeps the punctuation vocabulary small. The header reads left-to-right with natural pauses.
options.code:
loop i := 0, i < n, i += 1 { process(buf[i]) }
loop i := len, i > 0, i -= 1 { drain(q[i]) }

options.name: Keyword separators (while/step)
options.detail: Use keywords: . Self-documenting but verbose; adds two reserved words or repurposes existing ones.
options.code: loop i := 0 while i < n step i += 1 { process(buf[i]) }

options.name: Retire three-part form entirely
options.detail: Remove the three-part header. All counted loops use range iteration  or manual . Porting C loops requires rewriting them as range loops.

log.text: Raised as follow-up to D-LOOP-SEMICOLON1=C (redesign counted loop separator).
Closed as superseded — D-LOOP-SEMICOLON1 reversed to A (keep semicolons).

decisions.comment: Superseded: D-LOOP-SEMICOLON1 reversed to A — semicolons stay. No separator redesign needed.

jet doc

Documentation is integrated with the package toolchain.

decisions.title: Add C-style ++/-- increment and decrement operators?
decisions.gist: Jet already increments with `x += 1`. Should Jet also accept `++x`, `x++`, `--x`, and `x--` on mutable integers?
decisions.explainer: S17 ratified compound assignment (`+=`, `-=`, …) as the update-operator family. The owner asked for C-style `++`/`--`. Under I8 there should be one mechanical path — unless the owner explicitly chooses familiarity over uniformity on this site. The ballot covers full C semantics, permanent rejection, and three partial shapes (postfix-only, prefix-only, statement-only). Operand policy mirrors S17: mutable `var`, `mut` parameters, `self.field` on `mut self`, and index sites; integer types only (trap-on-overflow per D-NUMOPS2). No user-defined operator overloading.
decisions.story: Carla is porting a C sprite engine. Her game loop has `tick++` and `while (--lives > 0)` scattered through the original. She wants Jet to accept the same tokens so she can translate line-for-line, but she also wants beginners reading her code to understand what changed.

options.name: Full C-style ++/-- on mutable integer lvalues (pre + post)
options.detail: All four forms. Prefix returns the new value; postfix returns the old value. Operand must be a mutable integer lvalue (same LHS policy as S17). Applies to `Int` and sized integer widths; not `Float`. Overflow traps like `+= 1` (D-NUMOPS2). Gives C/C++ transliteration fidelity; spends a second increment spelling (I8 tension).

options.name: Reject ++/-- forever — keep `+= 1` / `-= 1` only (recommended)
options.detail: No increment/decrement operators. S17 compound assignment is the single canonical update path (I8). Matches Rust, Swift, Zig, Go, and Python. Users coming from C see a teaching error pointing at `+= 1`. Owner request is satisfied by documenting the transliteration table in the cookbook, not new syntax.

options.name: Postfix only (`x++`, `x--`) — no prefix forms
options.detail: Only postfix increment/decrement. Value of `x++` is discarded (statement form) or typed as `Void` — no old-value expression semantics. Covers the most common C loop idiom (`i++` at end of body) without prefix `--lives` in conditions. Still a second path beside `+= 1` but avoids prefix/precedence puzzles in conditions.

options.name: Prefix only (`++x`, `--x`) — no postfix forms
options.detail: Only prefix forms; they return the updated value (usable in expressions). Matches the `--lives > 0` condition pattern and `++it` iterator style. No postfix old-value trap. Rejects `tick++` at statement end — users write `tick += 1` or `++tick` there.

options.name: Statement-position only — both pre and post, never inside expressions
options.detail: Lexer/parser accept `++x`, `x++`, `--x`, `x--` only as standalone statements (or loop-header afterthought if D-LOOP-SURFACE B is extended). Using them where a value is expected is an error. Cuts the classic footgun (`arr[i] = i++`) while still letting Carla write familiar statement lines. Expression increment stays `+= 1`.

comparisons.note: Full four-form family; prefix/postfix differ in expression value. Decades of familiarity; also decades of postfix confusion.
No `++`/`--`. Updates use `+= 1`, `-= 1`, or `+=` with any step. Deliberate removal from C lineage.
No `++`/`--` (removed in Swift 3). `+= 1` / `-= 1` only.

decisions.recommendation: Reject `++`/`--` (Option B). S17 already owns increment/decrement; adding C operators duplicates that job and reintroduces prefix/postfix value semantics beginners stumble on. Choose A only if C transliteration ergonomics outweigh I8 on this site.

log.text: Ballot raised from increment-operators.md plan. Five options: full C-style, reject, postfix-only, prefix-only, statement-only. Rec B on I8 + beginner clarity.

decisions.title: Should methods be ordinary functions or macro-like rewrite hooks?
decisions.gist: Methods stay ordinary functions; the two things people actually love about Jai macro-methods — guaranteed inlining and DSL power — get honest homes: @Inline contracts now, E4 metaprogramming later.
decisions.explainer: Jet already ratifies methods as one structural placement for functions: inline, impl block, or external `fn Type.method(self)` all mean the same program. Treating methods as macros would blur call semantics, make refactoring up/down the hierarchy less predictable, and conflict with R11 source-fragment re-entry. The useful Jai insight is not “every method is a macro”; it is that refactoring should preserve shape and that library hooks should feel direct where the compiler blesses them.
decisions.story: Carla moves `Player.heal` from inside `struct Player` to an external method so her gameplay file reads top-down. She needs the call `p.heal(10)` to keep meaning exactly the same thing, not start participating in code rewriting because the method moved.
decisions.detail: Reworked 2026-07-01: the original options only gatekept. What Jai users love is (1) zero-cost abstraction they can TRUST (macros inline by construction) and (2) DSL authoring power. (1) translates as inline contracts: @Inline is a checked promise — if the compiler cannot inline, that is a compile error, not a silent regression; jet expand --facts inline shows every decision. (2) is real but belongs in E4 where expansion is auditable through the derive/build-message machinery — deferring it there routes the desire instead of killing it. Macro methods in v1 would make every call non-local and poison tooling.

options.name: Ordinary methods + checked @Inline / @InlineAlways contracts (recommended)
options.detail: The performance kernel of macro-methods without macro semantics. @InlineAlways failing to inline is a compile error naming why. Blessed hooks (Iterable/Index/Display) stay sema-owned traits.

options.name: Document the closed compiler-hook set only
options.detail: Iterable, Index, IndexMut, Display power syntax; nothing else does. Mostly current law; adds no answer for the perf-trust kernel.
options.code: impl Store.Iterable { fn iter(self) -> It { ... } }

options.name: Macro methods (call-rewrite hooks) in v1
options.detail: A method can receive syntax and emit source. Non-local call semantics, tooling blind spots; the power is E4’s to deliver auditable-y.
options.code: macro fn query(self, block) -> Source { ... }   // E4 question

comparisons.note: Jai exposes broad compile-time execution and compiler message loops. It is powerful and fast for game/tool authors, but trusts project code heavily.
comparisons.code:
#run build_tables();
#modify Some_Type { /* compiler message loop territory */ }

comparisons.note: Rust keeps methods and macros separate. Proc macros generate tokens that the compiler parses and checks again.

decisions.title: What symbol family owns metadata, compiler control, and comptime splices?
decisions.gist: Two planes with an eye-checkable law: @ states a contract on the declaration below; # instructs the compiler (modes, items, effects, quantities, queries); $ stays splice-only.
decisions.explainer: The question is not which sigil is easier to type — it is whether a reader can tell, from the first character, what kind of statement they are looking at. The v5 proposal (docs/reference/syntax-comparison-proposal.md) draws a line a reader can check by eye: @ only ever precedes a declaration and states a checkable contract about it (@Pure, @MustUse, @Codable, @Pub); # never states a contract — it changes what compiles, when it runs, what is legal, or supplies a compile-time value (#Unsafe, #Comptime, #Test, #(Fs), [T#N], pkg#1.2.3, #Caller()). $ remains the splice sigil inside generated Jet only.
decisions.story: Maya is exploring Jet in the LSP. She types `#` before a function and expects completions for tests, safety gates, FFI, purity, and build markers. She types `$` inside an expression and expects compile-time values, not another attribute namespace.
decisions.detail: Reworked 2026-07-01 after owner signaled comfort with @-attributes/#-directives (C++ framing). The line resolves every fuzzy case mechanically: @MustUse is a contract on callers, #Suppress changes legality in a scope; @Codable is a capability contract (derivation is implementation), #Derive is generation machinery you write; #Unsafe stays a directive even on items because it changes what is legal inside the body. Bonus: # stays rare and loud — #Unsafe/#Comptime scream instead of drowning in visibility/encoding markers. Tradition backs both instincts as-is: C’s #include/#pragma = machine instructions; Java/C#/Python @ = annotation on the declaration below. Grep law: rg '@\w' = every contract, rg '#\w' = every compiler instruction. Casing (PascalCase per D-CASING1 vs the v5 doc’s lowercase) is a separate knob — examples here keep the ratified PascalCase. Full worked law: proposal doc Sigil Law section + decision card D-META-PLANE.

options.name: One marker family: # for everything, $ splice
options.detail: One sigil to learn and grep; but # appears on every pub/codable item, diluting the alarm value of #Unsafe/#Comptime, and the attribute-vs-instruction distinction the reader still needs is no longer visible.

options.name: @ contracts / # directives / $ splices (recommended)
options.detail: The eye-checkable law: @ promises, # permits/controls. @ never appears inside a type or expression; # can (#(Fs), [T#N], #Caller()). ~ stays reserved.

options.name: $ as the compiler/comptime marker family
options.detail: Collapses "compute here" and "mark this item" into one sigil — the overload this whole family exists to avoid.
options.code: $Test "routing" { ... }   // and $name still a splice — muddled

comparisons.note: Jai leans on `#` directives for compile-time and compiler features.
Zig uses `@` for compiler builtins and `comptime` as a keyword. Search is good, but `@` becomes a second namespace every user must learn.
Rust uses `#[]` attributes; macros use `!`, creating a visible split between metadata and expansion.

decisions.title: Casing of the new @ contract plane: PascalCase like # markers, or lowercase?
decisions.gist: D-MARKER-FAMILY1 gave contracts the @ sigil but left casing open: @Pure/@Pre/@Persist or @pure/@pre/@persist. D-CASING1 mandated PascalCase for # markers only.
decisions.explainer: This batch itself is split: D-MARKER-FAMILY1 own examples are PascalCase (@Pure, @MustUse, @Codable — they are today PascalCase # markers moving over), but D-PREPOST1 (@pre/@post), D-PERSIST1 (@persist) and D-CAPBUNDLE1 (@numeric, @comparable, @printable, @codable_as_base) were ratified with lowercase spellings. Nothing can be implemented or renamed until one rule exists.
decisions.story: Walter writes his first contract. He knows #Test and #MustUse are PascalCase, so he types @Pre(amount > 0). If the plane is lowercase he gets an unknown-marker error on the spelling every # marker taught him.

options.name: PascalCase everywhere (recommended)
options.detail: Extend the D-CASING1 law to the @ plane: @Pure, @MustUse, @Codable, @Pre, @Post, @Persist, @Numeric, @Comparable, @Printable, @CodableAsBase. One casing rule for every marker in the language; markers moving from # keep their exact spelling.

options.name: Lowercase @ plane
options.detail: Contracts read as quiet prose annotations, visually distinct from SHOUTING # directives: @pure, @pre, @persist, @numeric. Cost: #Pure becomes @pure on the move — a rename AND a recase; two casing rules live forever.

options.name: Split: PascalCase derives, lowercase clauses
options.detail: @Codable/@Pure stay PascalCase (they name a capability), clause-like contracts with arguments go lowercase (@pre/@post). Matches how this batch was literally ratified; costs a judgment call per marker forever.

decisions.title: Which existing # markers move to the @ contract plane?
decisions.gist: D-MARKER-FAMILY1 states the law (@ = contract, # = directive) but only names three examples. This ballot fixes the exact move list so agents never guess per marker.
decisions.explainer: Clear moves under the law: #Pure, #MustUse, #Codable/#Encode/#Decode, and the maturity tags #Experimental/#Tested/#Hardened all state declaration promises. Clear stays: #Unsafe, #Test, #Bench, #Ref(Label), #Grant, #Target/#Js/#Wasm, #Extern/#Bindgen, #Uninit, #UnitFamily, #Layout (directives — the ballot names #Unsafe/#Test/#Ref itself). Genuinely ambiguous, needing your call: #Numeric (overlaps the new @numeric bundle from D-CAPBUNDLE1 — same job, two spellings unless merged), #PublishedSchema (a promise that also triggers snapshot machinery), #Redact (a promise about debug output that also drives codegen), and the serde field markers #Rename/#Skip/#Default/#Flatten (wire-format configuration, closer to generation machinery than contract).
decisions.story: Doris reviews a struct with #Codable, #Numeric, #Redact and #Rename("id") on it. Under the new law she should be able to read at a glance which are promises and which are compiler instructions — but only if every marker actually sits on its correct plane.

options.name: Minimal: only the three named families move
options.detail: #Pure -> @Pure, #MustUse -> @MustUse, #Codable/#Encode/#Decode -> @ plane. Everything else stays # until individually reopened. Smallest migration; leaves the maturity tags and #Numeric stating promises from the wrong plane.

options.name: Full application of the law (recommended)
options.detail: A plus: maturity tags -> @, #PublishedSchema -> @, #Redact -> @, and #Numeric merges into the D-CAPBUNDLE1 @numeric bundle (one mechanism, resolves that ballot open overlap). Serde field markers stay # (wire-format machinery, not promises). Every marker sits on its lawful plane; one migration pass, teaching errors on every old spelling.

options.name: Forward-only: nothing moves
options.detail: The @ plane starts with only the newly ratified markers (@pre/@post/@persist/bundles). Existing # markers keep their spellings; migration deferred to a later epoch sweep. Zero churn now; the law is immediately false for #Pure/#MustUse/#Codable — the ballot own canonical examples.

decisions.title: #Pure moved to @Pure — but #Pure also lives in TYPE position (callback bounds). What happens there?
decisions.gist: The @ plane law says @ only precedes declarations. `#Pure fn(Int) -> Int` is a live callback-type bound inside types, where @ never goes. The move list says Pure moves; the law says @ can’t go where #Pure lives.
decisions.explainer: D-MARKER-FAMILY1=B ratified: @ states a checkable promise and may only precede a declaration. D-MARKERMOVE1=B moved Pure to the @ plane. Neither addressed Parser/Types.rs:361: a function TYPE may be written `#Pure fn(T) -> U` to require a pure callback. Planning found the gap; parser work on the plane migration is gated on this answer.
decisions.story: Dot writes a numerics library and wants map() to accept only pure callbacks. She declares her own functions with @Pure now. When she writes the parameter type for map(), does the bound spell #Pure (old plane), @Pure (breaking the declarations-only law), or something else?
decisions.inWild:
fn map(items: [Int], f: #Pure fn(Int) -> Int) -> [Int] { ... }   // today

@Pure
fn double(x: Int) -> Int { x * 2 }   // after the move

map(nums, double)   // the bound and the declaration should visibly match
decisions.detail: Raised as gate G1 in docs/plans/epoch-3/marker-family.md. Blocking: parser work on the @ plane cannot start until the type-position surface is fixed.

options.name: Position split: @Pure on declarations, #Pure stays on callback-type bounds (recommended)
options.detail: The law stays exact: @ precedes declarations only. The type-position bound keeps its # spelling as wire-in machinery. Cost: one concept, two spellings, chosen by position — a taught rule, softened because you READ them in different places.

options.name: One spelling: @Pure allowed in the single type-position bound slot
options.detail: The law gains one carve-out: a contract marker may prefix a function TYPE to state a bound. One spelling everywhere Pure appears; the "declarations only" law becomes "declarations, plus contract bounds on function types".

options.name: Retire the type-position bound; purity is required at the parameter declaration
options.detail: No marker inside types at all. The parameter is itself a declaration, so the contract plane can annotate it. Grammar stays smallest; the bound moves left of the name instead of inside the type.

decisions.title: Which plane owns the remaining derive markers: #[Debug], #[Summarize], #[Comparable], user derives like #[Wire]?
decisions.gist: D-MARKERMOVE1=B moved only Codable/Encode/Decode among derive markers. The rest were not named. Default reading: they stay # (generation machinery, not promises) — confirm or move them.
decisions.explainer: The ratified two-plane law: @ states a checkable promise about the declaration; # is compiler machinery/directives. Codable moved because "this type round-trips" is a promise. #[Debug]/#[Summarize]/#[Comparable] and user derives (derive T.Wire bodies) generate code — the MARKERMOVE1 ballot itself frames user derives as directive machinery. Unaddressed, so the plane migration ships with a documented default that needs ratifying.
decisions.story: Walter just learned @Codable is a promise-plane contract. He types @Debug on his struct by analogy and gets a teaching error pointing back to #[Debug]. Is that the language he was promised, or should Debug have moved with Codable?
decisions.detail: Raised as gate G3 in docs/plans/epoch-3/marker-family.md. Non-blocking: the migration ships with the default (stay #) either way; this ballot ratifies or reverses it.

options.name: They stay # — derives are generation machinery (recommended)
options.detail: Only the three ratified movers (Codable/Encode/Decode) live on @. Everything that exists to GENERATE code, including all user derives, is # machinery. One teachable line: "@ promises, # generates."

options.name: All built-in derive markers move to @; user derives stay #
options.detail: Built-ins read as capability promises (@Debug = "this type is printable for debugging"). User derives stay machinery. Cost: the built-in/user line becomes the plane line — two kinds of derive spelling forever.

options.name: Case-by-case: promise-like derives move, mechanical ones stay
options.detail: Judgment call per marker (Comparable moves, Debug stays?). Maximal nuance, permanent ambiguity for every future derive.

decisions.comment: ALL derive markers INCLUDING USER DERIVES use @ - separation is ridiculous and defeats the purpose of separating anything at all. Use @ for all derive markers

decisions.title: What should the first-party CLI flag API look like?
decisions.gist: CLI args become the entry function’s typed signature: fn run(args: ServeArgs) — flags derived from fields, help generated from docs, subcommands are an enum. Zero parse ceremony, Go-flag simplicity kept.
decisions.explainer: What people love about Go’s flag package is that a small tool needs no framework: declare, run, get --help. Jet can beat it: the entry function already has a signature — let it take a typed args struct. Field names become flags, defaults become defaults, doc attributes become help text, an enum parameter becomes subcommands. The parser, help, completion, and man page all derive from the one struct the program was going to define anyway.
decisions.story: Nora writes a one-file asset packer. She wants `--input`, `--out`, and `--fast` parsed with good help text, and she wants tests to pass synthetic argv without mutating global process state.
decisions.detail: Reworked 2026-07-01: integrates the lifecycle-verbs proposal (jet <verb> -> fn <verb>(), syntax-comparison-proposal.md §36A / D-BUILDENTRY1). fn run() stays zero-arg for hello-world; adding a typed parameter opts into CLI parsing — magic default, one step to full control. Machinery is the same derive/reflection layer as Codable, no new syntax. Bad-flag errors are Jet diagnostics with what/why/fix. The explicit builder remains as the library floor for non-entry parsing (REPLs, plugins) — option A generates down onto it.

options.name: Typed entry signature: fn run(args: ServeArgs) (recommended)
options.detail: Flags from fields, help from @Doc, subcommands from an enum parameter. Hello-world keeps zero-arg fn run().

options.name: @[Cli] struct + explicit parse call
options.detail: Same derive, manual wiring: args :: cli.parse<ServeArgs>(io.args())?. Ships anyway as the layer under A; as the ONLY surface it keeps ceremony Go users came to avoid.
options.code: args :: cli.parse<ServeArgs>(io.args())?

options.name: Builder API only (status quo)
options.detail: args.spec().flag("verbose", ...) — works, stringly, help text drifts from the code that reads the values.
options.code: spec :: args.spec().flag("verbose", "print extra detail")

comparisons.note: The stdlib flag package is tiny and predictable, but global registration can make larger CLIs awkward.
Derive-based CLI parsing gives excellent UX but uses macro-heavy generated code.

decisions.title: Should Jet add a Jai-style `Any` for expert reflection boundaries?
decisions.gist: No top type — but deliver what Any is actually USED for: heterogeneous varargs over a trait (...Renderable) so anyone can write print-like functions, plus reflect/Data handles for tooling.
decisions.explainer: In real Jai code, Any overwhelmingly serves one need: writing your own print/log/assert that accepts anything displayable. Jet already covers consumption via interpolation. The missing piece is authorship: a variadic parameter constrained by a trait — parts: ...Renderable — where each argument is monomorphized at the call site. Full static typing, no boxing, no top type, and the print-like function is three lines.
decisions.story: Owen writes an inspector panel for game entities. He wants to show arbitrary field values in tooling, but his gameplay APIs should still say `Health`, `Position`, or `Inventory`, not `Any`.
decisions.detail: Reworked 2026-07-01: the original options only said no. The kernel is trait-bounded heterogeneous varargs: each call site compiles a shape-specialized body (same machinery as generics), so log_all("sev ", 3, incident) type-checks every argument against Renderable and fails with a teaching error naming the odd one out. Tooling/serialization keeps reflect.Value + Data (option B’s handle, now folded in as the expert floor rather than a rival). General Any stays rejected — D-DYNAMIC-TYPE1 stands.

options.name: Trait-bounded heterogeneous varargs + reflect handles (recommended)
options.detail: parts: ...Renderable monomorphizes per call site. Statically checked, zero boxing. reflect.Value/Data remain the tooling floor.

options.name: Expert core.reflect.Any handle only
options.detail: Library type carrying type info + value for reflection internals; construction gated behind reflection APIs. Covers tooling, not the print-authorship kernel.
options.code:
v :: reflect.value_of(incident)
print(v.type_name())

options.name: General Any top type
options.detail: Every value flows into Any. Repeats what D-DYNAMIC-TYPE1 closed; weakens the whole type system for one convenience.
options.code: fn log_all(parts: ...Any) { ... }

comparisons.note: Any is a type-info pointer plus value pointer. Useful for tooling/reflection, but weakens static guarantees if ordinary APIs accept it.
`Any` exists, but serious APIs prefer protocols/generics/enums to recover static meaning.

decisions.comment: Can we do A & B? also for A, we should be able to bind groups of traits, right? So we can require a specific set, not just one?

decisions.title: Should Jet adopt Jai-style dynamic-array type syntax?
decisions.gist: Keep [T] / [K,V] / [T#N] — but the real Jai kernel is the view/owning distinction: plan a labeled zero-copy View<T> riding the stored-ref machinery, instead of a second bracket spelling.
decisions.explainer: Jai’s [..]T reads well there because Jai has several array kinds to tell apart. Jet’s list family is already one-spelling-per-kind. What Jai users actually miss in Jet is not the bracket — it is the cheap non-owning VIEW: slicing without copying. Jet slices are inclusive copies by beginner law (safe, no dangling); the expert tier needs a real view type whose owner relationship the compiler tracks.
decisions.story: Iris ports a Jai particle system. She sees `particles: [..]$Particle` and asks for the Jet equivalent. The safest answer is a direct transliteration table, not new syntax.
decisions.inWild:
particles: [Particle] := []
particles.push(Particle.{ pos: .{0, 0}, vel: .{1, 0} })

ids: [Int#128] := fixed_ids()
decisions.detail: Reworked 2026-07-01: option A now carries a plan instead of a bare no. View<T> is a library type over the stored-reference machinery (D-REF-SHORTHAND1 labels/inference): window :: incidents.view(0..9) is zero-copy, compiler tracks that it borrows from incidents, and the expand lens distinguishes copy-slices from views in hot loops. Beginner law unchanged: [a..b] copies. Bracket spelling [..]T stays rejected — .. already means inclusive range/step, $ means splice, and a second dynamic-list spelling violates I8.

options.name: Keep the family; add zero-copy View<T> on stored-ref machinery (recommended)
options.detail: One spelling per collection kind. Views are the expert zero-copy tier with tracked owners; copy-slices stay the safe default.
options.code:
head :: incidents[0..9]              // beginner law: inclusive copy
window :: incidents.view(0..9)        // expert: zero-copy, owner tracked
sum :: window.fold(0, (a, i) => a + i.severity)

options.name: Add [..]T as a dynamic-list spelling
options.detail: Jai familiarity; duplicate semantics for [T], visual collision with ranges and splices.
options.code: ids: [..]String = []

options.name: Reserve [..]T for future slice/view syntax
options.detail: Keeps the option open; but if View<T> as a library type suffices, reserved grammar is a promise nobody needs.
options.code: // reserved, unused

comparisons.note: Dynamic-array type uses a compact bracket marker distinct from fixed arrays.
Slices are `[]T`; fixed arrays are `[N]T`; capacity-owning collections are library types.
comparisons.code:
var slice: []u8 = buffer[0..];
var fixed: [16]u8 = undefined;

decisions.title: Should Jet add a Jai-style `shift` primitive for stream parsers?
decisions.gist: The shift kernel — linear consume-from-front parsing — lands as core.binary.Reader with ?-composed methods, plus parse-pattern take for text (D-PARSESTR1). No new operator, full autocomplete and bounds diagnostics.
decisions.explainer: What makes Jai shift-style parsers pleasant is that a parser reads top-to-bottom in consumption order with no index bookkeeping. That is a cursor API shape, not an operator: a Reader owns position, every read advances, every read is fallible with ?. For text, the same motion composes with string parse patterns: cursor.take_pattern("inc-{id:Int} ")? consumes and binds in one line.
decisions.story: Sam writes a binary asset loader. He wants compact code that consumes a header, count, and payload from a byte buffer without hand-managing indices.
decisions.inWild:
cursor := bytes.cursor()
magic :: cursor.read_u32_le()?
count :: cursor.read_u16_le()?
items :: cursor.take(count)?
decisions.detail: Reworked 2026-07-01: option A upgraded from "methods if needed" to a designed core surface: binary.Reader (u8/u16/u32/u64 le/be, take(n), remaining, at_end) and text.Cursor (take_pattern, take_until, skip_ws), all fallible, all ?-composed — the linear read shape with bounds failures surfacing as ordinary Jet errors, not hidden truncation. Integrates D-PARSESTR1 (c8syntaxwave): one pattern syntax serves matching AND consuming. A shift operator stays rejected: domain punctuation for one idiom, hides failure behavior.

options.name: core.binary.Reader + text.Cursor with parse-pattern take (recommended)
options.detail: Consumption-ordered, fallible, discoverable. One pattern syntax shared with D-PARSESTR1.
options.code:
r :: binary.Reader.over(packet)
magic :: r.u32_be()?
len :: r.u16_be()?
body :: r.take(len)?

c :: text.Cursor.over(line)
c.take_pattern("inc-{id:Int} sev {sev:Int}")?
escalate(id, sev)

options.name: Builtin generic shift<T>(cursor) helper
options.detail: One blessed function instead of a designed surface; still needs the Reader type underneath, so it is A minus the API design.
options.code: magic :: shift<U32>(r)?

options.name: New shift operator/keyword
options.detail: Most compact, least general; syntax for one idiom, failure behavior hidden in punctuation.
options.code: magic :: r >> U32   // rejected shape

comparisons.note: Shift-style helpers make parsers compact by advancing a pointer/cursor as data is read.
Byte readers usually expose methods that advance internal position and return Results.

decisions.title: Should Jet support compact pointer-cast/deref chains like Jai?
decisions.gist: Keep casts and deref explicit inside `#Unsafe`; add docs for the Jai transliteration.
decisions.explainer: The Jai expression means: take a stored untyped pointer, cast it to pointer-to-bool, then dereference it. Jet already has raw pointer `*T` and postfix `p.*` under `#Unsafe`. The question is whether to add a compact cast/deref chain for reflection internals. Safety priority says no: every untyped pointer cast should be loud and gated.
decisions.story: Priya is implementing a debugger variable editor. A reflected slot tells her a field is Bool and gives a raw pointer. She needs to set the field, but only in audited tooling code.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: Jai’s chain is very readable to experts once learned and great in metaprogramming code. In Jet, the same compactness would normalize untyped pointer mutation. Keep it explicit, and make reflection APIs provide typed setters where possible so most code never casts.

options.name: Explicit cast + postfix deref inside `#Unsafe` (recommended)
options.detail: Current low-level model. Add docs/examples, not syntax.

options.name: Typed reflection setter API
options.detail: Avoid pointer syntax at call site; reflection library checks type before mutation.
options.code: slot.set_bool(true)?

options.name: Jai-style cast/deref chain
options.detail: Compact expert syntax, but hides two unsafe operations in one expression.
options.code: slot.value_pointer.(*Bool).* = true

comparisons.note: Type-info + pointer casts can be compact and expressive for reflection internals.
Raw pointer casts and dereferences are inside explicit unsafe blocks.

decisions.title: Does core.mem gain a `cast_ptr<T>` primitive (the ratified pointer-chain example uses one)?
decisions.gist: D-POINTERCHAIN1=A's worked example calls mem.cast_ptr<Bool>(...) — an API that does not exist in core.mem today. Confirm the addition (name + gating) or point at an existing cast.
decisions.explainer: The ratified option showed Jet's answer to Jai's `slot.value_pointer.(*bool).*` using an explicit, `#Unsafe`-gated cast step spelled mem.cast_ptr<T>. core.mem has no such function; nothing else currently does typed raw-pointer reinterpretation. Shipping the ratified example requires either adding the primitive (I1: only usable inside `#Unsafe("reason")` regions) or re-spelling the example onto an existing mechanism.
decisions.story: Frank ports a Jai interop layer. He reaches the reinterpret step, greps core.mem docs for cast, and either finds cast_ptr with a clear unsafe-gate error when used outside a gate — or finds nothing and stalls.
decisions.detail: Raised from docs/plans/epoch-3/jai-adoptions.md ambiguity 5. Blocking only the pointer-chain example/doc deliverable; nothing else rides it.

options.name: Add mem.cast_ptr<T>, #Unsafe-gated (recommended)
options.detail: The primitive the ratified example already teaches. Registered in core.mem beside rawptr machinery; calling it outside an #Unsafe region is the standard gate error; golden example under lowlevel/.
options.code: flag_ptr :: mem.cast_ptr<Bool>(raw)   // only inside #Unsafe("…") { }

options.name: Re-spell the example onto existing rawptr machinery
options.detail: If an existing cast (e.g. rawptr reinterpret via read-as) already covers it, the ratified example text is corrected to that spelling and no API is added. Only valid if the existing path truly exists — verify before choosing.
options.code: flag :: raw.read_as<Bool>()   // hypothetical existing spelling — verify first

comparisons.note: ptr::cast<T> is safe to form, unsafe to deref — Jet gates the whole region instead.

decisions.title: What spelling should visible uninitialized storage use?
decisions.gist: New option D: a lowercase `uninit` keyword in the initializer slot — bytes: [U8#1024] := uninit. Reads plainly, greps exactly, no punctuation soup; sema proves write-before-read regardless of spelling.
decisions.explainer: Visible uninitialized storage is a statement about the VALUE slot: "the initializer is: nothing yet." The most honest spelling puts that statement where the initializer goes. A keyword literal `uninit` is Jai’s --- with the mystery removed: newcomers read it aloud, rg 'uninit' finds every site, and the checker’s job (every path writes before any path reads) is identical under every option.
decisions.story: Leah fills a fixed buffer from a device packet. She needs storage before all fields are known, but she wants the compiler to reject any read before assignment.
decisions.inWild:
#Uninit header: PacketHeader
header.magic = cursor.read_u32_le()?
header.len = cursor.read_u16_le()?
process(header)
decisions.detail: Reworked 2026-07-01: added option D and moved the recommendation to it. Against A (#Uninit/@Uninit marker): a marker states a contract about the DECLARATION, but uninit-ness is a property of the initializer — the attribute plane is the wrong plane, and the marker line separates the fact from the = it modifies. Against B (---): visual noise beside ->, --, -=, ranges; unreadable aloud; muscle memory is the only argument. Against C (Uninit<T>): type-level wrapper for a value-slot fact, infects signatures. D maps 1:1 for Jai users (--- -> uninit), costs one contextual keyword legal only in initializer position.

options.name: @Uninit marker on the binding
options.detail: Searchable and marker-consistent, but states a value-slot fact on the declaration line — wrong plane, and the fact sits away from the = it modifies.
options.code:
@Uninit bytes: [U8#1024]
bytes[0] = 1

options.name: Jai-style := ---
options.detail: Compact, Jai muscle memory; punctuation with no pronunciation, visually adjacent to ->, --, -=, ranges.

options.name: Library wrapper Uninit<T>
options.detail: Explicit but infects types and signatures with a storage-state detail.
options.code: bytes: Uninit<[U8#1024]> := Uninit.new()

options.name: Contextual keyword: := uninit (recommended)
options.detail: The initializer says "nothing yet" in a word. Greppable, teachable, legal only in initializer position; checker proves write-before-read, reads of possibly-uninit slots are compile errors.

comparisons.note: `---` means intentionally uninitialized. Very terse, but punctuation-heavy.
`undefined` is explicit but keyword-like and can leak into ordinary code.
`MaybeUninit<T>` is library-explicit and unsafe to assume initialized.

decisions.title: Should stored-reference fields use `#Ref(Label)` or capability-style `~Type`?
decisions.gist: Middle path the ballot lacked: stored refs spell &T like every other shared borrow, the owner label is INFERRED when unambiguous, and @Ref(label) is required only to disambiguate — beginner-short, expert-precise.
decisions.explainer: The binder note asked: why is #Ref(Label) so long? Because diagnostics need to know WHOSE storage the field borrows. But that label is only informative when there are multiple candidate owners. In the common case — one owner in the construction context — the compiler can infer it, and field: &Incident is both short and honest: & already means shared borrow at call sites; a stored & extends the same word to fields. Unlike ~ (write authority) nothing is conflated.
decisions.story: Earl stores token text as a view into an arena-owned source buffer. The field is not “mutable access to String”; it is “this String view belongs to source”.
decisions.detail: Reworked 2026-07-01: added option D (recommended). Inference rule: if exactly one candidate owner exists at the construction site, it is inferred and jet expand --facts refs materializes it; if several candidates exist, compiling without @Ref(label) is an error that lists the candidates — the teaching moment arrives exactly when the information matters. This is the magic-default/expert-control shape applied to lifetimes: the beginner writes &T, the multi-arena expert writes @Ref(arena), and nobody writes a label the compiler already knows. ~T stays rejected (conflates write authority); bare-&-always (old C) stays rejected because ambiguous cases would get folklore defaults instead of diagnostics.

options.name: #Ref(Label) always required
options.detail: Every stored ref names its owner even when there is only one candidate — the repetition the binder note complained about.

options.name: field: ~T
options.detail: Short but conflates stored-borrow with call-time exclusive WRITE access, and still has no owner label for diagnostics.
options.code: struct Owner { primary: ~Incident }

options.name: field: &T always, never labeled
options.detail: Short everywhere, but multi-owner cases lose the label diagnostics need — errors degrade to "somewhere, something outlived."
options.code: struct Index { hot: &Incident }

options.name: &T with inferred owner + @Ref(label) to disambiguate (recommended)
options.detail: One candidate owner: inferred, zero ceremony. Several: compile error listing candidates, fixed by @Ref(label). Expand lens always shows the resolved owner.

comparisons.note: Stored references name a lifetime relationship; mutable access is a separate `&mut` concept.
comparisons.code:
struct View<'a> { text: &'a str }
fn edit(x: &mut String) {}

comparisons.note: Borrowing/consuming annotations are access-mode concepts, separate from object storage identity.

decisions.title: Stored-ref disambiguation label: #Ref(label) or @Ref(label)?
decisions.gist: Two decisions ratified the same day contradict each other on one sigil: does the stored-ref owner label stay a # directive or move to the @ contract plane?
decisions.explainer: D-MARKERMOVE1 (=B, ratified 2026-07-01) explicitly lists `#Ref(Label)` under markers that CLEAR STAY on the # directive plane — it names #Ref itself as an example of a directive, alongside #Unsafe/#Test/#Bench. D-REF-SHORTHAND1 (=D, ratified the same day) chose an option whose own worked code sample spells the disambiguation label `@Ref(pool)` on the @ contract plane. Both are ratified; they cannot both be true once the marker-family @ plane actually ships (this card, c7markerfamily/#167). The label just names which in-scope value owns a `&T` field when inference is ambiguous — it is not, on its own, a promise about the declaration (the plane law's test), which reads closer to `#`'s job of supplying compiler-needed data, not stating a contract. This ballot exists purely to pick the one spelling that ships.
decisions.story: Walter is implementing the ref-shorthand card and hits the fork in the road: the marker-family law card says #Ref, the ref-shorthand ballot's own code sample says @Ref. He should not guess which ratified decision wins — a one-line owner call closes the gap and the exact same label (whichever spelling) gets typed into every stored-ref struct in the codebase from here on.

options.name: #Ref(label) — directive plane (recommended)
options.detail: Matches D-MARKERMOVE1's explicit text, which names #Ref(Label) as a clear-stays example in the same breath as #Unsafe/#Test/#Bench. The label supplies compiler-needed disambiguation data at a specific construction site — it is not a checkable promise about the type itself the way @Codable or @MustUse are (those hold regardless of any call site; a ref label only matters when inference is ambiguous).
