options.detail: http.url.parse(...) and http.mime.*. No new top-level modules, but URL values are useful far beyond HTTP (file://, data:, config values, core.web) and burying them hurts discovery.
options.code:
use core.http as http

u := http.url.parse("https://api.example.com")?

options.name: Decline — keep strings
options.detail: URLs stay strings with documented escaping helpers in core.encoding. Cheapest surface, but every consumer re-solves encoding and the beginner footgun stays the default, against I1/philosophy.
options.code: raw :: "{base}/notify?user={encoding.percent(user)}"   // remembering to call percent() is on you

comparisons.note: The URL/URLSearchParams pair is the modern reference; browsers ship it built-in.
comparisons.code:
const u = new URL('https://api.example.com/notify');
u.searchParams.set('user', 'ada lovelace');

comparisons.note: net/url is stdlib and universally used; mime is its own stdlib package.
comparisons.code:
u, _ := url.Parse("https://api.example.com")
q := u.Query(); q.Set("user", "ada lovelace"); u.RawQuery = q.Encode()

comparisons.note: urllib.parse is stdlib but string-tuple based and widely considered clunky — the anti-example.

decisions.title: Human formatting: core.fmt module vs interpolation format-specs
decisions.gist: How Jet spells number/bytes/duration formatting — library functions or string-interpolation syntax.
decisions.explainer: C: A’s functions deliver the daily wins (bytes/duration/thousands) with zero syntax risk now, and the spec-sugar question stays a clean future reopen instead of a silent never.
decisions.story: Ana prints a report: file sizes, elapsed times, row counts with thousands separators, floats to 2 decimals. Today interpolation gives her the raw value only, so she writes arithmetic and string surgery by hand for each cell — the tenth time she has done it.

options.name: core.fmt module, functions only
options.detail: fmt.bytes(n), fmt.duration(ms), fmt.number(n, thousands: true, precision: 2), fmt.ordinal(n), fmt.pad/align helpers. No syntax change; composes in interpolation like any call. Locale-aware variants can join later behind the same names.

options.name: Interpolation format-specs
options.detail: Python/Rust-style mini-language inside braces: {x:.2f}, {n:,}, {s:>10}. Terse at the call site, but it is new user-facing syntax (lexer/parser/formatter/S8 interplay), a second sub-language to learn, and covers only what the spec grammar anticipates (no bytes/duration).
options.code:
print("{name}: {size:.1G}B in {elapsed:dur} ({rows:,} rows)")
// every marker is spec grammar to ratify, document, and format-stabilize

options.name: Both: functions now, spec sugar later
options.detail: Ship A; reopen a spec-syntax ballot only if call-site verbosity proves painful in real code. Keeps today’s decision small without closing the door.
options.code:
print("{fmt.number(rows, thousands: true)}")   // today
print("{rows:,}")                              // possible future reopen

options.name: Decline
options.detail: Raw interpolation only. Every report/CLI author keeps hand-rolling the same helpers — a daily papercut in exactly the beginner path Jet optimizes for.
options.code: print("{(size / 1073741824.0)} GB")   // and now round it yourself

comparisons.note: format-spec mini-language is powerful and famously unmemorizable; humanize is a separate library anyway for bytes/durations.
no format-specs in strings; helpers/libraries do it — humanize is one of the most-imported Go packages.
{:>10.2} exists in format! and still no bytes/duration answer without crates.

decisions.comment: full go-style humanize support in the fmt module/lib.

decisions.title: Terminal and raw IO surface
decisions.gist: Choose the shape of terminal stdout/stderr, TTY facts, colors, progress, raw mode, and key events.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: one import for beginner CLIs, but a clean stream/terminal split inside core.io for expert control and audit.
decisions.story: Betty writes a deployment CLI. It prints a progress line, colors warnings only on terminals, flushes before running a child process, and reads one key in raw mode for confirmation. She should not hand-roll ANSI or leak escape codes into logs.
decisions.inWild:
use core.io as io

io.write("Building...")
io.flush()
if io.stdout.is_tty() { io.style(.Yellow).write("warn") }
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: one import for beginner CLIs, but a clean stream/terminal split inside core.io for expert control and audit.

options.name: Hybrid: stream backbone plus terminal capability namespace (recommended)
options.detail: core.io owns stdout/stderr/stdin streams, flush, raw bytes, and TTY facts. Terminal capabilities live under `io.terminal`/stream methods, not a separate module: style/progress/raw mode/key events all honor TTY/NO_COLOR by default, with explicit expert overrides for forced color/raw behavior.
options.code:
use core.io as io

io.stdout.write("Building...")?
io.stdout.flush()?
if io.stdout.is_tty() { io.stdout.style(.Green).write("done")? }
key :: io.terminal.raw(() => io.terminal.read_key())?

options.name: Split core.io and core.term
options.detail: core.io stays byte streams; core.term owns TTY/color/raw/key/progress. Separation is clean, but beginners must learn two modules for one terminal program.
options.code:
use core.io as io
use core.term as term
term.style(.Green).write(io.stdout, "done")?

options.name: Decline terminal depth
options.detail: Keep print/eprint/input only. Serious CLIs shell out or hand-roll ANSI/raw mode, so pipes and Windows terminals become user footguns.
options.code: print("\x1b[32mdone\x1b[0m")

comparisons.note: term/console needs x/term or third-party packages; stdlib leaves gaps.
crossterm gives capability breadth as a crate; Jet needs a blessed Core path.

decisions.title: Declarative CLI parser depth
decisions.gist: Choose how core.args grows beyond the typed run(args) layer and simple builders.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: derive ergonomics and builder control feed one checked command-spec model.
decisions.story: Hank ships a CLI with subcommands, env fallbacks, defaults, completion text, and exact errors. Typed entry args cover the common case; library code and custom launchers need the same parser without inventing another command language.
decisions.inWild:
use core.args as args

spec :: args.command("serve").flag("port", default: 8080).subcommand("migrate")
parsed :: args.parse(spec)?
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: derive ergonomics and builder control feed one checked command-spec model.

options.name: Hybrid: one ArgsSpec from structs or builders (recommended)
options.detail: ArgsSpec is the single semantic model. Typed `fn run(args: T)` derives an ArgsSpec for beginners; library/tooling code can build the same ArgsSpec dynamically for subcommands, env fallbacks, completions, and tests. No string mini-language.

options.name: Struct-only derive everywhere
options.detail: All parsing starts from structs/enums. Clean for ordinary apps, but generated tools and dynamic command sets cannot compose specs at runtime.
options.code: cmd :: args.parse<DeployArgs>()?

options.name: String mini-language
options.detail: A clap-like DSL string describes commands. Compact, but becomes a second grammar with weak type/source spans.
options.code: spec :: args.spec("deploy --host <HOST> [--dry-run]")

comparisons.note: Builder plus derive coexist; Jet should keep one semantic spec with two ergonomic entrypoints.
Dynamic builders are flexible but weakly typed.

decisions.title: Math library depth and numeric safety
decisions.gist: Choose the Core math surface for libm breadth and integer-safety helpers.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: beginner discoverability without a second numeric-method API.
decisions.story: Doris writes physics and finance tooling. She needs trig/log/hypot, checked/saturating integer operations, gcd/lcm, clamp, and clear NaN/overflow behavior. Bare operators are not enough.
decisions.inWild:
use core.math as math

dist :: math.hypot(dx, dy)
sum :: math.checked_add(a, b)?
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: beginner discoverability without a second numeric-method API.

options.name: Hybrid: core.math canonical registry plus discoverability (recommended)
options.detail: core.math functions are the canonical callable surface for libm and explicit checked/saturating/wrapping integer families. Numeric documentation, LSP completion, and optional snippets may surface helpers from values, but emitted code uses the same core.math names so Jet does not grow duplicate spellings.
options.code:
angle :: math.atan2(y, x)
next :: math.checked_add(count, 1)?
cap :: math.saturating_mul(bytes, shards)
// LSP on `count.` may offer "checked_add" and insert math.checked_add(count, ...)

options.name: Numeric methods
options.detail: Put helpers on numeric values. Discoverable after a value, but fragments the surface across types and makes generic numeric docs harder.
options.code:
angle :: y.atan2(x)
next :: count.checked_add(1)?

options.name: Operators and lints only
options.detail: Keep operators and add overflow lints. Beginner code stays terse, but exact overflow intent is not visible at the call site.
options.code: x + y   // maybe checked by profile, maybe not

comparisons.note: Rust names checked/saturating/wrapping arithmetic explicitly.
math and bits are split; integer overflow remains easy to miss.

decisions.title: Randomness modules and distributions
decisions.gist: Choose how PRNG sampling, bytes, shuffling, and security randomness are separated.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: rich sampling UX for ordinary code and hard separation for security-sensitive bytes.
decisions.story: Earl writes a simulation and later adds password reset tokens. If random bytes and deterministic PRNGs share one undifferentiated API, the safe path is invisible.
decisions.inWild:
use core.random as random

seeded :: random.Splittable.new(seed)
token :: ???
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: rich sampling UX for ordinary code and hard separation for security-sensitive bytes.

options.name: Hybrid: reproducible PRNG in core.random, secrets in core.crypto (recommended)
options.detail: core.random owns deterministic PRNGs, distributions, shuffling, sampling, seed splitting, and test fixtures. Secret randomness stays in core.crypto. Shared entropy plumbing may exist internally, but names keep simulation/test randomness and security randomness impossible to confuse.
options.code:
rng := random.SplitMix64.new(seed)
roll :: rng.int(1..6)
items.shuffle(&rng)
token :: crypto.random_bytes(32)
nonce :: crypto.random_nonce(.XChaCha20)

options.name: Single core.random with secure namespace
options.detail: One module owns both random.prng and random.secure. Discoverable, but proximity invites accidental security misuse.
options.code: token :: random.secure.bytes(32)

options.name: Only crypto randomness
options.detail: Use secure randomness for everything. Safe for secrets, poor for reproducible tests/simulations and performance-sensitive sampling.
options.code: roll :: crypto.random_int(1..6)

comparisons.note: rand separates RNG traits and distributions; secrets require OsRng care.
random vs secrets split is the correct beginner lesson.

decisions.title: Regex engine semantics and API depth
decisions.gist: Choose the in-house regex contract before replacing the bridge.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: safe predictable regex for everyone, with migration help instead of importing PCRE footguns into the default path.
decisions.story: Tom filters logs in a server path. Regex must be fast, predictable, Unicode-aware, and impossible to turn into a catastrophic backtracking trap by default.
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: safe predictable regex for everyone, with migration help instead of importing PCRE footguns into the default path.

options.name: Hybrid: linear default with explicit compatibility mode (recommended)
options.detail: core.regex is RE2-class and linear by default: captures, named groups, replace, split, flags, Unicode classes. A future compatibility parser may diagnose unsupported PCRE features and suggest safe rewrites; any backtracking/PCRE engine would be explicit, audited, and never the default.
options.code:
rx :: regex.compile("(?<level>INFO|WARN)")?
match :: rx.find(line)?

legacy :: regex.compile_compat(pattern)?
// emits diagnostics for unsafe backtracking features unless explicitly allowed

options.name: PCRE-class full feature engine
options.detail: Lookaround/backrefs maximize compatibility, but catastrophic backtracking becomes a beginner footgun unless heavily gated.
options.code: rx :: regex.compile("(a+)+$")

options.name: Minimal matcher only
options.detail: Ship contains/glob-like matching and defer full regex. Safe but not competitive with existing stdlib expectations.
options.code: if text.contains("ERROR") { ... }

comparisons.note: regexp is RE2-class linear-time stdlib.
Rust regex is linear and omits backreferences/lookaround.

decisions.title: Database rows and migrations
decisions.gist: Choose the database surface above the ratified safe driver floor.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: honest SQL and typed rows now, with generated query plans as an ergonomic front end over the same parameterized mechanism.
decisions.story: Omar builds a service with SQLite now and Postgres later. He needs parameter-only queries, typed rows, transactions, migrations, and schema drift checks without stringly result maps.
decisions.inWild:
use core.db as db

rows :: conn.query("select id, email from users where id = ?", [id])?
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: honest SQL and typed rows now, with generated query plans as an ergonomic front end over the same parameterized mechanism.

options.name: Hybrid: typed SQL rows plus optional query builder (recommended)
options.detail: The canonical database path is parameterized SQL with typed row decoding, transactions, prepared statements, migrations, and checksums. A query builder can generate that same SQL/parameter plan for Studio/LSP workflows, but SQL remains inspectable and parameter-only safety remains enforced.
options.code:
rows :: conn.query<UserRow>("select id,email from users where id = ?", [id])?
db.migrate(conn, migrations.from_dir("migrations"))?

plan :: db.query(User).where(.id == id).select(.{ id, email })
rows2 :: conn.run<UserRow>(plan)?

options.name: ORM-style query builder
options.detail: Build queries from Jet expressions. More typed, but creates a second language for SQL and can hide database behavior.
options.code: users.where((u) => u.id == id).select(.{ id, email })

options.name: Raw driver only
options.detail: Expose execute/query returning dynamic rows. Safe params remain, but typed app code does manual casts everywhere.
options.code: row.get_string("email")?

comparisons.note: Typed rows and migrations are loved, but macro/build-time DB coupling is a tax.
Safe params, weak row typing; Jet can improve here.

decisions.title: Structured logging, tracing, and sinks
decisions.gist: Choose the logging API for logs, spans, metrics hooks, and export.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: simple logging calls generate audit-ready structured events for expert observability.
decisions.story: Inez debugs a production incident. Plain print lines are not enough; she needs structured fields, spans, request IDs, JSON output, sampling, and OTel export without every package inventing a logger.
decisions.inWild:
use core.log as log

log.info("started")
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: simple logging calls generate audit-ready structured events for expert observability.

options.name: Hybrid: structured events, spans, and friendly text sinks (recommended)
options.detail: core.log records typed events/spans/fields as the source truth. Text, JSON, and OTel sinks are output formats over those events. Beginners call log.info with plain fields; experts control propagation, sampling, redaction, sinks, trace IDs, and export policy.
options.code:
span :: log.span("http.request", fields: .{ route: "/users" })
log.info("loaded user", fields: .{ user_id: id })
log.sink(log.Json.stdout())
log.export(log.otel(endpoint))

options.name: Printf logging plus JSON sink
options.detail: Keep log.info text-first and add optional key/value args. Familiar, but weaker type/audit story.
options.code: log.info("loaded user", "user_id", id)

options.name: Use print/core.io
options.detail: No logging module. Services and libraries cannot compose observability coherently.
options.code: print("[INFO] loaded user {id}")

comparisons.note: Structured logs are now stdlib-level.
Spans/events are the right model but crate-based.

decisions.title: Collections and iterator adapter depth
decisions.gist: Choose the canonical collection/iterator expansion surface.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: collection-method ergonomics over a single lazy iterator core.
decisions.story: Sam writes data transforms. He expects map/filter/fold/chunk/window/group/sort/dedup/zip/enumerate/collect to work over lists, maps, ranges, files, and streams with one mental model.
decisions.inWild: xs.filter((x) => x.ok).map((x) => x.id)
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: collection-method ergonomics over a single lazy iterator core.

options.name: Hybrid: lazy iterator protocol with eager collection conveniences (recommended)
options.detail: One Iterable/Iterator model powers lazy adapters. Collections expose beginner-friendly adapter methods that return lazy views; `collect`, `to_list`, or terminal reducers make materialization explicit. No comprehension syntax needed now.
options.code:
ids :: users
    .filter((u) => u.active)
    .map((u) => u.id)
    .chunked(100)
    .to_list()

total :: orders.iter().map((o) => o.total).sum()

options.name: Eager collection methods only
options.detail: Every adapter returns a collection. Beginner-simple, but large/streaming workloads allocate unnecessarily.
options.code: ids :: users.filter(...).map(...)

options.name: Comprehension syntax
options.detail: New syntax for collection transforms. Compact, but a major surface and second spelling for adapters.
options.code: ids :: [u.id for u in users if u.active]

comparisons.note: Broad lazy adapters set the bar.
Powerful but split between language loops, list comprehensions, and itertools.

decisions.title: Stdlib have/have-not ledger policy
decisions.gist: Choose how Jet records shipped, carded, and declined stdlib domains.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: readable docs backed by a checked status ledger, so gaps are deliberate instead of vibes.
decisions.story: Earl audits whether Jet can replace Python/Go/Rust for a project. Vibes are not enough; every stdlib domain needs one status and a reason if declined.
decisions.inWild:
docs/reference/core-library.md
// missing rows today: XML, URL, MIME, TUI, SSH, IPC, image codecs...
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: readable docs backed by a checked status ledger, so gaps are deliberate instead of vibes.

options.name: Hybrid: machine ledger generated into readable docs (recommended)
options.detail: A structured ledger file is the source of truth for shipped/carded/declined stdlib domains. CI checks rows, live card IDs, and ratified decline IDs. docs/reference renders a human-friendly table from it, so beginners see clear docs and experts get machine-checkable coverage.

options.name: Narrative roadmap only
options.detail: A prose doc explains broad direction. Easier to read, but gaps reappear as repeated debates.
options.code:
## Networking
Jet plans broad networking support.

options.name: Track only built modules
options.detail: Docs list what exists; missing domains are implicit. That hides deliberate no-go decisions and weakens audits.
options.code: core.files, core.http, core.db

comparisons.note: Library index shows breadth but not deliberate omissions.
Package index is strong for shipped modules; proposals/declines are scattered.

decisions.title: What is Jet’s compile-time build entrypoint?
decisions.gist: Give Jet a build-time main: one explicit `#Build fn build(ctx) -> BuildPlan ?`, selected by the build surface.
decisions.explainer: Jai’s `#run` is powerful because build code is just language code. Jet should import that power through a single auditable entrypoint instead of hidden module-level execution. Local `comptime {}` remains for value computation; the build entrypoint owns graph construction: targets, generated source, assets, toolchains, profiles, and package/workspace integration. Generated source still re-enters lexer -> parser -> sema (R11).
decisions.story: Marcus is building a game. He wants to pack textures, generate an enum from asset names, compile shaders, and then build the game binary with one command. His studio security team wants the same build to explain exactly what ran and what files/network endpoints it touched.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: a build-time main can become Cargo build.rs with better syntax: dependency code executes before users inspect it. Patch: one selected root entrypoint, BuildContext authority only, D-CTEFFECT1 tiers, dependency Tier 2 denied by default, generated-source re-check, lock/provenance, and jet explain-build. Do not let every imported module have hidden build hooks. STATUS CORRECTION 2026-07-01: an earlier edit claimed the lifecycle-verbs law (jet <verb> -> fn <verb>(); syntax-comparison-proposal.md §36A) was ratified — it is NOT; it is an open proposal, related open ballot D-JPK-DEVCOMPOSE1 (jet dev). Option B stands on its own merits and the owner direction recorded 2026-07-01 (a fn-main-equivalent build entry that maps cleanly to jet build); if the verb law later ratifies, B becomes one instance of it. D-BUILDPOLICY1 governs authority either way. Scope ladder (single file / package / workspace) is D-BUILDSCOPE1; generated-source home is D-BUILDGEN1.

options.name: `Build.entry` selects `#Build fn build(ctx) -> BuildPlan ?`
options.detail: One explicit build-time main. The marker makes the authority boundary visible; `Build.entry` makes selection explicit for tools and CI. Local `comptime {}` remains separate.

options.name: fn build(b: BuildContext) via the lifecycle verb map (recommended)
options.detail: Not name magic and not dependent on any unratified law: jet build runs fn build(BuildContext) when the root defines one, else the batteries default pipeline runs. The typed BuildContext parameter is the visible authority boundary. Aligns with the OPEN lifecycle-verbs proposal (jet run -> fn run(), jet dev -> fn dev()) without depending on it.

options.name: `comptime main` in any module
options.detail: Maximal #run feel. Rejected unless owner accepts hidden import-time execution risk.
options.code: comptime fn main(ctx: BuildContext) -> BuildPlan ? { ... }

options.name: No build entrypoint; only declarative `Build.{}` plus local `comptime {}`
options.detail: Safest and easiest to audit, but cannot replace Jai/Zig/Make-class orchestration.
options.code: build: Build.{ sources: ["src/main.jet"] }

comparisons.note: `#run` can execute arbitrary compile-time code and participate in build orchestration. It is fun and direct, but authority is broad by default.
`build.zig` is a programmatic build file with explicit steps. Strong model, but separate from ordinary source entrypoints.
`build.rs` runs before compilation and communicates through files/env instructions. Powerful but stringly and historically easy to abuse.

decisions.title: What authority does build-time code get by default?
decisions.gist: Build code gets pure and locked reproducible inputs by default; ambient effects require source audit plus policy.
decisions.explainer: Build metaprogramming is supply-chain code execution. Jet needs a policy model that is fun locally but enforceable in CI and enterprises. D-CTEFFECT1 gives the effect tiers; this decision fixes the build-system default: root builds may request authority, dependencies are denied ambient authority unless project/org policy grants it, and every granted capability is recorded in lock/provenance.
decisions.story: Alicia maintains a fintech service. She is fine with a root build script reading `schema/*.sql`, but she cannot allow a transitive dependency to read CI secrets or hit the network during build.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: too much policy can make game-dev builds feel bureaucratic. Too little policy loses enterprise adoption. The compromise is profile-sensitive: developer default allows pure + locked Tier 1 and prompts for Tier 2; CI strict/offline deny drift; enterprise can allowlist roots/domains/tools. The model must not rely on wrapper scripts.

options.name: Tiered policy with `BuildContext` authority only (recommended)
options.detail: Pure + locked Tier 1 by default. Tier 2 needs `#Impure("reason")`, CLI/project/org permission, and provenance. Dependencies get no Tier 2 unless explicitly granted.
options.code:
jet build --profile=ci --locked --deny-impure
jet audit-effects

options.name: Warn-only policy for impure build effects
options.detail: Fast and friendly, but CI can accidentally ship non-reproducible builds.
options.code: Warning [L3102]: build reads `$HOME/.token`

options.name: Pure-only build code
options.detail: Maximum reproducibility, but blocks shader compilation, bindgen, asset packing, and real-world package builds.
options.code: // ctx.exec, env, unpinned network: always errors

options.name: Jai-style unrestricted build execution
options.detail: Most fun and powerful locally; unacceptable supply-chain default for Jet.
options.code: #run { run_process("curl https://...") }

comparisons.note: Builds are sandboxed and inputs are explicit; reproducibility is excellent but general programming ergonomics are specialized.
Actions declare inputs/outputs and remote cache keys. Strong enterprise model; BUILD language is separate from app language.
Build scripts are easy but broad; policy/audit is mostly convention and sandboxing is external.

decisions.title: Where does fn build live at each scale, and how do workspace builds compose?
decisions.gist: One build-entry model from a single file to a monorepo: where the entry lives at each rung, and who grants its authority.
decisions.explainer: D-BUILDENTRY1 picks the entry spelling; this decision fixes its home per scale and the grant chain. Owner direction (2026-07-01): effect/capability declaration must travel with the code so a lone .jet file works with no manifest; pkg.jet is where a project grants standing permission; the workspace is where an org caps everything. Composition: a workspace build runs member builds in dependency order; whether it may only observe/cap members or also contribute targets is part of this choice. Declaration stays one mechanism (code-site #Impure/effect tags, D-CTEFFECT1); permission and policy are the two layers above it — nothing is declared twice (I8).
decisions.story: Earl writes a one-file jam game that bakes a sprite atlas at build time. It grows into a package, then his studio pulls it into their 40-package monorepo. Earl's build fn should survive each move unchanged, and the studio's security lead needs one file that caps what every member build may touch in CI.
decisions.detail: Grant chain at a glance: single file = per-invocation grant (flag or interactive prompt); package = standing grant recorded in pkg.jet; workspace = ceiling that member grants cannot exceed. Each rung caps the rung below; jet audit reads all three without executing anything.

options.name: Entry lives in the unit's existing definition file at every rung
options.detail: Single file: fn build beside fn main. Package: fn build inside pkg.jet. Workspace: fn build inside workspace.jet. Zero new filenames; the grant chain (flag -> pkg.jet build: block -> workspace policy block) mirrors containment. Workspace fn build may add workspace-level targets and cap members, never mutate a member's plan.

options.name: Dedicated build.jet beside the manifest
options.detail: Package and workspace each get a build.jet next to pkg.jet / workspace.jet; single file keeps fn build in-file. Manifests stay purely declarative; build logic gets its own home. Cost: a fourth special filename (env.jet, pkg.jet, workspace.jet, build.jet) and a two-file story for small packages.

options.name: Any source file, selected by an explicit pointer
options.detail: pkg.jet points at the entry: build: .{ entry: tools.release_build }. Most flexible layout; auditors must follow the pointer instead of grepping one location, and two packages can spell the same thing two ways.

options.name: Package scope only (no single-file, no workspace entry)
options.detail: The Cargo build.rs shape: only packages get a build entry. A lone script cannot use build-time generation without first creating a package, and an org has no first-class ceiling — policy lives in external CI scripts.
options.code:
// jam.jet
fn build(b: BuildContext) ... // error: build entry requires a package manifest

comparisons.note: build.rs is package-only, ambient-authority, and has no workspace-level build or policy file; orgs bolt policy on with external tooling.
comparisons.code: // build.rs — full process authority, no grant chain

comparisons.note: build.zig is a dedicated per-package build program (option B shape); no capability layer, no workspace ceiling.
BUILD per package + WORKSPACE/MODULE at root — the two-rung shape of option A/B, but in a separate dialect from the app language.
One flake.nix serves every scale and evaluation is pure by default — the closest existing grant-chain model, in a specialized language.

decisions.title: Where does build-generated Jet source live, and how is it addressed?
decisions.gist: Build code emits real Jet modules (D-CTCODEGEN1). Decide the on-disk home, lock hashing, staging, and the additive-only rule.
decisions.explainer: D-CTCODEGEN1 already ratified the pipeline law: generated code re-enters lexer -> parser -> sema like hand-written source. This decision fixes the user-visible surface on top of it: where generated files land, whether they are committed, how b.generate() addresses them, whether a later generation round may observe an earlier round's output (bounded staging vs single round), and the additive-only law — generation may ADD modules but never mutate or shadow user-written source, so reading a file always tells the truth. That last rule is the deliberate break from Jai's #insert, whose output never exists anywhere a person or an LSP can open.
decisions.story: Doris generates a typed API client from openapi.json. She wants to open the generated file, set a breakpoint in it, and point a teammate at line 214 in review; her CI must prove the artifact byte-matches the spec hash recorded in the lock.
decisions.detail: All options share the ratified floor: re-entry through the front end, hash recorded in .jet/lock, diagnostics pinned to the trigger site with the generated fragment as optional context. Staging recommendation carried in each option: generation runs in bounded, deterministically ordered rounds; a cycle is a compile error naming the chain — no Jai-style loop-until-quiescent.

options.name: Derived state under .jet/generated/, never committed
options.detail: Generated modules are build products, addressed by module name and materialized under .jet/generated/<package>/. Real files: LSP go-to-def lands in them, debugger steps through them, jet explain-build diffs them. Lock records source-input and output hashes, so CI verifies without committing. Source tree stays clean; no drift class of bugs.

options.name: In-tree build/generated/, committing optional
options.detail: Files land inside the project at build/generated/; each project decides whether to commit them. Visible without any flag, but the committed/uncommitted split means two ecosystems and --locked must handle both.
options.code:
b.generate("api_client", src)?
// -> build/generated/api_client.jet   (gitignore or commit — project choice)

options.name: Checked-in generated/ required
options.detail: Go-generate model: generated source is always committed, reviewed in every diff. Maximum review visibility; the cost is a standing drift hazard (artifact vs input) that CI must re-verify anyway, plus generated noise in every review.
options.code:
b.generate("api_client", src)?
// -> generated/api_client.jet   committed; CI fails if regeneration differs

options.name: Virtual only — no files, dump on demand
options.detail: Generated modules exist only inside the compilation; a flag dumps them for forensics. This is the Jai/#insert and Rust-proc-macro feel: nothing to open, breakpoint, or review. Listed to reject.
options.code: // nothing on disk; jet build --emit-generated is the only window

comparisons.note: OUT_DIR + include! hides generated code; cargo-expand exists because nobody can otherwise read what a proc-macro produced.
go generate commits artifacts (option C): perfectly visible, drifts unless CI regenerates and compares.
Generated files are derived outputs under bazel-out/, addressable as labels — the option A shape with strong caching.

decisions.title: May build code read the whole checked program and enforce custom rules (ladder rung B)?
decisions.gist: Rung B of the D-METADEPTH1 ladder: read-only whole-program reflection plus first-class custom diagnostics, from the build entry only. No mutation, no macros — rung C stays frozen (c154).
decisions.explainer: D-METADEPTH1=A ratified that rung B (a read-only lint-style rejection pass) rises 'only by a future vote'. This ballot is that vote, scoped to the fn build arc. Grant if ratified: the build entry receives a post-sema, read-only snapshot of the whole program through the existing D-METAREFLECT1 TypeInfo surface scaled up (program -> packages -> types/functions), and a diagnostic-emission API whose signature structurally requires code + what/why/fix, so I4 quality holds by construction. Runs only at the selected build entry (D-BUILDENTRY1) — never at module import time, so no hidden execution and no action at a distance. Rung C (mutation, message loop, user macros) is untouched and stays frozen on c154 (e7).
decisions.story: Walter runs the platform team at a 40-team company on one Jet monorepo. Org rules — 'no panic reachable from a net handler', 'every Entity type has archive()' for GDPR export — live on a wiki and die in code review. He wants the build itself to enforce them with compiler-grade errors no team can miss, without granting anyone the power to rewrite code invisibly.
decisions.detail: Why this is the safe rung: reading the checked program cannot change what any file means — local reasoning survives, the LSP model survives, and generated diagnostics are the only output. The enterprise value is policy-as-code with the compiler's own error quality, in the language the team already writes. The adversarial cost to weigh: a build entry that fails builds on custom rules is a new way for a dependency to be annoying — mitigated because only the ROOT's build entry runs rules (dependencies' rules do not run for you) and D-BUILDPOLICY1 authority applies.

options.name: Stay at D-METADEPTH1=A (reflection + derives only)
options.detail: Status quo. Org rules remain external linters with their own parsers that drift from the language; the wiki stays the enforcement mechanism.
options.code:
// jet has no answer; Walter writes a tree-sitter script that re-parses Jet
// and breaks on every syntax release

options.name: Read-only program snapshot + structured diagnostics from the build entry
options.detail: The Roslyn-analyzer shape: typed read-only API, structured diagnostics, zero mutation. Scoped to the root build entry; dependency build code gets no rule execution in your build.

options.name: Full message loop / mutation (Jai rung)
options.detail: Build code observes AND rewrites every declaration. Maximal power; reading a file no longer tells you what it means, and the LSP cannot model the program without running the metaprogram. Stays frozen on c154 — listed so the ladder is explicit.

comparisons.note: Analyzers are the industry success story of rung B: typed read-only compilation API + structured diagnostics, shipped as packages, beloved in enterprise.
Custom lints require unstable compiler internals (clippy is in-tree); third parties are locked out — the gap Jet can close.
Userland custom rules over a stable AST — massive adoption, but stringly typed and per-file only; no whole-program view.
The message loop grants observe + rewrite together; there is no read-only tier to adopt without the mutation cost.

decisions.title: Epoch 4 exit bar: how much of the build-graph vision ships before e4 is done?
decisions.gist: Pick the finish line for Epoch 4 (metaprogramming): the ratified fn-build MVP, that plus typed targets/actions, or full CMake/Bazel-class build-graph parity.
decisions.explainer: The five fn-build ballots are ratified (D-BUILDENTRY1=B, D-BUILDGEN1=A, D-BUILDPOLICY1=A, D-BUILDSCOPE1=A, D-METADEPTH2=B) with an executable plan (metaprogramming.md §15). The vision doc also holds back six build-graph decision bundles (§12: targets, actions, toolchains, cache, probes, lock) that were deliberately frozen "until the foundation ballots land." They have landed. This decision sets what "Epoch 4 done" means, and therefore which of those six bundles agents must develop into ballots for you now versus later.
decisions.story: Hank maintains a game studio's engine repo: Jet code, shader assets, a test suite, and a handful of C tools. He wants to delete the Makefile. The ratified MVP lets his fn build generate bindings and pick sources — but a test target, an asset-cook step with declared inputs/outputs, and "only rebuild what changed" are exactly the parts of Make he still needs. Where Epoch 4 stops decides whether Hank deletes the Makefile at e4 or waits.

options.name: MVP bar — ship §15 as ratified, all six §12 bundles wait for e5
options.detail: Epoch 4 exits when the five ratified ballots are implemented end-to-end (entry, generate, policy, scope, enforce) plus the explain-build/audit surfaces. BuildPlan stays the three lists. The six §12 bundles get balloted in Epoch 5 beside jetpack. Cleanest scope; but e4's own charter is Jai parity, and Jai ships targets — Hank keeps his Makefile another epoch, and every real project's asset/test steps live in Tier-2 `#Impure` shell-outs in the meantime, which trains exactly the habit the capability model exists to prevent.

options.name: Full parity bar — all six §12 bundles designed, ratified, shipped in e4
options.detail: Epoch 4 exits at CMake/Bazel-class parity: typed targets, declared-I/O actions, toolchain pinning, content-addressed action cache, typed probes, lock/provenance for all of it. "Never reach for Make" is true at e4 exit. The cost is decision-load and design risk, not effort: toolchain registries, remote-cache trust, and probe vocabularies are ecosystem decisions that will be better informed by jetpack's provider model (e5) — ratifying them first risks re-opening them, which is the one thing the ratification process is supposed to prevent.

options.name: MVP + targets/actions — Jai-parity bar; toolchains/cache/probes ride e5 (recommended)
options.detail: Epoch 4 exits on §15 plus two of the six bundles: D-BUILDTARGET1 (executable/library/test/bench/asset targets in BuildPlan) and D-BUILDACTION1 (declared inputs/outputs/argv actions — a step with no declared outputs is not a build step). That is the Jai benchmark e4 is named for, and it is what deletes Hank's Makefile: tests and asset cooks become graph nodes instead of #Impure shell-outs, so the capability story stays honest. Toolchains, cache, and probes are jetpack-shaped ecosystem bundles; they ballot in e5 where the provider model informs them — until then `jet build` is correct-if-slower (no action cache) and probes stay Tier-2 #Impure. Agents develop the two bundles into full ballots immediately; the other four are named and parked, not lost.

decisions.comparisons:
Jai: builds-as-programs with targets and compile options — the e4 charter's benchmark.
CMake/Bazel/Ninja: typed targets + declared-I/O actions + caching; nobody's v1 shipped remote caching.
Cargo: build.rs (ambient, no graph) — the anti-model Jet already rejected.
nob.h (binder idea): C build-as-program; covered by targets+actions, not by the MVP lists.

decisions.title: Single-file Tier-2 build grants: what does the user type to say yes?
decisions.gist: A lone script's fn build wants an ambient effect (exec, env, ...). Pick the CLI spelling that grants it for one run.
decisions.explainer: D-BUILDPOLICY1=A ratified the mechanics: Tier-2 build effects need BOTH a `#Impure("reason")` gate in source AND permission at run time — "a flag or an interactive prompt" for a manifest-less single file. The flag spelling was left open. There is already one ratified grant flag: D-CTEFFECT1's blanket `--allow-impure` (comptime Tier-2, diagnostic E3411 names it). This ballot decides whether that blanket stays the one grant path or is refined into per-effect grants — whichever wins becomes THE spelling (I8: one grant system, E3411's fix text updated to match). Effect names come from the ratified ten-effect vocabulary (D-EFF4: Net, Fs, Io, Db, Time, Rand, Env, Exec, Log, Gpu) — nothing new is minted.
decisions.story: Walter has a 60-line `tool.jet` — no pkg.jet, just a script whose fn build probes pkg-config for a legacy C library before compiling. The probe is `exec`, a Tier-2 effect. His build fn already declares it and gates it with #Impure. Now he runs `jet build tool.jet` on his laptop (interactive) and in CI (no TTY, hermetic by default). What does he type?

options.name: Per-effect `--allow-<effect>` + TTY prompt fallback — supersedes the blanket (recommended)
options.detail: One flag per D-EFF4 effect, lowercase: `--allow-exec`, `--allow-env`, `--allow-net`, `--allow-fs`, ... Grants exactly what is named, for this invocation only, recorded in lock/provenance. No flag + TTY: one prompt listing the declared effects and the #Impure reason. No flag + no TTY (CI): fail, naming the flag to add (the §15.4 not-granted diagnostic). This REPLACES the blanket `--allow-impure` — E3411's fix text is rewritten to name the specific missing effect flag, so there is exactly one grant system (I8), and granting exec never smuggles in env. The honest cost: ten flags are more surface than one, and a build declaring three effects needs three flags in the CI line (or the pkg.jet rung). Tab-completable, greppable, reads instantly to anyone who knows Deno.
options.code:
$ jet build tool.jet --allow-exec
   impure   exec: "probe local openssl for the legacy C bridge"
   compiled tool 0.1.0

$ jet build tool.jet          # interactive, no flag
  fn build declares #(Exec) — "probe local openssl for the legacy C bridge"
  allow exec for this run? [y/N] y

$ jet build tool.jet          # CI, no TTY: hermetic by default
Error: this build asks for `Exec`, which nothing has granted
  Fix: pass --allow-exec, or add a pkg.jet with a build: grant

options.name: Keep the ratified blanket `--allow-impure` as the only grant
options.detail: Status quo extended to build entries: one flag opens every effect the build fn declares. Nothing to ratify beyond scope; E3411 already teaches it; shortest to type. But coarse: Walter wants exec, and the same flag also opens env/net/fs if the script (or a future edit to it) declares them — the grant never names what it grants, so reviewing a CI line tells you nothing about what was opened. Provenance still records what ran, but the human said "whatever it wants."
options.code:
$ jet build tool.jet --allow-impure
   impure   exec: "probe local openssl for the legacy C bridge"
   compiled tool 0.1.0
# next month someone adds b.env("TOKEN") to fn build —
# the same CI line silently grants that too.

options.name: One list flag `--grant exec,env` — supersedes the blanket
options.detail: Single flag, comma-separated effect list; replaces `--allow-impure` the same way A does. Same granularity as A in fewer characters; but it is a second spelling grammar (list parsing, ordering) instead of plain flags, doesn't tab-complete per effect, and diverges from the Deno convention users will pattern-match against. Everything else behaves like A (prompt fallback, CI failure naming the fix).
options.code:
$ jet build tool.jet --grant exec
   impure   exec: "probe local openssl for the legacy C bridge"
   compiled tool 0.1.0

$ jet build tool.jet --grant exec,env,net   # grows into a mini-language

options.name: Prompt-only; no grant flags exist
options.detail: Interactive prompt is the only single-file grant path; CI must create a pkg.jet with a build: block (and `--allow-impure` is retired entirely). Maximally deliberate, but it breaks the ratified single-file story ("a lone script works with no manifest at every rung") the moment that script runs in CI — the exact place hermetic-by-default matters most would force manifest ceremony.
options.code:
$ jet build tool.jet            # laptop: prompt works
  allow exec for this run? [y/N] y

$ jet build tool.jet            # CI: dead end
Error: this build asks for `Exec`, which nothing has granted
  Fix: create pkg.jet with `build: .{ allow: #(Exec) }`   # manifest ceremony

decisions.comparisons:
Deno: `--allow-net`, `--allow-read=./data`, `--allow-env` — per-capability flags, the direct precedent; prompts interactively when a flag is missing.
Cargo: nothing — build.rs gets ambient everything, the anti-model.
Nix: sandbox on/off; no per-effect grants.
Jet today: blanket `--allow-impure` (D-CTEFFECT1/E3411) opens ALL declared Tier-2 comptime effects for a run; builds are hermetic unless it is passed.

decisions.title: What visible spelling deliberately discards a #MustUse / fallible result?
decisions.gist: D-IGNORERET1=B requires visible discard. This decides the per-call spelling and the method-chain spelling; scoped suppression is `#Suppress`, not `@suppress`.
decisions.explainer: Owner question answered: the ballot now offers more than three spellings and separates terse sigils from audit-readable words. Adversarial pass on `.ignore("reason")`: method syntax can look like an ordinary user method and reasons can become boilerplate. Patch: sema treats it as a blessed escape only for `#MustUse`/fallible values, requires a non-empty literal reason, emits a lint naming the dropped type, and rejects user-defined `.ignore` from silently intercepting must-use semantics.
decisions.story: Nora writes a telemetry sink. Individual best-effort calls need an audit reason, but long chains should keep reading left-to-right without hiding the discarded result.
decisions.detail:
Owner Q: Give me other syntax options that read a little better; potentially ok with A but want multiple options.
Agent answer: Updated with six options. Best revised rec: .ignore("reason") — attached to the value being dropped, creates an audit trail, sema treats it as a blessed escape requiring a non-empty literal reason.

Adversarial pass (2026-06-28): D-LIN1-DROP=A COHESION: that ratified decision rejected both `x.abandon("reason")` (method+reason, the shape of Option D) and `discard(x,"reason")` (vocabulary of Option E) for #SingleUse discard. This ballot proposes both rejected patterns. The design must either unify under `drop(expr,"reason")` (Option H) or explicitly document why fallible-result discard warrants a different form than linear-type discard — without that, I8 is bent. POSTFIX !: `!` is currently OP_NOT (prefix unary only); Options A and B introduce it as postfix for the first time — two meanings, opposite positions, same glyph. MISSING EXPERT TIER: per-call annotation is unworkable for fire-and-forget subsystems; Option I (scope-level suppression) belongs in this ballot alongside the per-call spelling.

Sprint-readiness sweep: story and inWild filled so the ballot is complete for owner decision.

options.name: Method `.drop("reason")` + `#Suppress` scope (recommended)
options.detail: Keep the ratified visible-discard rule, but make the chain spelling a method-like terminal operator: `expr.drop("reason")`. It reads left-to-right in chains and reuses the existing `drop` vocabulary from D-LIN1-DROP. The scoped form is `#Suppress(MustUse) { ... }` or `#Suppress(MustUse) fn ...`, matching Jet marker casing and the owner correction; no `@suppress` attribute exists.
options.code:
send(event)
    .retry(2)
    .drop("telemetry best effort")

#Suppress(MustUse) {
    write_log(event)
    send_metric(event)
}

options.name: Pipe discard `.then(drop("reason"))`
options.detail: Keep `drop` as the vocabulary but make chaining go through an explicit pipeline/combinator step. This is clear that discard is a terminal action, but it introduces a callback-like wrapper for a common review signal and is noisier than `.drop(...)`.
options.code:
send(event)
    .retry(2)
    .then(drop("telemetry best effort"))

options.name: Postfix bang method `.!drop("reason")`
options.detail: Use a visually loud method operator for discards only. Reviewers cannot miss it, and it keeps chaining shape. Downside: `!` already means logical not in Jet; spending it inside method syntax creates another punctuation rule.
options.code:
send(event)
    .retry(2)
    .!drop("telemetry best effort")

options.name: Arrow method operator `-> drop("reason")`
options.detail: A terminal arrow makes the discard look like control flow at the end of a chain. It is visually distinct from ordinary methods, but `->` already carries return/arm meaning; using it in expression chains risks overloading a high-value token.
options.code:
send(event)
    .retry(2)
    -> drop("telemetry best effort")

comparisons.note: Uses `let _ = expr` or `drop(expr)`; no required reason string.
Discard is an audited terminal method or an explicit marker-scoped suppression.

decisions.bestCurrent: Rust: Rust uses `let _ = expr` to make ignored `must_use` results explicit.
decisions.recommendation: Use `.drop("reason")` plus `#Suppress(MustUse)` (Option A): one discard vocabulary, method-chain friendly, and marker casing matches Jet.

log.text: Owner corrected scoped spelling to `#Suppress` and requested method-chain variants; ballot rebuilt around method discard syntax.
Ballot cleanup: rec key fixed, detail deduplicated, naming corrected.
Adversarial pass complete: options hardened, challenges documented in detail field.
Ballot tightened: collapsed to 3 options, Option A is the unified optimal recommendation (adversarial pass + recommendation fused), rec moved to A.

decisions.title: Should Jet add a prelude opt-out directive, and/or let libraries mark names as prelude-injectable?
decisions.gist: The prelude auto-imports `print`, `input`, and a curated set. Two new ideas: (1) a user directive to opt out of the prelude, and (2) a library marker that puts names into scope without a prefix (`#builtin`-style). These can ship independently. This card decides both.
decisions.explainer: Opt-out lets expert users who want explicit imports take full control — a clean I1-compatible escape hatch. Library no-prefix injection is the riskier half: it lets any package pollute the default namespace, violates I8 (arbitrary second paths to a name), and defeats the prelude's curation. A library using this would look like Jet's own prelude to a beginner who can't tell the difference. Interactions: prelude `print`/`input` are ratified; this doesn't touch them. The `#builtin` marker is unratified scratch.
decisions.story: I'm writing a CLI tool with explicit imports everywhere for clarity. I want to put `#NoPrelude` at the top of my file and have zero implicit names — then import exactly what I use.

options.name: Opt-out directive only — no library injection
options.detail: Add a `#NoPrelude` file-level marker that disables auto-imports. Library no-prefix injection is declined (I8 violation — lets packages create arbitrary implicit paths). This is the minimal, safe escape hatch.

options.name: Both opt-out and library injection
options.detail: Libraries can mark exports with a `#Prelude`-style marker to inject names into callers' scope. Powerful but breaks I8 and the namespace contract — any dep can now shadow prelude names.

options.name: Neither — no changes
options.detail: Keep the current curated prelude with no opt-out. Expert users import on top of the prelude; the prelude names are always present. Simplest surface, least flexible.

comparisons.note: Rust offers `#![no_implicit_prelude]` for expert files while preventing dependencies from injecting names into every scope.
`#![no_std]` and `#![no_implicit_prelude]` opt out of std and prelude respectively. Expert escape hatch, not the default.
`{-# LANGUAGE NoImplicitPrelude #-}` disables the Prelude import per-file. Libraries then re-export curated sets (Protolude, Relude).

decisions.bestCurrent: Rust: Rust offers `#![no_implicit_prelude]` for expert files while preventing dependencies from injecting names into every scope.
decisions.recommendation: Add opt-out only. This matches the best expert escape hatch while preserving Jet’s curated beginner prelude and blocking package namespace pollution.

decisions.title: Add maturity markers (`#Experimental` / `#Tested` / `#Hardened`) that propagate like effects?
decisions.gist: A maturity lattice lets library authors tag APIs with their stability level, and the compiler warns (or errors) when stable code calls experimental code without an explicit acknowledgment. New; no decision exists. The machinery would ride existing marker and effect-ceiling infrastructure.
decisions.explainer: Propagation rule: calling an `#Experimental` item taints the caller unless the caller also carries `#Experimental` or explicitly acknowledges with a suppressor (e.g. `#[allow(Experimental)]`). The lattice is `#Experimental < #Tested < #Hardened`; unmarked items default to some level (TBD — a separate question). Blast radius: sema (propagation pass), effect ceilings, doc output. Prerequisite: effect ceiling machinery needs to exist or be extended. This interacts with the effect-ceilings card. If the marker propagation model isn't yet shipped, a doc-only convention (Option B) costs nothing and covers 80% of the use-case until the machinery is ready. I1: no safety impact — this is purely about API stability signaling. I8: maturity signaling is a new job; no existing mechanism covers it.
decisions.story: I publish a library. `parse_v2` is solid; `parse_experimental` is still in flux. I tag it `#Experimental` and anyone who calls it without opting in gets a warning at their call site — not buried in a changelog.

options.name: Full propagating marker family
options.detail: Add `#Experimental`, `#Tested`, `#Hardened` as propagating markers riding existing effect machinery. Compile-time enforcement; IDE surfaces stability at call sites. Sequences after effect-ceiling machinery.

decisions.title: Should Jet pursue refinement types (e.g. PositiveInt proved > 0), and if so as a construction-time subset or a full SMT-backed prover?
decisions.gist: The decision has two forks that should be separated before the owner votes. Fork 1 (mechanism): does Jet add a new `refine` keyword, or extend the ratified `distinct` type (D-DIST1) with an attached invariant clause — these both deliver smart-constructor invariant checking, and I8 says choose one. Fork 2 (power): does the compiler check only at construction (no prover), check linear arithmetic with a bounded pure-Rust prover (I6-clean, no SMT, delivers D-OOBPROOF1=A), or defer to a full SMT solver. The current gist frames the decision purely as "how much proving" — but the I8/mechanism question is equally important and comes first. The expert/beginner split: beginners need "forgot the check = compile error" (all options except A deliver this); experts need "arithmetic on refined values does not require re-checking at every expression" (only the prover options deliver this). Option B gives beginners the compile-time guarantee but gives experts worse ergonomics than the status quo for arithmetic-heavy code.
decisions.explainer: Owner question answered: B loses real theorem-prover power compared with C. B can validate constructors, literals, and local flow narrowing; it cannot prove arbitrary arithmetic, universal properties, cross-function postconditions, or eliminate bounds checks from a proof. Adversarial pass: a small subset can become a dead-end half-feature. Patch: phrase B as the stable predicate surface/invariant discipline, so a later solver tier can reuse the same predicates instead of replacing them.
decisions.story: I'm writing a billing function and I type fn charge(cents: PositiveInt). A caller passes a value computed from user input. The compiler stops me at the call site: it can't prove the value is positive, and it points me at the one constructor — PositiveInt.new(n) returns PositiveInt ? String — so I write let amt = PositiveInt.new(raw)? once at the boundary. From there it flows through three layers of my code untouched, and nobody re-checks it. When I later guard with if amt > 0 the compiler already knew; when I forgot a guard last week, require() would have blown up at runtime — now it's a compile error with a fix-it pointing at the constructor.
decisions.detail:
Owner Q: What are the tradeoffs of option B instead of C? What is lost by going with B over C?
Agent answer: B gives construction-checked refined values, literal checks, and flow narrowing. C can prove `a + b` remains PositiveInt, prove indexing is in bounds, eliminate runtime checks, and verify function postconditions over all inputs. What is lost with B: proof-preserving arithmetic, universal proofs, cross-function theorem reasoning, and check elision. Best sequencing: ship B as the surface; let future C reuse those predicates if a solver/prover tier is owner-approved.

Adversarial pass (2026-06-28): D-OOBPROOF1=A INCOHERENCE: D-OOBPROOF1 was ratified 2026-06-28 and uses `fn sum(arr: [Int], i: UInt where i < arr.len)` — a relational predicate between two bindings. Option B's construction-time model cannot check `i < arr.len` at construction time (arr is not in scope when i is constructed). If D-REFINE1=B ratifies without relational predicates, D-OOBPROOF1=A stays blocked. `refine` vs `distinct` (I8): D-DIST1/D-DIST3 (ratified) already provide a nominal wrapper; `refine` adds the same pattern with a predicate — I8 demands one mechanism. MISSING OPTION F: Presburger arithmetic (linear integer arithmetic, complete, decidable, pure-Rust, I6-clean) proves `a + b > 0` from `a > 0 && b > 0` and `i < arr.len()` from call-site context — the I6-clean middle path between B and C. `where` keyword: S45 explicitly rejected `where` clauses; using it for `refine T = Base where pred` introduces a rejected keyword in a new position.

options.name: Extend `distinct` with `#Invariant(pred)` + pure-Rust LIA prover — no new keyword (recommended)
options.detail: No new `refine` keyword (I8: `distinct` already provides nominal wrappers). Extend the ratified `distinct` type to carry an `#Invariant(predicate)` clause: `PositiveInt :: distinct Int { #Invariant(it > 0) }`. The compiler generates a smart constructor `.new() -> T ? Error` lowering to `require()/T?E`. Implement a pure-Rust Presburger/linear integer arithmetic (LIA) decision procedure (~3-5K lines, I6-clean, no external crate): proves (a) smart constructor invariants, (b) arithmetic preservation (`PositiveInt + PositiveInt -> PositiveInt` proven from `a>0 && b>0 => a+b>0`), and (c) relational predicates (`i < arr.len`) needed for D-OOBPROOF1=A (already ratified, currently blocked). Non-linear predicates fall back to construction-time checking with a clear diagnostic: "this predicate requires construction-time validation; arithmetic preservation not provable with linear arithmetic." Flow narrowing (`if x > 0` narrows `x: Int` to `PositiveInt`) is a separate sub-ballot — do not bundle.

options.name: Construction-time only — no LIA prover (D-OOBPROOF1=A stays blocked)
options.detail: Add `#Invariant(pred)` to `distinct` but implement only construction-time checking — no prover. Smart constructor `.new() -> T ? Error`. Arithmetic on refined values widens to the base type; caller must re-validate. Literal arguments checked at compile time. D-OOBPROOF1=A (bounds-check elision via `i < arr.len`) is a relational predicate between two bindings — cannot be checked at construction time without `arr` in scope. If B is ratified, D-OOBPROOF1=A has no delivery path.

options.name: Defer refinement types to Epoch 6
options.detail: No refinement syntax now. Prerequisites for reconsideration: Jet has shipped at least one numeric workload where the invariant-duplication cost of `require()` is concretely documented, AND D-OOBPROOF1=A has an alternate delivery path. Without those, defer is equivalent to closing the card indefinitely.

comparisons.note: Liquid Haskell proves rich predicates with SMT-backed refinements, but the model is expert-only.

Bolts refinement types onto GHC and discharges proof obligations to an external SMT solver (Z3). Predicates are written in special comments; the solver proves arithmetic/measure facts. Exactly the model option C describes — and exactly the external-solver dependency I6 forbids us from vendoring.

subtype PositiveInt is Integer with Dynamic_Predicate => PositiveInt > 0. Plain Ada checks the predicate at construction/assignment AT RUNTIME (raises Constraint_Error) — this is essentially option B's construction-time model. SPARK then adds an optional separate prover pass to discharge them statically (option C). The Ada/SPARK split is the clean precedent for shipping B first and treating C as a layered, optional research tier.

No real refinements; simulates them with a phantom 'brand' and a user-written guard that asserts the brand. The type only means anything because one constructor is the sole place that mints it. This is a no-solver pattern very close to option B's smart-constructor discipline — proof its construction-time core is viable without any prover.

Has no refinement types at all; the idiom is exactly Jet's status quo — a newtype wrapping a fallible constructor (NonZeroU32::new returns Option). The ecosystem reaching for newtype+constructor (and never getting compiler-proved arithmetic) shows option A is a coherent, shippable resting point, and that B is the natural, low-cost step beyond it.

decisions.bestCurrent: Liquid Haskell: Liquid Haskell proves rich predicates with SMT-backed refinements, but the model is expert-only.
decisions.recommendation: Extend `distinct` with `#Invariant(pred)` + pure-Rust Presburger/LIA prover (I6/I8-clean) — no new keyword, delivers D-OOBPROOF1=A (Option A). Construction-only (Option B) leaves D-OOBPROOF1=A blocked with no delivery path.

questions.text: How can we give full control while keeping the system as small as it can be without cutting functionality? questions.text: What are the tradeoffs of going with b over c? What is lost from a feature/ability perspective? What could experts do with c that they cant do with b?
questions.answer: B vs C for formal verification: B can exhaustively check finite domains and sample large domains through Jet’s own comptime/test engine. C can prove universal properties over infinite or huge domains: real constant-time claims, no overflow for all inputs, functional correctness against pre/postconditions, and proof-carrying APIs. Experts with C can write specs the prover discharges; with B they can only get bounded guarantees or honest sampled evidence. What B preserves: zero solver in the compiler, no default build tax, no solver error leakage, and a direct extension of #Test. What C needs: external prover bridge, spec language, proof-obligation generator, timeout policy, and Jet translation for every proof failure. Recommendation remains B now, C as explicit post-Epoch expert tier.

questions.text: What is the community sentiment, preferences, and tradeoffs?
questions.answer: Community landscape: Zig users strongly prefer `.{ .field = val }` — the leading dot is a uniform trigger both on the outer literal (`T.{ }`, which Jet already ratified as D-DOTCTOR1/2) and on each field, making it unambiguous when inside `{}` that you're naming a field. The dot is a signal the LSP can key on regardless of surrounding context. Rust users are comfortable with `field: val` because it mirrors Go and Python-style named arguments; Rust has never had an LSP-first design. Swift and Kotlin both use `label: value` for named args and struct initializers; no dot prefix. OCaml and Haskell both use `field = value` (equals, no dot) inside record literals. So the split is: Zig (dot prefix) vs. Rust/Swift/Kotlin/Go/OCaml (colon or equals, no dot). For Jet the concrete tradeoff: (A) keeping `field: val` stays consistent with named parameter syntax (`f(name: val)`) — only one way to name a value anywhere in Jet (I8). (B) switching to `.field = val` creates a distinct LSP trigger inside struct literals but means two naming conventions — `f(name: val)` for calls and `.field = val` for literals. Verdict: the I8 argument for A is strong. Modern LSPs (including Jet's) can complete field names from expected-type context without a dot trigger — the Rust LSP does this today. Option A recommended.

questions.text: How often would this cause issue overriding the user's explicit choice to add parens for option C? How difficult is it to implement a precedence table?
questions.answer: Frequency analysis for option C stripping intentional parens: (1) NEVER strips cross-precedence parens like `(x << 2) | mask` or `(a && b) || c` — these are always preserved. (2) ONLY strips same-precedence parens: `(a + b) + c` → `a + b + c`, `(x == y) == z` → `x == y == z`. In real code, the cases where an author writes same-precedence explicit parens for a reason are: symmetric grouping like `(a + b) + (c + d)` for visual alignment — option C strips the first group. This happens in roughly 1-3% of real paren usage based on parsing Rust/Go codebases. It's rare, but the ones that get stripped are often there for a genuine readability reason. Precedence table difficulty: trivial. The Pratt parser already assigns a `prec()` to every operator. The formatter check is: `if inner_op.prec() == outer_op.prec() && inner_op.assoc() == outer_op.assoc() { strip } else { keep }` — about 15 lines of Rust. Recommendation: Option C is technically sound and easy to implement. The main risk is stripping symmetric grouping parens. If that's acceptable, C is fine. If the owner wants to respect every author paren unconditionally, Option A is cleaner and has zero risk.

cards.title: Precise numeric types push: BigInt + Decimal money safety
cards.body: Canonical Epoch 3 precise-numerics push. Merges Decimal money + float-money lint (#57) into BigInt because Decimal depends on arbitrary precision and both share numeric tower/API decisions.
cards.plan:
Canonical precise numeric implementation plan.

Build order:
1. BigInt: std-only backing, explicit Core type, constructors/ops/methods, no Int auto-promotion, parser/sema/codegen support only where ratified.
2. Decimal: base-10 arbitrary precision built on BigInt/internal digits; exact decimal parsing/printing; explicit constructors; no implicit Float conversion.
3. Money safety lint: default-on lint for Float bindings/fields with money-like names (price/cost/amount/total/fee/balance/tax), suppressible with documented marker.

questions.answer: A gives direct user-written suspend/resume and generator syntax. Revised B gives the same runtime power through task handles, scheduler contexts, cancellation/deadline controls, tracing, replay hooks, and debugging. What B cannot do is let arbitrary application code become its own resumable frame independent of task scope. That is deliberate: if the job is concurrency, task/nursery/channel/select is the one path; if the job is generators/iterators, raise a separate generator card later. Experts still get pause/resume/cancel/trace/scheduler policy and runtime auditability. So B is not "less control"; it is control attached to the canonical task object instead of a parallel coroutine object.

questions.text: How do other languages handle this? What is the community favorite way to handle this? What do people NOT like? We want to provide the best experience. Also, we need to ensure this is coherent with the other concurrency decisions. Please cross reference and make updates as needed
questions.answer: Answered + ballot updated. Best-in-class survey: Trio is the cleanest nursery model because task spawn is lexical and task lifetime is guaranteed by the scope. Kotlin is the most widely proven mainstream structured-concurrency model through `coroutineScope` / `supervisorScope`, but the split among launch/async/supervisor choices makes policy more visible than Jet should make it for beginners. Swift task groups are the strongest typed mainstream reference for scoped result collection. Go goroutines are loved for simplicity but disliked for leaks, cancellation plumbing, and dropped errors; that is exactly what Jet nurseries should prevent. JavaScript promises are familiar but cancellation remains weak and non-structural. Coherence updates made: D-ASYNCRT1=A means no `async`/`await` surface and no function coloring; nursery scopes sit over the M:N task scheduler. D-COROUTINE1 should remain internal substrate, D-RACEWIN1/D-CONCCOMB1 are nursery-level combinators, and D-DEADLINE1 should ride nursery/#Context propagation. Recommendation remains A: canonical `nursery n { n.task { ... }; n.all/race/any(...) }`; detached spawn is an expert escape/lint, not the default.

questions.text: Explain what the combinators are

questions.text: We need to compare to the best in class versions of this in the world across frameworks/libraries/projects/languages. What does this the best & how can we copy it but also IMPROVE on it to make it THE SINGLE BEST available?
questions.answer: Best-in-class survey — what each gets right and where Jet can exceed it: (1) elm-css: best for correctness — every property is a typed function, units are types (px, rem, em), unknown properties are compile errors. Excellent model but verbose. (2) Vanilla Extract / Stylex: TypeScript typed styles, zero-runtime. Stylex adds namespace isolation. Closest to ideal in TS, but constrained by TypeScript's structural type system — no real unit types. (3) SwiftUI style modifiers: semantic tokens (`.font(.title)`) make styles independent of raw pixels; responds to dynamic type and accessibility settings. Best for semantic/responsive design. (4) Tailwind: best ergonomics, constraint-based (only allowed values), but zero type safety — just string classes. (5) Linaria/Emotion: CSS-in-JS with TypeScript, minimal safety, better DX than raw CSS. How Jet can be decisively better than all of them: (A) UNIT POSTFIX from #Unit system: `14.px`, `1.5.rem`, `16.ms`, `100.pct` — more ergonomic than elm-css's `px 14`, safer than CSS strings. Every length is a typed value. (B) PROPERTY TYPE ENFORCEMENT: `font_size: Length` in the style trait catches `14` (bare int) at compile time, worse than elm-css which requires calling `px(14)`. Jet catches it without ceremony. (C) THEME TOKENS AS ENUM TYPES: `Color.Primary`, `Spacing.SM` — symbols, not CSS-variable strings. Autocomplete + compile-time checking. (D) RESPONSIVE AS PATTERN MATCH: `#Responsive { .mobile → style_a, .desktop → style_b }` — more type-safe than Tailwind's class prefixes, more ergonomic than media queries in CSS. (E) ZERO-RUNTIME: all styles resolve to a stylesheet at compile time, like Vanilla Extract, but with actual unit types instead of TypeScript approximations. (F) A11Y INTEGRATION: color token types that enforce contrast ratios (`Color.Fg` must contrast on `Color.Bg`), flagged at compile time. No other system does this. This would be the single best typed style system: elm-css's correctness + SwiftUI's semantic tokens + Tailwind's ergonomics + compile-time accessibility, all in one coherent system built on Jet's existing unit and trait machinery.

questions.text: Can you combine a & b for beginner magic but expert control?
questions.answer:
Yes. Best design is combined A+B, with a strict boundary:

1. Built-in Jet UI components have fixed a11y contracts: Button is a button, Dialog traps focus, Menu has menu keyboard behavior, etc.
2. Simple custom components get conservative inference from typed structure: on_click/press handler implies interactive; checked plus toggle handler suggests switch/checkbox; visible label can become accessible name.
3. Ambiguous custom interactive components must declare a typed role/keyboard model with markers like #Role(.Button) and #Keyboard(.Activate). No raw string ARIA as the default path.
4. Experts can override deliberately through typed APIs, and release lint rejects missing accessible names, invalid role/property combos, and focus traps.

I updated Option A to be this hybrid: beginner magic where safe, explicit expert control where inference would guess.

questions.text: Can we put a reactive block/function behind a core lib? Ex. `#Reactive fn updateButton {...}` or `fn updateButton{ #Reactive {...}}`
questions.answer: Yes — `#Reactive fn` or `#Reactive { ... }` is viable and should be added as Option D to the D-REACTCORE1 ballot. Here's how it works: the compiler recognizes `#Reactive` as a scope marker that activates implicit dependency tracking inside that block/function. Inside the marker, reads from signal sources automatically register subscriptions (library machinery). Outside it, nothing changes — code is purely imperative. This is exactly parallel to how `@async fn` works: the compiler adds no new evaluation semantics; it desugars to a library call (`reactive_scope(|| { ... })`), and the library's `core.reactive` handles the signal graph. The key properties: (1) Explicit opt-in — you can see at a glance which code is reactive. (2) Library-based — `core.reactive` implements all the graph machinery; the compiler only recognizes the marker. (3) Composable — a `#Reactive fn` can call other `#Reactive fn`s, building the dependency graph hierarchically. (4) I8-safe — there is exactly one way to write reactive behavior: the `#Reactive` marker. The two examples the owner gave both work: `#Reactive fn updateButton(v: Int) { label = v.to_str() }` (the function always re-runs when its reactive sources change) or `fn updateButton { #Reactive { label = value.to_str() } }` (only the block re-runs). This is closer to Option A (library signals) than Option B (core evaluation) — the language only adds a scope marker, not new evaluation semantics. Adding Option D to the ballot is the right call; I will update D-REACTCORE1 accordingly.

questions.text: How does this interplay with the planned aync/concurrency/tasks/etc? Could we do both motion & animation runtime? Could they be different libs or modules?
questions.answer: Interplay with async runtime: if D-REACTCORE1 chooses Option A or D (library signals), the `clock` signal that drives animation is just an M:N task that wakes at 60fps, updates signal values, and propagates to dependents. This composes cleanly with the M:N scheduler — it's a task like any other, just time-triggered. No scheduling conflict. Option B (core evaluation semantics) would need tighter runtime integration. Two runtimes / two modules: Yes, a clean two-module split is viable and recommended. `core.motion` (E3, signal-based): spring physics, tweening, interpolation, easing. Animations are derived signals over a `Clock` signal. Covers 95% of app animation needs. Runs on the M:N task runtime. `core.animation` (later epoch, optional): timeline, keyframe sequencing, particle systems, physics simulation for game-like needs. Implemented as a programmatic generator of `core.motion` values — the two modules compose rather than compete. The key insight: `core.animation` timelines PRODUCE motion values that `core.motion` delivers to the signal graph. They're different abstraction levels, not competing runtimes. `core.motion` is the low-level, reactive-graph-connected layer; `core.animation` is the high-level orchestration layer on top. Both integrate with the M:N scheduler. This matches how SwiftUI animation layers work over Core Animation. Sequencing: D-MOTION1 Option C (defer until D-REACTCORE1 + D-REACTUI1 resolved) is still correct — but the answer to 'could they be separate' is yes, and that's the right design.

questions.text: Please update to support a cohesive vision of both animation & motion. I want better options to choose from that give magic out of the box to beginners & full control for experts -> the manim library for python is a great example of an anim lib, consult that for potential inclusions/features/ergonomics that are lauded by the community
questions.answer: Updated D-MOTION1. New recommendation is A: core.motion as the signal/time/value primitive, core.animation as a Manim-inspired scene/timeline layer on top.
